title: Chapter 5: Medical and Health Insurance/Takaful (MHIT)
text:
This chapter covers the critical area of medical and health insurance in Malaysia. With rising healthcare costs and regulatory changes, understanding MHIT products is ESSENTIAL for exam success and client advisory.
Exam Weight: 15-18% of total exam
Study Time Recommendation: 10-12 hours




By the end of this chapter, you must be able to:

Define medical and health insurance scope and importance
Describe all types of MHIT products (Medical Reimbursement, Critical Illness, Long-term Care, Hospital Income, Dental, Disability Income)
Understand healthcare issues in Malaysia
Compute disability income needs
Compare different health plans and select appropriate policies
Analyze policy features, exclusions, and disclosure requirements







Definition: Medical and Health Insurance (MHIT) = umbrella term for insurance contracts mitigating health-related risks.
Historical Terminology Evolution: - Accident insurance - Health insurance
- Accident and health insurance - Accident and sickness insurance - Disability insurance → Now unified as: Medical and Health Insurance (MHIT)
Why MHIT is Essential:








Factor
Impact
Malaysian Context




Spiraling Medical Costs
Substantial financial burden
Private hospital costs escalating 10-15% annually


Unpredictable Health
Anyone can fall ill anytime
Thousands hospitalized annually


Financial Strain
Medical bills can devastate finances
Single major surgery: RM50,000-300,000+


Growing Awareness
More people recognize need
Market expansion in Malaysia



⚠️ EXAM ALERT: MHIT is not just “nice to have” - it’s a NECESSITY in modern risk management.
📌 EXAM QUESTION LINK: Q3, Q4 test understanding of health concerns and definition of health insurance.

Problem

Growing Demand

Factors Affecting Quality: - Funding availability - Resource allocation - Access to technology - Medical expertise availability - Governance and oversight
Private vs Public: - Private (urban): Advanced tech, high expertise, high cost - Public (subsidized): Variable quality, longer wait, affordable

📝 EXAM QUESTION 5 (Links to Section 5.1)
Question: “Several issues associated with healthcare in Malaysia. Main concerns from list below: i. Lack of qualified medical personnel ii. Increasing healthcare costs iii. Inadequate access and uneven distribution iv. Consistent high quality throughout country”
Answer: C (i, ii & iii only)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Option (iv) is a TRAP! It says “consistent HIGH quality” - but quality is NOT consistent; it VARIES significantly between urban and rural. This is actually an ISSUE (variation), not a positive achievement.
KEYWORDS TO REMEMBER: - ✅ “Lack/Shortage” of personnel - ✅ “Increasing/Rising” costs - ✅ “Inadequate access” and “uneven distribution” - ❌ NOT “consistent quality” (quality actually VARIES)





SIX Main Categories (MUST MEMORIZE):
MHIT PRODUCTS
├── 1. Medical Reimbursement Insurance
├── 2. Critical Illness (Dread Disease) Insurance
├── 3. Long-term Care Insurance
├── 4. Hospital Income Insurance
├── 5. Dental Insurance
└── (Related: Disability Income Insurance)




Definition: Reimburses actual medical expenses incurred for treatment.
Also Known As: - Hospital and Surgical Insurance - Hospitalization Insurance - Major Medical Insurance



What’s Covered (Typical):








Category
Examples
Malaysian Context




Hospitalization
Room & board, ICU
Private hospital: RM200-1,000+/day


Surgery
Surgical fees, operating room
Major surgery: RM10,000-100,000+


Specialist Fees
Consultation, treatment
RM200-500+ per visit


Diagnostic Tests
X-ray, MRI, CT scan, blood tests
MRI: RM1,000-3,000


Medication
Prescribed drugs during hospitalization
Variable


Emergency Treatment
A&E services
Critical in accidents


Pre/Post Hospitalization
Before/after hospital visits
Usually 60/90 days coverage







Definition: Maximum amount insurer pays per policy year.
Common Annual Limits in Malaysia:









Plan Type
Annual Limit
Typical Premium (Monthly)
Suitability




Basic
RM50,000 - RM100,000
RM100 - RM200
Budget-conscious, young, healthy


Standard
RM150,000 - RM300,000
RM250 - RM400
Average needs, families


Comprehensive
RM500,000 - RM1,000,000
RM500 - RM800
High coverage needs, chronic conditions risk


Premium
RM1,000,000+
RM800+
Maximum protection, serious illness risk



⚠️ EXAM TIP: Higher annual limit = Higher premium, but better protection against catastrophic medical costs.




Definition: Maximum total amount insurer pays over entire policy lifetime.
Modern Trend: Many insurers now offer NO LIFETIME LIMIT or very high limits (RM5-10 million).
Why Important: - Chronic diseases require ongoing treatment - Multiple hospitalizations over lifetime - Major illnesses (cancer) can exceed annual limits multiple times




Common Exclusions (MUST MEMORIZE):








Exclusion Type
Examples
Rationale




Pre-existing Conditions
Illnesses diagnosed before policy
Adverse selection prevention


Cosmetic Surgery
Elective procedures for appearance
Not medically necessary


Normal Pregnancy
Standard childbirth
Not illness/injury


Dental Treatment
Unless accident-related
Separate dental coverage


War/Riot Injuries
Conflict-related injuries
Uninsurable/unpredictable


Self-inflicted Injuries
Suicide attempts, self-harm
Moral hazard


HIV/AIDS
Some policies exclude
Risk management


Alternative Medicine
Traditional/complementary therapies
Unless specified


Experimental Treatments
Unproven procedures
Medical necessity


Routine Checkups
Preventive health screenings
Not treatment for illness



⚠️ EXAM ALERT: “Normal pregnancy” is excluded, but complications of pregnancy may be covered.




Definition: Time period after policy inception before certain benefits payable.
Types of Waiting Periods:









Type
Duration
Purpose
Applies To




Initial Waiting Period
30 days
Prevent immediate claims after purchase
All illnesses (except accidents)


Specific Illness Waiting Period
120 days
High-cost conditions
Specified illnesses only


Pre-existing Condition
12-36 months OR permanent exclusion
Prevent adverse selection
Known conditions



Example:
Policy Start Date: January 1, 2025

Accident (Feb 1): ✅ COVERED (no waiting for accidents)
Flu (Feb 15): ❌ NOT COVERED (within 30-day initial waiting)
Surgery for hernia (March 1): ✅ COVERED (after 30 days, not specified illness)
Cancer treatment (April 1): ❌ NOT COVERED (within 120-day specific illness waiting)
Cancer treatment (June 1): ✅ COVERED (after 120 days for specified illness)
⚠️ EXAM ALERT: Accidents have NO waiting period; coverage is immediate.




Definition: Medical condition that existed BEFORE policy purchase, whether diagnosed or not.
Three Approaches:
Approach 1: Permanent Exclusion
Pre-existing: Diabetes diagnosed before policy
Coverage: Never covered throughout policy life
Approach 2: Waiting Period (12-36 months)
Pre-existing: Hypertension known before policy
Waiting: Not covered for 24 months
After 24 months: ✅ Covered for hypertension
Approach 3: Loaded Premium
Pre-existing: Heart condition
Coverage: Covered from start
Premium: Higher premium charged
📌 EXAM TIP: Most policies EXCLUDE pre-existing conditions permanently or impose long waiting periods.




Definition: Amount insurer deems reasonable for specific treatment in specific geographic area.
How R&C is Determined: 1. Survey of charges in the area 2. Medical necessity of treatment 3. Complexity of procedure 4. Doctor’s qualifications/experience 5. Hospital classification
Example Scenario:
Treatment: Appendectomy in Kuala Lumpur
Hospital A Bill: RM15,000
Hospital B Bill: RM12,000  
Hospital C Bill: RM10,000
Insurer's R&C Assessment: RM12,000 (median/average)

If you go to Hospital A:
Your Bill: RM15,000
Insurer Pays (R&C): RM12,000
You Pay: RM3,000 (excess over R&C)




Definition: Direct billing between hospital and insurer; policyholder doesn’t pay upfront.
How It Works:
Traditional Method (Reimbursement):
Step 1: Hospital bills patient → Patient pays RM50,000
Step 2: Patient submits claim to insurer
Step 3: Insurer reimburses patient RM50,000
Issue: Need upfront cash
Cashless Method:
Step 1: Hospital bills insurer directly → Patient pays RM0 upfront
Step 2: Insurer pays hospital RM50,000
Step 3: Patient only pays excess (if any)
Benefit: No upfront payment needed




Definition: Rate at which medical costs increase annually.
Malaysian Context:








Type
Rate
Impact




General Inflation
3-5% annually
Overall price increases


Medical Inflation
10-15% annually
Healthcare costs rise faster



Why Medical Inflation Higher: - Advanced technology costs - New expensive treatments - Specialized care demand - Pharmaceutical costs - Aging population
📌 EXAM TIP: Choose policies with inflation-adjusted annual limits to maintain coverage value.




Definition: High-limit insurance for catastrophic health events; bridges gap that basic plans don’t cover.
Key Features:








Feature
Description
Modern Trend




Extensive Coverage
Broad range of medical expenses
Comprehensive


High Maximum Limits
RM1 million+
Now RM1-2 million common


Top-Up Options
Secondary riders to increase limit
Add RM500,000-1 million more


Flexibility
Often paired with hospitalization plans
Customizable


Deductibles
Predetermined amount before insurer pays
Various options


Co-insurance
Cost-sharing mechanism
Percentage split



⚠️ EXAM ALERT: Major Medical Insurance is classified under Medical Reimbursement category.

📝 EXAM QUESTION 6 (Links to Section 5.2.a)
Question: “All of following are health insurance schemes in Malaysia, EXCEPT: A. Critical illnesses insurance B. Funeral insurance C. Major medical insurance D. Hospital and surgical insurance”
Answer: B (Funeral insurance)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Funeral insurance pays a benefit when someone DIES - that’s LIFE INSURANCE, not health insurance.
DISTINCTION TO REMEMBER: - Health Insurance = Covers TREATMENT while ALIVE (illness, injury, hospitalization) - Life Insurance = Pays on DEATH (funeral, estate, beneficiaries)
KEYWORDS: - ✅ Critical illness = Health (pays on diagnosis during life) - ✅ Major medical = Health (pays for treatment) - ✅ Hospital & surgical = Health (pays for hospitalization) - ❌ Funeral = Life (pays on death)





Origin: 1980s in South Africa; expanded globally including Malaysia.
Definition: Lump sum payment upon diagnosis of specified critical illnesses.



Common Covered Illnesses (Malaysian Context):








Category
Illnesses Typically Covered
LIAM Guidelines




Cancer
Major cancers (all stages)
✅ Standard


Heart Conditions
Heart attack, coronary artery bypass surgery
✅ Standard


Stroke
Cerebrovascular accident with permanent symptoms
✅ Standard


Kidney Failure
End-stage renal failure requiring dialysis
✅ Standard


Major Organ Transplant
Heart, lung, liver, kidney, pancreas, bone marrow
✅ Standard


Neurodegenerative
Parkinson’s, Alzheimer’s, multiple sclerosis
Extended coverage


Others
Paralysis, blindness, deafness, coma
Extended coverage



⚠️ EXAM ALERT: Life Insurance Association of Malaysia (LIAM) provides guideline list, but coverage VARIES between insurers.

Policy Structure Options:
1. Standalone Critical Illness Policy
Function: Independent policy, not attached to life insurance
Premium: Separate premium payment
Payout: Lump sum on diagnosis
Death Benefit: Only if death from covered illness within survival period
2. Critical Illness Rider (Attached to Life Policy)
Function: Attached to life insurance policy
Premium: Lower than standalone (shared with life policy)
Payout: Two sub-types:
  a) Accelerated Benefit: Reduces life insurance death benefit
  b) Non-Accelerated (Additional): Separate payout, doesn't affect death benefit




Feature 1: Single vs. Multiple Claim Policies









Type
Description
Example
Suitability




Single Claim
Pays once then terminates
Cancer diagnosed → RM200,000 paid → Policy ends
Lower cost, basic protection


Multiple Claim
Allows additional claims for different illnesses
Heart attack → RM200,000 → Policy continues → Later: Stroke → Another RM200,000
Higher cost, comprehensive protection



Multiple Claim Conditions: - Different illness category - Waiting period between claims (e.g., 1-3 years) - May have limit on total claims (e.g., 3 claims maximum)

Feature 2: Coverage for Early to Advanced Stages
Traditional: Only pays for advanced/late-stage illness Modern: Staged benefits
Example:
Total Sum Assured: RM200,000

Early Stage Cancer (Stage 1):
Payout: 25% = RM50,000
Remaining Coverage: RM150,000

Intermediate Stage Cancer (Stage 2-3):
Payout: 50% = RM100,000
Remaining Coverage: RM50,000

Advanced Stage Cancer (Stage 4):
Payout: 100% = RM200,000 (full remaining amount)
📌 EXAM TIP: Early/intermediate stage benefits provide financial support for treatment sooner.

Feature 3: Waiting and Survival Periods
Waiting Period:
Definition: Time after policy inception before claims can be made
Typical: 90-120 days
Exception: Accidents have NO waiting period

Example:
Policy Date: Jan 1, 2025
Cancer diagnosed: March 1, 2025 (Within 90 days)
Result: NOT COVERED (within waiting period)

Cancer diagnosed: May 1, 2025 (After 90 days)
Result: ✅ COVERED
Survival Period:
Definition: Time insured must survive after diagnosis to qualify for payout
Typical: 14-30 days
Purpose: Confirm illness severity

Example:
Diagnosis: Heart attack on June 1
Survival Period: 14 days
Must survive until: June 15
Payout: If alive on June 15 ✅
If dies June 10: Survival period not met ❌ (but life insurance pays instead if rider)
⚠️ EXAM ALERT: Both waiting period (before diagnosis) and survival period (after diagnosis) must be met.

Feature 4: Accelerated vs. Non-Accelerated Benefits
Accelerated Benefit (More Common):
Setup:
Life Insurance Sum Assured: RM500,000
CI Rider Sum Assured: RM200,000

Scenario: Cancer diagnosed
CI Payout: RM200,000 ✅
Remaining Life Insurance: RM500,000 - RM200,000 = RM300,000

If later dies:
Death Benefit: RM300,000 only
Non-Accelerated Benefit (Additional Benefit):
Setup:
Life Insurance Sum Assured: RM500,000
CI Rider Sum Assured: RM200,000 (Additional)

Scenario: Cancer diagnosed
CI Payout: RM200,000 ✅
Life Insurance: RM500,000 (UNCHANGED)

If later dies:
Death Benefit: RM500,000 (full amount)
Total Received: RM200,000 (CI) + RM500,000 (Death) = RM700,000
📌 EXAM TIP: - Accelerated = CI reduces death benefit (more common, lower premium) - Non-Accelerated = CI additional to death benefit (less common, higher premium)

📝 EXAM QUESTION 7 (Links to Section 5.2.b)
Question: “Which health insurance often issued with life policy, covers list of dread diseases only? A. Critical illnesses insurance B. Healthcare rider insurance C. Major medical insurance D. Hospital and surgical insurance”
Answer: A (Critical Illnesses Insurance)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Three phrases in question point to Critical Illness:

“issued with life policy” = Can be attached as rider to life insurance ✅
“dread diseases” = Another name for critical illnesses ✅
“list” = Specified illnesses covered (not all conditions) ✅

KEYWORDS TO MATCH: - “Dread disease” = Critical illness terminology - “List” = Specified conditions (cancer, heart attack, stroke, etc.) - “With life policy” = Rider capability





Global Context: - USA: 40% of elderly need nursing home care; 60% by age 75 - Malaysia: Underdeveloped market, growing need due to aging population
Definition: Covers costs when individuals cannot perform daily activities independently due to illness, disability, or cognitive impairment.



Activities of Daily Living (ADLs) - CRITICAL CONCEPT:








ADL
Description
Example




Bathing
Ability to wash oneself
Can shower independently


Dressing
Ability to put on clothes
Can dress without help


Toileting
Ability to use bathroom
Can use toilet independently


Transferring
Ability to move from bed to chair
Can walk/move without assistance


Continence
Bladder and bowel control
Can control bodily functions


Feeding
Ability to eat independently
Can feed self



LTC Trigger: Typically inability to perform 2-3 ADLs independently.













Care Type
Setting
Services
Malaysian Context




Nursing Home Care
Nursing facility
24-hour skilled nursing
Limited facilities in Malaysia


Assisted Living
Assisted living facility
Help with ADLs, medication management
Growing in urban areas


Home Care Services
Patient’s home
Skilled nursing, PT, OT at home
Preferred in Malaysian culture


Adult Day-care
Day-care center
Supervision, social activities, ADL assistance
Limited availability


Respite Care
Various
Temporary relief for family caregivers
Important for family support




📝 EXAM QUESTION 10 (Links to Section 5.2.c)
Question: “Coverage of long-term care insurance includes: i. Nursing home care ii. Home care services iii. Social services iv. Assisted living facilities
A. i & ii only B. i, ii & iii only C. i, ii & iv only D. All the above”
Answer: C (i, ii & iv only)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Option (iii) “Social services” is the TRAP!
Why “Social services” NOT covered: - Too BROAD and general - LTC covers SPECIFIC HEALTHCARE settings/services - Social services include non-medical support (welfare, community programs, social work) - LTC focuses on MEDICAL/HEALTHCARE support for ADLs
WHAT IS COVERED: - ✅ Nursing home = Medical care facility (24-hour skilled nursing) - ✅ Home care = Healthcare services at home (nursing, PT, OT) - ✅ Assisted living = Residential facility with ADL support & medication management - ❌ Social services = Too general, not healthcare-specific
MEMORY TIP: LTC covers MEDICAL/HEALTHCARE care settings, not general social welfare programs.





Definition: Daily cash benefit for each day hospitalized; NOT reimbursement of actual costs.
Key Distinction: - Medical Reimbursement: Pays actual bills - Hospital Income: Pays fixed daily amount regardless of actual costs



Daily Cash Benefit Structure:
Example:
Policy: RM200/day hospital income
Hospitalization: 5 days for illness
Actual Hospital Bill: RM30,000 (paid by medical insurance or self)
Hospital Income Payout: RM200 × 5 = RM1,000 (regardless of actual bill)
Use: Can use RM1,000 for any purpose (loss of income, transport, childcare, etc.)
Flexibility of Use: - Cover household expenses - Compensate for lost income - Transportation costs - Childcare during hospitalization - Meals for family members - Any other needs
📌 EXAM TIP: Hospital Income provides cash flow during hospitalization, complementing medical reimbursement insurance.





Also Called: Permanent Health Insurance ✅ (This is the exam term!)
Definition: Replaces portion of income lost due to disability from illness or injury.



Purpose: Provide monthly benefits to replace lost income when unable to work due to disability.
Key Points: - Does NOT cover medical expenses (that’s medical insurance) - Covers INCOME LOSS only - Typically replaces 50-70% of income (not 100%) - Prevents over-insurance and malingering

📝 EXAM QUESTION 1 (Links to Section 5.3)
Question: “Disability Income Insurance is also called ___. A. Disability care insurance B. Total disability insurance C. Permanent health insurance D. Income loss insurance”
Answer: C (Permanent Health Insurance)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: “Permanent Health Insurance” is British/traditional terminology for disability income insurance.
WHY “Permanent Health”? - “Permanent” = Long-term income protection (not temporary) - “Health” = Health-related inability to work - Used in UK, Malaysia, and former British colonies
TERMINOLOGY VARIATIONS: - UK/Malaysia: Permanent Health Insurance ✅ - USA: Disability Income Insurance - Modern: Both terms used interchangeably
EXAM TIP: When you see “Permanent Health Insurance” in exam, immediately think DISABILITY INCOME replacement.




TWO Main Approaches:
1. Own Occupation (More Liberal):
Definition: Unable to perform duties of YOUR SPECIFIC occupation
Example: Surgeon who loses hand dexterity
Result: Considered totally disabled (can't do surgery)
Even if: Could work in another field
2. Any Occupation (More Restrictive):
Definition: Unable to perform duties of ANY occupation for which reasonably qualified
Example: Surgeon who loses hand dexterity
Result: NOT considered totally disabled if can do admin work, teaching, etc.
Only disabled if: Can't do ANY job at all
📌 EXAM TIP: “Own Occupation” is MORE FAVORABLE to policyholder but has HIGHER premiums.

Income-Loss Approach (Modern Definition):
Focus: Loss of income of the insured (not job performance)

📝 EXAM QUESTION 2 (Links to Section 5.3.a.ii)
Question: “How does income-loss approach define disability? A. Focuses on loss of income of insured B. Focuses on level of job performance C. Focuses on hurt to family D. Focuses on length and severity”
Answer: A (Focuses on loss of income)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: The name says it all: INCOME-LOSS approach!
MODERN vs TRADITIONAL: - Traditional: Can you do your job? (job duties focus) - Income-Loss: How much income have you lost? (financial impact focus)
EXAMPLE TO UNDERSTAND:
Traditional Approach:
Question: Can surgeon perform surgery?
Answer: No → Disabled

Income-Loss Approach:
Question: How much income lost?
Before: RM15,000/month (surgery)
Now: RM7,500/month (teaching/consulting)
Answer: 50% income loss → Partial disability benefit based on loss percentage
KEYWORDS: “Income-loss” = Financial focus, not job duty focus




Defining Injury: - Accidental bodily harm - Must be unforeseen - NOT self-inflicted - Differentiates accidental vs. deliberate
Defining Sickness: - Manifests AFTER policy in effect - Excludes pre-existing conditions - Diagnosed and treated during active policy period




Partial Disability:
Definition: Inability to perform SOME (but not all) duties of occupation
Typical Benefit: 50% of total disability monthly indemnity
Duration: Up to 6 months
Requirement: Usually follows period of total disability

Example:
Total Disability Benefit: RM3,000/month
Partial Disability Benefit: RM1,500/month (50%)
Maximum Duration: 6 months

Residual Disability:
Definition: Can perform some work but suffers loss of income
Benefit: PROPORTIONATE to income loss
Formula: (Loss of Income / Prior Income) × Monthly Indemnity
🔢 CRITICAL FORMULA (MUST MEMORIZE):
Residual Indemnity = (Loss of Income / Prior Income) × Monthly Indemnity
Example Calculation:
Prior Income: RM3,000/month
Current Income: RM1,500/month (due to disability)
Loss of Income: RM3,000 - RM1,500 = RM1,500
Monthly Indemnity: RM2,500

Residual Indemnity = (RM1,500 / RM3,000) × RM2,500
                   = 0.5 × RM2,500
                   = RM1,250/month
📌 EXAM TIP: Residual disability formula is HIGH PROBABILITY exam question. Practice calculations!

📝 EXAM QUESTION 8 (Links to Section 5.3)
Question: “Following statements regarding disability income insurance are incorrect, EXCEPT: A. Provides monthly benefits to policyholders who lose jobs due to illness/accidents, replacing portion of lost income B. Typically covers 100% of policyholder’s income C. Also known as critical illness insurance D. Presumptive disability = completely unable to perform occupation”
Answer: A (Correct statement)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Analyze each statement carefully:
A ✅ CORRECT - This is the accurate definition: - “Monthly benefits” = Regular income replacement ✅ - “Portion” = 50-70%, NOT 100% ✅ - “Lost income” = Focus on income loss ✅
B ❌ WRONG - NOT 100%! - Typical: 50-70% of income only - Why not 100%? Prevent malingering (faking disability to avoid work)
C ❌ WRONG - Completely different products: - Disability Income = Monthly income replacement when can’t work - Critical Illness = Lump sum on diagnosis of specific disease - NOT the same!
D ❌ WRONG - Misunderstands presumptive disability: - Presumptive Disability = Specific losses (e.g., loss of 2 limbs, sight in both eyes, hearing in both ears) that AUTOMATICALLY qualify as total disability - Doesn’t require proving can’t work - Even if COULD work, still considered totally disabled
KEYWORDS TO REMEMBER: - “Monthly benefits” ✅ - “Portion” (not 100%) ✅ - “Lost income” ✅





Purpose: Calculate appropriate coverage amount for disability income insurance.
Approach: Similar to Capital Conservation from Chapter 3.
🔢 FORMULA:
Capital Needed = Annual Income to Replace / Interest Rate

OR

Capital = A / r
Where: - A = Annual income that needs to be replaced - r = Expected investment return rate (as decimal)

Example 1:
Current Monthly Income: RM6,000
Annual Income: RM6,000 × 12 = RM72,000
Income to Replace: 60% = RM43,200 (typical replacement ratio)
Interest Rate: 6% = 0.06

Capital Needed = RM43,200 / 0.06 = RM720,000

Interpretation: Need RM720,000 capital which, invested at 6%, generates RM43,200 annually to replace lost income.

Factors to Consider:








Factor
Consideration
Impact




Replacement Ratio
Typically 50-70%, not 100%
Lower than actual income to prevent malingering


Existing Coverage
EPF, SOCSO, group insurance
Reduce individual need


Expenses
Fixed expenses continue during disability
May need full amount


Savings
Emergency fund available
Can supplement


Family Support
Dual income household
May reduce need









1. Exclusion Clauses
Standard Exclusions: - Pre-existing conditions - Specific illness waiting periods - War-related injuries - Elective cosmetic surgery - Self-inflicted injuries - Normal pregnancies (complications may be covered)

2. Benefit Period
Definition: Duration benefits are payable after onset of condition.
Options: - Short-term: 1-2 years - Medium-term: 5 years - Long-term: To age 60, 65, or lifetime
📌 EXAM TIP: Longer benefit period = Higher security but Higher premium.

3. Deferred/Elimination Period
Definition: Time from disability onset during which NO benefits paid.
Purpose: Exclude minor/short-term conditions.
Common Periods: - 30 days - 60 days - 90 days - 180 days
⚠️ EXAM ALERT: Longer elimination period = Lower premium (client bears more risk initially).

4. Waiver of Premium
Definition: Premiums waived during extended illness/disability.
Typical Trigger: Total disability for 6+ months.
Benefit: Coverage continues without premium payment burden.





Enhanced Standards (Bank Negara Malaysia):


Approval Process:
Life Insurers: - Appointed actuary approval required - Premium rates must be actuarially sound - Marketing materials approved
Lodgment with BNM: - 30 days BEFORE market introduction - All products, premium rates, marketing materials - BNM pre-launch review

📝 EXAM QUESTION 9 (Links to Section 5.9)
Question: “Objective of minimum standards for disclosure and transparency in insurance: A. Prevent mis-selling B. Avoid monopolies within industry C. Ensure customers only purchase one MHI policy D. Allow customers share information”
Answer: A (Prevent mis-selling)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Disclosure + Transparency = Consumer Protection = Prevent Mis-selling
UNDERSTANDING THE CONCEPT: - Mis-selling = Selling product that’s unsuitable or misrepresenting features - Disclosure = Full, clear information about product - Transparency = Honest, visible pricing and terms
WHY DISCLOSURE REQUIREMENTS EXIST: 1. Complex products (hard for average person to understand) 2. Information asymmetry (insurer knows more than buyer) 3. Long-term commitments (decades of premiums) 4. High stakes (health coverage needs)
WHAT REGULATION REQUIRES: - Clear explanation of benefits ✅ - Visible exclusions/limitations ✅ - Premium rate tables ✅ - Historical premium increases ✅ - Sample policy contracts ✅ - 30-day BNM pre-launch review ✅
KEYWORDS: - “Disclosure” = Make information known - “Transparency” = Clear and visible - “Prevent mis-selling” = Consumer protection goal

📝 EXAM QUESTION 3 (Links to Section 5.0 - Health Concerns)
Question: “Heddy Chan worried about health. Main concerns if health fails? i. Escalating costs of medical treatment ii. Lost EPF contributions iii. Loss of income”
Answer: C (i & iii only)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Distinguish between PRIMARY and SECONDARY concerns!
PRIMARY CONCERNS (IMMEDIATE & MAJOR): - ✅ (i) Medical costs - Immediate, huge financial burden - Surgery: RM50,000-300,000+ - Hospitalization: RM1,000+ per day - Treatment: Ongoing expenses - Direct impact on finances NOW

✅ (iii) Income loss - Can’t work, no money coming in

Family support needs continue
Bills still need to be paid
Lifestyle affected immediately
Loss of earning capacity


SECONDARY CONCERN (INDIRECT): - ❌ (ii) EPF contributions - Yes, contributions stop, but: - Not an immediate crisis - EPF is for retirement (future) - Can be addressed later - Not a primary worry when facing health crisis
ANALOGY:
House on fire (health crisis):
- Primary concern: Put out fire (medical costs), save family (income for support)
- Secondary concern: Missing next month's house insurance payment (EPF contributions)
EXAM TIP: When question asks for MAIN/PRIMARY concerns, focus on IMMEDIATE, DIRECT, CRITICAL impacts.

📝 EXAM QUESTION 4 (Links to Section 5.0)
Question: “Following insurance classified as health insurance, EXCEPT: A. Accident insurance B. Disability insurance C. Life insurance D. Sickness insurance”
Answer: C (Life insurance)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Simple but crucial distinction!
HEALTH INSURANCE: - Purpose: Pay for TREATMENT of illness/injury - Trigger: ILLNESS or INJURY occurs - Payout: WHILE ALIVE - Examples: - ✅ Accident insurance (treatment of injuries) - ✅ Disability insurance (income when can’t work due to health) - ✅ Sickness insurance (treatment of illnesses)
LIFE INSURANCE: - Purpose: Financial protection for BENEFICIARIES - Trigger: DEATH of insured - Payout: AFTER DEATH - Example: - ❌ Life insurance (pays on death, not for treatment)
MEMORY TIP:
HEALTH = ALIVE + TREATMENT
LIFE = DEATH + BENEFICIARIES
COMMON CONFUSION: Some think life insurance is health-related because: - Can die from illness - May have health requirements to qualify - BUT: Payout is on DEATH, not for health treatment!








1. Residual Disability:
Residual Indemnity = (Loss of Income / Prior Income) × Monthly Indemnity
2. Disability Capital Need:
Capital Needed = Annual Income to Replace / Interest Rate

Definition: Medical and Health Insurance (MHIT) = umbrella term for insurance contracts mitigating health-related risks.

📝 EXAM QUESTION 5 (Links to Section 5.1)
Question: “Several issues associated with healthcare in Malaysia. Main concerns from list below: i. Lack of qualified medical personnel ii. Increasing healthcare costs iii. Inadequate access and uneven distribution iv. Consistent high quality throughout country”
Answer: C (i, ii & iii only)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Option (iv) is a TRAP! It says “consistent HIGH quality” - but quality is NOT consistent; it VARIES significantly between urban and rural. This is actually an ISSUE (variation), not a positive achievement.
KEYWORDS TO REMEMBER: - ✅ “Lack/Shortage” of personnel - ✅ “Increasing/Rising” costs - ✅ “Inadequate access” and “uneven distribution” - ❌ NOT “consistent quality” (quality actually VARIES)

Definition: Time period after policy inception before certain benefits payable.
Types of Waiting Periods:









Type

Known conditions



Example:
Policy Start Date: January 1, 2025

Accident (Feb 1): ✅ COVERED (no waiting for accidents)
Flu (Feb 15): ❌ NOT COVERED (within 30-day initial waiting)
Surgery for hernia (March 1): ✅ COVERED (after 30 days, not specified illness)
Cancer treatment (April 1): ❌ NOT COVERED (within 120-day specific illness waiting)
Cancer treatment (June 1): ✅ COVERED (after 120 days for specified illness)
⚠️ EXAM ALERT: Accidents have NO waiting period; coverage is immediate.




Definition: Medical condition that existed BEFORE policy purchase, whether diagnosed or not.
Three Approaches:
Approach 1: Permanent Exclusion
Pre-existing: Diabetes diagnosed before policy
Coverage: Never covered throughout policy life
Approach 2: Waiting Period (12-36 months)
Pre-existing: Hypertension known before policy
Waiting: Not covered for 24 months
After 24 months: ✅ Covered for hypertension
Approach 3: Loaded Premium
Pre-existing: Heart condition
Coverage: Covered from start
Premium: Higher premium charged
📌 EXAM TIP: Most policies EXCLUDE pre-existing conditions permanently or impose long waiting periods.




Definition: Amount insurer deems reasonable for specific treatment in specific geographic area.
How R&C is Determined: 1. Survey of charges in the area 2. Medical necessity of treatment 3. Complexity of procedure 4. Doctor’s qualifications/experience 5. Hospital classification
Example Scenario:
Treatment: Appendectomy in Kuala Lumpur
Hospital A Bill: RM15,000
Hospital B Bill: RM12,000  
Hospital C Bill: RM10,000
Insurer's R&C Assessment: RM12,000 (median/average)

If you go to Hospital A:
Your Bill: RM15,000
Insurer Pays (R&C): RM12,000
You Pay: RM3,000 (excess over R&C)




Definition: Direct billing between hospital and insurer; policyholder doesn’t pay upfront.
How It Works:
Traditional Method (Reimbursement):
Step 1: Hospital bills patient → Patient pays RM50,000
Step 2: Patient submits claim to insurer
Step 3: Insurer reimburses patient RM50,000
Issue: Need upfront cash
Cashless Method:
Step 1: Hospital bills insurer directly → Patient pays RM0 upfront
Step 2: Insurer pays hospital RM50,000
Step 3: Patient only pays excess (if any)
Benefit: No upfront payment needed

📝 EXAM QUESTION 6 (Links to Section 5.2.a)
Question: “All of following are health insurance schemes in Malaysia, EXCEPT: A. Critical illnesses insurance B. Funeral insurance C. Major medical insurance D. Hospital and surgical insurance”
Answer: B (Funeral insurance)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Funeral insurance pays a benefit when someone DIES - that’s LIFE INSURANCE, not health insurance.
DISTINCTION TO REMEMBER: - Health Insurance = Covers TREATMENT while ALIVE (illness, injury, hospitalization) - Life Insurance = Pays on DEATH (funeral, estate, beneficiaries)
KEYWORDS: - ✅ Critical illness = Health (pays on diagnosis during life) - ✅ Major medical = Health (pays for treatment) - ✅ Hospital & surgical = Health (pays for hospitalization) - ❌ Funeral = Life (pays on death)





Origin: 1980s in South Africa; expanded globally including Malaysia.
Definition: Lump sum payment upon diagnosis of specified critical illnesses.



Common Covered Illnesses (Malaysian Context):








Category
Illnesses Typically Covered
LIAM Guidelines




Cancer
Major cancers (all stages)
✅ Standard


Heart Conditions
Heart attack, coronary artery bypass surgery
✅ Standard


Stroke
Cerebrovascular accident with permanent symptoms
✅ Standard


Kidney Failure
End-stage renal failure requiring dialysis
✅ Standard


Major Organ Transplant
Heart, lung, liver, kidney, pancreas, bone marrow
✅ Standard


Neurodegenerative
Parkinson’s, Alzheimer’s, multiple sclerosis
Extended coverage


Others
Paralysis, blindness, deafness, coma
Extended coverage



⚠️ EXAM ALERT: Life Insurance Association of Malaysia (LIAM) provides guideline list, but coverage VARIES between insurers.

Policy Structure Options:
1. Standalone Critical Illness Policy
Function: Independent policy, not attached to life insurance
Premium: Separate premium payment
Payout: Lump sum on diagnosis
Death Benefit: Only if death from covered illness within survival period
2. Critical Illness Rider (Attached to Life Policy)
Function: Attached to life insurance policy
Premium: Lower than standalone (shared with life policy)
Payout: Two sub-types:
  a) Accelerated Benefit: Reduces life insurance death benefit
  b) Non-Accelerated (Additional): Separate payout, doesn't affect death benefit




Feature 1: Single vs. Multiple Claim Policies









Type
Description
Example
Suitability




Single Claim
Pays once then terminates
Cancer diagnosed → RM200,000 paid → Policy ends
Lower cost, basic protection


Multiple Claim
Allows additional claims for different illnesses
Heart attack → RM200,000 → Policy continues → Later: Stroke → Another RM200,000
Higher cost, comprehensive protection



Multiple Claim Conditions: - Different illness category - Waiting period between claims (e.g., 1-3 years) - May have limit on total claims (e.g., 3 claims maximum)

Feature 2: Coverage for Early to Advanced Stages
Traditional: Only pays for advanced/late-stage illness Modern: Staged benefits
Example:
Total Sum Assured: RM200,000

Early Stage Cancer (Stage 1):
Payout: 25% = RM50,000
Remaining Coverage: RM150,000

Intermediate Stage Cancer (Stage 2-3):
Payout: 50% = RM100,000
Remaining Coverage: RM50,000

Advanced Stage Cancer (Stage 4):
Payout: 100% = RM200,000 (full remaining amount)
📌 EXAM TIP: Early/intermediate stage benefits provide financial support for treatment sooner.

Feature 3: Waiting and Survival Periods
Waiting Period:
Definition: Time after policy inception before claims can be made
Typical: 90-120 days
Exception: Accidents have NO waiting period

Example:
Policy Date: Jan 1, 2025
Cancer diagnosed: March 1, 2025 (Within 90 days)
Result: NOT COVERED (within waiting period)

Cancer diagnosed: May 1, 2025 (After 90 days)
Result: ✅ COVERED
Survival Period:
Definition: Time insured must survive after diagnosis to qualify for payout
Typical: 14-30 days
Purpose: Confirm illness severity

Example:
Diagnosis: Heart attack on June 1
Survival Period: 14 days
Must survive until: June 15
Payout: If alive on June 15 ✅
If dies June 10: Survival period not met ❌ (but life insurance pays instead if rider)
⚠️ EXAM ALERT: Both waiting period (before diagnosis) and survival period (after diagnosis) must be met.

Feature 4: Accelerated vs. Non-Accelerated Benefits
Accelerated Benefit (More Common):
Setup:
Life Insurance Sum Assured: RM500,000
CI Rider Sum Assured: RM200,000

Scenario: Cancer diagnosed
CI Payout: RM200,000 ✅
Remaining Life Insurance: RM500,000 - RM200,000 = RM300,000

If later dies:
Death Benefit: RM300,000 only
Non-Accelerated Benefit (Additional Benefit):
Setup:
Life Insurance Sum Assured: RM500,000
CI Rider Sum Assured: RM200,000 (Additional)

Scenario: Cancer diagnosed
CI Payout: RM200,000 ✅
Life Insurance: RM500,000 (UNCHANGED)

If later dies:
Death Benefit: RM500,000 (full amount)
Total Received: RM200,000 (CI) + RM500,000 (Death) = RM700,000
📌 EXAM TIP: - Accelerated = CI reduces death benefit (more common, lower premium) - Non-Accelerated = CI additional to death benefit (less common, higher premium)

📝 EXAM QUESTION 7 (Links to Section 5.2.b)
Question: “Which health insurance often issued with life policy, covers list of dread diseases only? A. Critical illnesses insurance B. Healthcare rider insurance C. Major medical insurance D. Hospital and surgical insurance”
Answer: A (Critical Illnesses Insurance)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Three phrases in question point to Critical Illness:

“issued with life policy” = Can be attached as rider to life insurance ✅
“dread diseases” = Another name for critical illnesses ✅
“list” = Specified illnesses covered (not all conditions) ✅

KEYWORDS TO MATCH: - “Dread disease” = Critical illness terminology - “List” = Specified conditions (cancer, heart attack, stroke, etc.) - “With life policy” = Rider capability





Global Context: - USA: 40% of elderly need nursing home care; 60% by age 75 - Malaysia: Underdeveloped market, growing need due to aging population

Services
Malaysian Context

24-hour skilled nursing
Limited facilities in Malaysia

📝 EXAM QUESTION 10 (Links to Section 5.2.c)
Question: “Coverage of long-term care insurance includes: i. Nursing home care ii. Home care services iii. Social services iv. Assisted living facilities
A. i & ii only B. i, ii & iii only C. i, ii & iv only D. All the above”
Answer: C (i, ii & iv only)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Option (iii) “Social services” is the TRAP!
Why “Social services” NOT covered: - Too BROAD and general - LTC covers SPECIFIC HEALTHCARE settings/services - Social services include non-medical support (welfare, community programs, social work) - LTC focuses on MEDICAL/HEALTHCARE support for ADLs
WHAT IS COVERED: - ✅ Nursing home = Medical care facility (24-hour skilled nursing) - ✅ Home care = Healthcare services at home (nursing, PT, OT) - ✅ Assisted living = Residential facility with ADL support & medication management - ❌ Social services = Too general, not healthcare-specific
MEMORY TIP: LTC covers MEDICAL/HEALTHCARE care settings, not general social welfare programs.





Definition: Daily cash benefit for each day hospitalized; NOT reimbursement of actual costs.
Key Distinction: - Medical Reimbursement: Pays actual bills - Hospital Income: Pays fixed daily amount regardless of actual costs



Daily Cash Benefit Structure:
Example:
Policy: RM200/day hospital income
Hospitalization: 5 days for illness
Actual Hospital Bill: RM30,000 (paid by medical insurance or self)
Hospital Income Payout: RM200 × 5 = RM1,000 (regardless of actual bill)
Use: Can use RM1,000 for any purpose (loss of income, transport, childcare, etc.)
Flexibility of Use: - Cover household expenses - Compensate for lost income - Transportation costs - Childcare during hospitalization - Meals for family members - Any other needs
📌 EXAM TIP: Hospital Income provides cash flow during hospitalization, complementing medical reimbursement insurance.





Also Called: Permanent Health Insurance ✅ (This is the exam term!)
Definition: Replaces portion of income lost due to disability from illness or injury.



Purpose: Provide monthly benefits to replace lost income when unable to work due to disability.
Key Points: - Does NOT cover medical expenses (that’s medical insurance) - Covers INCOME LOSS only - Typically replaces 50-70% of income (not 100%) - Prevents over-insurance and malingering

📝 EXAM QUESTION 1 (Links to Section 5.3)
Question: “Disability Income Insurance is also called ___. A. Disability care insurance B. Total disability insurance C. Permanent health insurance D. Income loss insurance”
Answer: C (Permanent Health Insurance)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: “Permanent Health Insurance” is British/traditional terminology for disability income insurance.
WHY “Permanent Health”? - “Permanent” = Long-term income protection (not temporary) - “Health” = Health-related inability to work - Used in UK, Malaysia, and former British colonies
TERMINOLOGY VARIATIONS: - UK/Malaysia: Permanent Health Insurance ✅ - USA: Disability Income Insurance - Modern: Both terms used interchangeably
EXAM TIP: When you see “Permanent Health Insurance” in exam, immediately think DISABILITY INCOME replacement.




TWO Main Approaches:
1. Own Occupation (More Liberal):
Definition: Unable to perform duties of YOUR SPECIFIC occupation
Example: Surgeon who loses hand dexterity
Result: Considered totally disabled (can't do surgery)
Even if: Could work in another field
2. Any Occupation (More Restrictive):
Definition: Unable to perform duties of ANY occupation for which reasonably qualified
Example: Surgeon who loses hand dexterity
Result: NOT considered totally disabled if can do admin work, teaching, etc.
Only disabled if: Can't do ANY job at all
📌 EXAM TIP: “Own Occupation” is MORE FAVORABLE to policyholder but has HIGHER premiums.

Income-Loss Approach (Modern Definition):
Focus: Loss of income of the insured (not job performance)

📝 EXAM QUESTION 2 (Links to Section 5.3.a.ii)
Question: “How does income-loss approach define disability? A. Focuses on loss of income of insured B. Focuses on level of job performance C. Focuses on hurt to family D. Focuses on length and severity”
Answer: A (Focuses on loss of income)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: The name says it all: INCOME-LOSS approach!
MODERN vs TRADITIONAL: - Traditional: Can you do your job? (job duties focus) - Income-Loss: How much income have you lost? (financial impact focus)
EXAMPLE TO UNDERSTAND:
Traditional Approach:
Question: Can surgeon perform surgery?
Answer: No → Disabled

Income-Loss Approach:
Question: How much income lost?
Before: RM15,000/month (surgery)
Now: RM7,500/month (teaching/consulting)
Answer: 50% income loss → Partial disability benefit based on loss percentage
KEYWORDS: “Income-loss” = Financial focus, not job duty focus




Defining Injury: - Accidental bodily harm - Must be unforeseen - NOT self-inflicted - Differentiates accidental vs. deliberate
Defining Sickness: - Manifests AFTER policy in effect - Excludes pre-existing conditions - Diagnosed and treated during active policy period




Partial Disability:
Definition: Inability to perform SOME (but not all) duties of occupation
Typical Benefit: 50% of total disability monthly indemnity
Duration: Up to 6 months
Requirement: Usually follows period of total disability

Example:
Total Disability Benefit: RM3,000/month
Partial Disability Benefit: RM1,500/month (50%)
Maximum Duration: 6 months

Residual Disability:
Definition: Can perform some work but suffers loss of income
Benefit: PROPORTIONATE to income loss
Formula: (Loss of Income / Prior Income) × Monthly Indemnity
🔢 CRITICAL FORMULA (MUST MEMORIZE):
Residual Indemnity = (Loss of Income / Prior Income) × Monthly Indemnity
Example Calculation:
Prior Income: RM3,000/month
Current Income: RM1,500/month (due to disability)
Loss of Income: RM3,000 - RM1,500 = RM1,500
Monthly Indemnity: RM2,500

Residual Indemnity = (RM1,500 / RM3,000) × RM2,500
                   = 0.5 × RM2,500
                   = RM1,250/month
📌 EXAM TIP: Residual disability formula is HIGH PROBABILITY exam question. Practice calculations!

📝 EXAM QUESTION 8 (Links to Section 5.3)
Question: “Following statements regarding disability income insurance are incorrect, EXCEPT: A. Provides monthly benefits to policyholders who lose jobs due to illness/accidents, replacing portion of lost income B. Typically covers 100% of policyholder’s income C. Also known as critical illness insurance D. Presumptive disability = completely unable to perform occupation”
Answer: A (Correct statement)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Analyze each statement carefully:
A ✅ CORRECT - This is the accurate definition: - “Monthly benefits” = Regular income replacement ✅ - “Portion” = 50-70%, NOT 100% ✅ - “Lost income” = Focus on income loss ✅
B ❌ WRONG - NOT 100%! - Typical: 50-70% of income only - Why not 100%? Prevent malingering (faking disability to avoid work)
C ❌ WRONG - Completely different products: - Disability Income = Monthly income replacement when can’t work - Critical Illness = Lump sum on diagnosis of specific disease - NOT the same!
D ❌ WRONG - Misunderstands presumptive disability: - Presumptive Disability = Specific losses (e.g., loss of 2 limbs, sight in both eyes, hearing in both ears) that AUTOMATICALLY qualify as total disability - Doesn’t require proving can’t work - Even if COULD work, still considered totally disabled
KEYWORDS TO REMEMBER: - “Monthly benefits” ✅ - “Portion” (not 100%) ✅ - “Lost income” ✅





Purpose: Calculate appropriate coverage amount for disability income insurance.
Approach: Similar to Capital Conservation from Chapter 3.
🔢 FORMULA:
Capital Needed = Annual Income to Replace / Interest Rate

OR

Capital = A / r
Where: - A = Annual income that needs to be replaced - r = Expected investment return rate (as decimal)

Example 1:
Current Monthly Income: RM6,000
Annual Income: RM6,000 × 12 = RM72,000
Income to Replace: 60% = RM43,200 (typical replacement ratio)
Interest Rate: 6% = 0.06

Capital Needed = RM43,200 / 0.06 = RM720,000

Interpretation: Need RM720,000 capital which, invested at 6%, generates RM43,200 annually to replace lost income.

Factors to Consider:








Factor
Consideration
Impact




Replacement Ratio
Typically 50-70%, not 100%
Lower than actual income to prevent malingering


Existing Coverage
EPF, SOCSO, group insurance
Reduce individual need


Expenses

May need full amount


Savings
Emergency fund available
Can supplement


Family Support
Dual income household
May reduce need









1. Exclusion Clauses
Standard Exclusions: - Pre-existing conditions - Specific illness waiting periods - War-related injuries - Elective cosmetic surgery - Self-inflicted injuries - Normal pregnancies (complications may be covered)

2. Benefit Period
Definition: Duration benefits are payable after onset of condition.
Options: - Short-term: 1-2 years - Medium-term: 5 years - Long-term: To age 60, 65, or lifetime
📌 EXAM TIP: Longer benefit period = Higher security but Higher premium.

3. Deferred/Elimination Period
Definition: Time from disability onset during which NO benefits paid.
Purpose: Exclude minor/short-term conditions.
Common Periods: - 30 days - 60 days - 90 days - 180 days
⚠️ EXAM ALERT: Longer elimination period = Lower premium (client bears more risk initially).

4. Waiver of Premium
Definition: Premiums waived during extended illness/disability.
Typical Trigger: Total disability for 6+ months.
Benefit: Coverage continues without premium payment burden.





Enhanced Standards (Bank Negara Malaysia):


Approval Process:
Life Insurers: - Appointed actuary approval required - Premium rates must be actuarially sound - Marketing materials approved
Lodgment with BNM: - 30 days BEFORE market introduction - All products, premium rates, marketing materials - BNM pre-launch review

📝 EXAM QUESTION 9 (Links to Section 5.9)
Question: “Objective of minimum standards for disclosure and transparency in insurance: A. Prevent mis-selling B. Avoid monopolies within industry C. Ensure customers only purchase one MHI policy D. Allow customers share information”
Answer: A (Prevent mis-selling)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Disclosure + Transparency = Consumer Protection = Prevent Mis-selling
UNDERSTANDING THE CONCEPT: - Mis-selling = Selling product that’s unsuitable or misrepresenting features - Disclosure = Full, clear information about product - Transparency = Honest, visible pricing and terms
WHY DISCLOSURE REQUIREMENTS EXIST: 1. Complex products (hard for average person to understand) 2. Information asymmetry (insurer knows more than buyer) 3. Long-term commitments (decades of premiums) 4. High stakes (health coverage needs)
WHAT REGULATION REQUIRES: - Clear explanation of benefits ✅ - Visible exclusions/limitations ✅ - Premium rate tables ✅ - Historical premium increases ✅ - Sample policy contracts ✅ - 30-day BNM pre-launch review ✅
KEYWORDS: - “Disclosure” = Make information known - “Transparency” = Clear and visible - “Prevent mis-selling” = Consumer protection goal

📝 EXAM QUESTION 3 (Links to Section 5.0 - Health Concerns)
Question: “Heddy Chan worried about health. Main concerns if health fails? i. Escalating costs of medical treatment ii. Lost EPF contributions iii. Loss of income”
Answer: C (i & iii only)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Distinguish between PRIMARY and SECONDARY concerns!
PRIMARY CONCERNS (IMMEDIATE & MAJOR): - ✅ (i) Medical costs - Immediate, huge financial burden - Surgery: RM50,000-300,000+ - Hospitalization: RM1,000+ per day - Treatment: Ongoing expenses - Direct impact on finances NOW

✅ (iii) Income loss - Can’t work, no money coming in

Family support needs continue
Bills still need to be paid
Lifestyle affected immediately
Loss of earning capacity


SECONDARY CONCERN (INDIRECT): - ❌ (ii) EPF contributions - Yes, contributions stop, but: - Not an immediate crisis - EPF is for retirement (future) - Can be addressed later - Not a primary worry when facing health crisis
ANALOGY:
House on fire (health crisis):
- Primary concern: Put out fire (medical costs), save family (income for support)
- Secondary concern: Missing next month's house insurance payment (EPF contributions)
EXAM TIP: When question asks for MAIN/PRIMARY concerns, focus on IMMEDIATE, DIRECT, CRITICAL impacts.

📝 EXAM QUESTION 4 (Links to Section 5.0)
Question: “Following insurance classified as health insurance, EXCEPT: A. Accident insurance B. Disability insurance C. Life insurance D. Sickness insurance”
Answer: C (Life insurance)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Simple but crucial distinction!
HEALTH INSURANCE: - Purpose: Pay for TREATMENT of illness/injury - Trigger: ILLNESS or INJURY occurs - Payout: WHILE ALIVE - Examples: - ✅ Accident insurance (treatment of injuries) - ✅ Disability insurance (income when can’t work due to health) - ✅ Sickness insurance (treatment of illnesses)
LIFE INSURANCE: - Purpose: Financial protection for BENEFICIARIES - Trigger: DEATH of insured - Payout: AFTER DEATH - Example: - ❌ Life insurance (pays on death, not for treatment)
MEMORY TIP:
HEALTH = ALIVE + TREATMENT
LIFE = DEATH + BENEFICIARIES
COMMON CONFUSION: Some think life insurance is health-related because: - Can die from illness - May have health requirements to qualify - BUT: Payout is on DEATH, not for health treatment!

title: Chapter 2: Risk Management and Insurance Planning
text:
This chapter builds on Chapter 1’s foundation and introduces the systematic process of managing risks in financial planning. Understanding the 6-step risk management process is CRITICAL for exam success, as it forms the framework for all practical risk management questions.
Exam Weight: Expect 15-20% of exam questions from this chapter - one of the highest weighted chapters.
Study Time Recommendation: 10-12 hours




By the end of this chapter, you must be able to:

Distinguish between speculative and pure risks in financial planning contexts
Apply the 6-step risk management process systematically
Evaluate and select appropriate risk management techniques for different scenarios
Analyze case studies to recommend suitable risk management strategies
Identify different types of pure risks (personal, property, liability)



















Category
Focus
Primary Risks
Risk Type
Examples in Malaysia




Wealth Accumulation
Growing assets through investments
Market volatility, currency fluctuations, economic conditions
SPECULATIVE RISKS
Unit trusts, equity investments in Bursa Malaysia, property speculation


Wealth Conservation
Protecting accumulated wealth to sustain lifestyle
Health issues, disability, premature death, inability to liquidate assets
PURE RISKS
Critical illness, disability, death affecting dependents



⚠️ EXAM ALERT: Module 2 focuses on PURE RISK (insurance-related). Speculative risks are covered in Module 3.
📌 CRITICAL DISTINCTION: - Speculative Risk = Possibility of GAIN or LOSS (investment activities) - Pure Risk = Possibility of LOSS or NO LOSS (insurable events)




Definition: Risks involving the possibility of gaining or losing based on market fluctuations or economic conditions.
Key Characteristics: 1. Potential for profit 2. Voluntarily undertaken 3. NOT insurable through traditional insurance 4. Managed through investment strategies
Malaysian Examples:








Investment Type
Speculative Risks Involved
Management Approach




Bursa Malaysia stocks
Market volatility, company performance, sector-specific risks
Portfolio diversification, asset allocation


Property investment

Market research, diversification across areas


Currency trading
Exchange rate fluctuations, geopolitical factors
Hedging strategies, limit exposure


Unit trust funds
Market downturns, fund manager performance
Dollar-cost averaging, fund selection



Impact on Financial Planning Decisions: - Asset allocation strategies - Portfolio diversification requirements - Risk tolerance assessment - Cash holdings for liquidity
⚠️ EXAM TIP: If question mentions “investment”, “market volatility”, or “potential for gain” → Speculative Risk




Definition: Risks representing the possibility of losses WITHOUT the opportunity for gain.
Key Characteristics: 1. No potential for profit 2. Fortuitous (happen by chance) 3. INSURABLE 4. Definite and measurable
Three Main Types of Pure Risks:









Type
Definition
Malaysian Examples
Insurance Solutions




Personal Risks
Risks affecting individual’s earning capacity and life
Premature death, disability, critical illness, unemployment
Life insurance, disability income, critical illness, medical insurance


Property Risks
Risks of financial loss from damage/destruction of property
House fire, flood damage, car accidents, burglary
Fire insurance, home insurance, motor insurance


Liability Risks
Risks of being held legally responsible for injury/damage to others
Car accident injuring others, domestic worker injury, professional negligence
Third-party motor insurance, employer’s liability, professional indemnity



📌 MEMORY AID - “PPL”: - Personal (affects YOU) - Property (affects YOUR STUFF) - Liability (affects OTHERS through YOUR actions)




Four Major Categories (MUST MEMORIZE):









Risk Type
Definition
Financial Impact
Example




Risk of Premature Death

Breadwinner dies at 40, leaving family with mortgage


Risk of Retirement
Outliving financial resources
Insufficient retirement income, erosion of purchasing power
Living to 90 but savings only planned for 75


Risk of Health Deterioration
Illness or medical conditions requiring treatment
Medical expenses, loss of income during treatment
Critical illness like cancer requiring expensive treatment


Risk of Unemployment
Loss of employment/income
Inability to meet financial obligations
Retrenchment during economic downturn



⚠️ EXAM QUESTION PATTERN: “Which pure risk situations fall under personal risks?” Answer: ALL FOUR categories above (Premature death, Retirement, Health deterioration, Unemployment)







MEMORIZE THIS: Risk management is the systematic process of dealing with risks faced by an individual.
⚠️ EXAM TRAP: - ❌ NOT “eliminating all risks” (impossible) - ❌ NOT “using insurance as sole method” (only one technique) - ❌ NOT “reducing risk exposures to increase wealth” (too narrow) - ✅ “Systematic process of DEALING with risks”




Key Concept: Risks are NOT static; they evolve with changes in: - Individual circumstances (marriage, children, career changes) - Economic conditions (recession, inflation, market crashes) - Regulatory environment (new laws, tax changes) - Technology (cybersecurity risks, digital fraud) - Demographics (aging population, healthcare advances)
Malaysian Context Examples:








Dynamic Factor
How It Changes Risk
Impact on Risk Management




COVID-19 Pandemic
Increased health risks, business disruptions, job losses
Higher demand for medical insurance, business interruption coverage


EPF/SOCSO Regulation Changes
Modified contribution rates, coverage expansions
Adjust retirement planning, review social security adequacy


Digital Economy Growth
New cybersecurity risks, digital fraud
Need for cyber insurance, data protection measures


Aging Population
Increased healthcare needs, longer retirement periods
More critical illness coverage, longer-term retirement planning


Climate Change
More frequent floods, landslides in Malaysia
Enhanced property insurance, location-based risk assessment



⚠️ EXAM TIP: Questions about changing circumstances or evolving risks test understanding of risk dynamics.

Risk Evaluation Criteria:
Frequency Analysis: - High Frequency, Low Severity → Risk Retention or Loss Control (e.g., minor car scratches - use own funds) - Low Frequency, High Severity → Risk Transfer/Insurance (e.g., death - buy life insurance) - High Frequency, High Severity → Risk Avoidance (e.g., dangerous activities - don’t do them) - Low Frequency, Low Severity → Risk Retention (e.g., losing wallet - accept and budget for replacement)

Making Informed Decisions:
Key Principles: 1. Not every risk needs to be managed - Prioritize based on impact and probability 2. Resource limitations require prioritization - Focus on most significant risks first 3. Purpose: Select and apply cost-effective risk management techniques.
Four Main Risk Management Techniques (MUST MEMORIZE)










Technique
Description
When to Use
Strategies
Examples




1. Risk Avoidance
Completely avoid the risk
When risk is unacceptable and can be avoided
Elimination, Substitution, Separation, Rational Planning
Don’t engage in dangerous hobbies; Don’t invest in extremely volatile assets; Don’t drive if vision impaired


2. Risk Control (Loss Control)
Reduce likelihood or severity of losses
When risk cannot be avoided but can be managed
Loss Prevention, Loss Reduction, Loss Sharing
Install fire alarm (prevention); Use sprinkler system (reduction); Form business partnership (sharing)


3. Risk Retention
Accept and retain the risk, cover losses yourself
When risk impact is affordable or unavoidable
Active Retention (deliberate), Passive Retention (unintentional)
Maintain emergency fund; Self-insure small losses; Accept deductibles in insurance


4. Risk Transfer
Transfer risk to another party
When risk impact is too high to retain
Non-insurance Transfer, Insurance Transfer
Lease instead of buy equipment; Purchase life insurance; Buy property insurance

Strategy
Definition
Example

Type

1. Simon Lim bought a house for RM600,000. Which best describes the pure risk situation? - A. Risk that house may be burnt down in a fire accident ✅ - B. Risk that house value may drop in a downturn - C. Risk of losing money had he invested elsewhere - D. None of the above
Explanation: - A = Pure risk (only loss or no loss, no gain) - B = Speculative risk (property value can go up or down) - C = Opportunity cost/speculative risk Exam Tip: Pure risk = NO possibility of profit, only loss or no loss.

2. Which best defines risk management? - A. Methods used in eliminating all risks faced by an individual - B. Systematic process of dealing with risks faced by an individual ✅ - C. Use of insurance as the sole method to manage risks - D. Process of increasing wealth by reducing risk exposures
Explanation: - A = Wrong - cannot eliminate ALL risks - B = Correct definition - SYSTEMATIC PROCESS of DEALING (not eliminating) - C = Wrong - insurance is only ONE technique - D = Wrong - too narrow, focus is on managing risks not just wealth increase Exam Tip: Word-for-word definition question - memorize “systematic process of dealing with risks”

3. As a financial practitioner, which best describes “risk”? - A. Uncertainty about financial losses from an exposure ✅ - B. Certainty about financial losses from an exposure - C. Exposure to investment risks - D. Exposure to systemic risks
Explanation: - A = Correct - exact definition from Chapter 1 & 2 - B = Wrong - UNCERTAINTY not certainty - C = Wrong - too narrow (only investment) - D = Wrong - too narrow (only systemic) Exam Tip: This is the MODULE 2 definition of risk - know it word-for-word

4. Fill in the blanks: In risk management, _____ is the unpleasant outcome of _____. - A. Loss; risk ✅ - B. Risk; Loss - C. Exposure; loss - D. Loss; business ventures
Explanation: - LOSS is the unpleasant OUTCOME (result) - RISK is what might cause it (the possibility) - Therefore: Loss is outcome OF risk Exam Tip: Think cause and effect - Risk causes Loss

5. There are two forms of loss. _____ is a loss that may happen; _____ is a loss that has precipitated. - A. Occurred loss; loss exposure - B. Loss exposure; occurred loss ✅ - C. Loss event; loss risk - D. Potential loss; actual loss (also acceptable, but B is the terminology used in the text)
Explanation: - Loss EXPOSURE = potential/may happen (future) - Occurred/Precipitated loss = already happened (past) Exam Tip: “Exposure” = future possibility; “Occurred/Precipitated” = already happened

6. Harban Singh (construction worker, high-risk area, large accident policy, single, no dependents, pressed by credit card debt). Insurer turns down proposal. What are likely grounds?

High physical hazard: works in high-risk area
Likely moral hazard: in debts
Possible morale hazard: no dependents


A. i only
B. i & ii
C. None of the above
D. All the above ✅

Explanation: - i = TRUE: High-risk job = physical hazard - ii = TRUE: Debt + large policy = potential fraud (moral hazard) - iii = TRUE: No dependents + large policy = may not care about safety (morale hazard) All three concerns valid - insurer right to decline Exam Tip: Multiple hazards can exist simultaneously in one scenario

7. _____ is a risk that affects the entire economy; _____ is a risk that affects only individuals. - A. Fundamental risk; particular risk ✅ - B. Particular risk; fundamental risk - C. Speculative risk; pure risk - D. Static risk; dynamic risk
Explanation: - Fundamental = affects MANY (economy/community) - Particular = affects FEW (individuals) Exam Tip: “Fundamental” sounds big = affects everyone; “Particular” sounds specific = affects specific person

8. Which are the three main types of pure risk faced by individuals? - A. Group risks, personal risks, and liability risks - B. Insurable risks, property risks, and liability risks - C. Personal risks, property risks, and liability risks ✅ - D. Death risks, disability risks, and illness risks
Explanation: The “PPL” framework: - Personal risks - Property risks - Liability risks Exam Tip: Memorize “PPL” - these are the three categories of pure risks




9. Which pure risk situations fall under personal risks?

Risk of Premature death
Risk of Retirement
Risk of Health Deterioration
Risk of Unemployment


A. i & ii only
B. ii & iii only
C. i, ii & iii only
D. All of the above ✅

Explanation: ALL FOUR are personal risks: - Premature death = affects earning capacity - Retirement = outliving resources - Health deterioration = medical costs + lost income - Unemployment = loss of income Exam Tip: When in doubt with personal risks, usually “all of the above” if all relate to the person’s earning/living capacity

10. (Fire scenario - Mr. Kong’s factory) Property loss can be direct or indirect. Which loss is classified as INDIRECT? - A. Loss of the factory - B. Loss of the special printing machines - C. Loss of profits ✅ - D. Loss of printing materials
Explanation: - Direct loss = Physical damage (factory, machines, materials) - Indirect loss = Consequential/resulting loss (profits, rental income, business interruption) Exam Tip: Direct = You can TOUCH it (physical); Indirect = You CANNOT touch it (consequential)

11. Which of the following is a speculative risk? - A. Risk of house fire - B. Risk of car accident - C. Risk of starting a new business ✅ - D. Risk of critical illness
Explanation: - A, B, D = Pure risks (only loss or no loss) - C = Speculative (business can profit OR lose) Exam Tip: If there’s potential for GAIN/PROFIT = Speculative

12. A young family with a new baby is considering insurance. Which risk should be the HIGHEST priority? - A. Travel insurance - B. Investment-linked policy - C. Life insurance for breadwinner ✅ - D. Car comprehensive insurance
Explanation: Priority for family with dependent: 1. Life insurance (protect dependent if breadwinner dies) = CRITICAL 2. Medical insurance (healthcare for family) 3. Critical illness (protect income) 4. Others (travel, car comprehensive) = lower priority Exam Tip: Dependent child = Life insurance becomes CRITICAL priority




13. Which risk management technique involves completely avoiding the risk? - A. Risk control - B. Risk avoidance ✅ - C. Risk retention - D. Risk transfer
Explanation: Four techniques: - Avoidance = Eliminate completely - Control = Reduce frequency/severity - Retention = Accept and self-pay - Transfer = Shift to others Exam Tip: “Avoid” = “Eliminate” = don’t do the risky activity

14. Installing a fire alarm system is an example of: - A. Risk avoidance - B. Loss prevention ✅ - C. Loss reduction - D. Risk transfer
Explanation: - Fire alarm = Detects early = PREVENTS fire from growing - Fire alarm is part of RISK CONTROL technique - Specifically: LOSS PREVENTION (reduces FREQUENCY) Exam Tip: Prevention = BEFORE/STOP it happening; Reduction = MINIMIZE damage AFTER it starts

15. Installing sprinkler systems in a building is an example of: - A. Risk avoidance - B. Loss prevention - C. Loss reduction ✅ - D. Risk retention
Explanation: - Sprinklers activate AFTER fire starts = don’t prevent, but REDUCE damage - Part of RISK CONTROL - Specifically: LOSS REDUCTION (reduces SEVERITY) Exam Tip: Sprinkler/fire extinguisher = REDUCTION (fire already started, minimize damage)

16. Maintaining an emergency fund to cover unexpected medical expenses is: - A. Risk avoidance - B. Risk control - C. Risk retention ✅ - D. Risk transfer
Explanation: - Emergency fund = Prepare to SELF-PAY when loss occurs - This is RISK RETENTION (accept risk, plan to cover it yourself) - Specifically: ACTIVE retention (deliberate with preparation) Exam Tip: Emergency fund = Retention (you’re retaining/accepting the risk)

17. Purchasing comprehensive motor insurance is an example of: - A. Risk avoidance - B. Risk control - C. Risk retention - D. Risk transfer ✅
Explanation: - Buying insurance = Transfer risk to insurer - Pay premium, insurer pays claims - This is INSURANCE-BASED TRANSFER Exam Tip: Buying insurance = always TRANSFER technique

18. Which technique is most appropriate for LOW frequency, HIGH severity risks? - A. Risk avoidance - B. Risk control - C. Risk retention - D. Risk transfer (Insurance) ✅
Explanation: Frequency-Severity Matrix: - Low frequency + High severity = INSURANCE (transfer) - Rarely happens, but devastating when it does - Examples: Death, major accident, house fire Exam Tip: Low frequency + High severity = classic insurance situation

19. Which technique is most appropriate for HIGH frequency, LOW severity risks? - A. Risk avoidance - B. Risk control - C. Risk retention ✅ - D. Risk transfer
Explanation: - High frequency + Low severity = Self-pay (retention) - Happens often but small impact - Insurance would be too expensive - Examples: Minor car scratches, small medical consultations Exam Tip: High frequency + Low severity = too expensive to insure, better to self-pay

20. Leasing equipment instead of buying it is an example of: - A. Risk avoidance - B. Risk control - C. Non-insurance transfer ✅ - D. Insurance transfer
Explanation: - Leasing = Lessor retains ownership and risks - Risk transferred through CONTRACT, not insurance - This is NON-INSURANCE TRANSFER Exam Tip: Contract-based shift = Non-insurance transfer; Premium-based = Insurance transfer




21. What is the FIRST step in the risk management process? - A. Gather information - B. Establish risk management objectives ✅ - C. Analyze risks - D. Develop a plan
Explanation: 6-Step Process: 1. Establish objectives (define what you want to achieve) 2. Gather information 3. Analyze and evaluate 4. Develop plan 5. Implement 6. Review and revise Exam Tip: Must know goals BEFORE gathering data

22. Which step involves identifying whether risks are high or low priority? - A. Step 2: Gather information - B. Step 3: Analyze and evaluate risks ✅ - C. Step 4: Develop plan - D. Step 5: Implement plan
Explanation: - Step 3 = ANALYZE information to IDENTIFY and EVALUATE (prioritize) risks - Evaluation includes assessing frequency, severity, and priority Exam Tip: “Evaluate” and “prioritize” happen in Step 3 (Analysis)

23. EPF death benefit is classified as: - A. Cash in bank - B. Cash resources ✅ - C. Cash equivalent resources - D. Non-liquid resources
Explanation: Table 2-1 Classifications: - Cash in bank = Immediately accessible - Cash resources = Received in cash on death within reasonable time (EPF, insurance, gratuities) - Cash equivalent = Can convert to cash (unit trusts, shares) - Non-liquid = Hard to convert (property) Exam Tip: EPF death benefit = Cash Resources (NOT cash in bank - needs processing time)

24. Listed shares on Bursa Malaysia are classified as: - A. Cash in bank - B. Cash resources - C. Cash equivalent resources ✅ - D. Non-liquid resources
Explanation: - Listed shares = Can sell on exchange = Convert to cash easily - Not immediate like bank account - Not cash received on death - Therefore: CASH EQUIVALENT Exam Tip: Shares, unit trusts, bonds = Cash Equivalent (can liquidate fairly easily)

25. Which is NOT a step in the risk management process? - A. Gather information for analysis - B. Develop a risk management plan - C. Eliminate all identified risks ✅ - D. Review, monitor, and revise the plan
Explanation: - Cannot eliminate ALL risks (unrealistic) - Risk management = MANAGE risks (not eliminate all) - Options A, B, D are actual steps in the 6-step process Exam Tip: “Eliminate all risks” = red flag wrong answer

26. How often should a risk management plan be reviewed? - A. Only when a claim is made - B. Once every 5 years - C. Annually and when life circumstances change ✅ - D. Never - set it and forget it
Explanation: Review triggers: - Annual review (comprehensive) - Major life changes (marriage, child, job change) - Financial changes (promotion, inheritance) - Asset acquisition (house, car) Exam Tip: Risk management is CONTINUOUS, not one-time




27. A retiree couple on fixed income is choosing medical insurance. They should prioritize: - A. Lowest premium regardless of deductible - B. Highest deductible to save on premium - C. Lower deductible even if premium is higher ✅ - D. No insurance - use government hospitals
Explanation: - Fixed income = predictable expenses important - Lower deductible = lower out-of-pocket when claim - Higher premium = predictable monthly cost - Better than high deductible with unpredictable large out-of-pocket Exam Tip: Fixed income + retiree = prefer predictable costs = lower deductible

28. A young couple with first child and mortgage should prioritize: - A. Investment-linked policy for returns - B. Term life insurance covering mortgage and family expenses ✅ - C. Saving for child’s university - D. Comprehensive motor insurance
Explanation: Priority ranking: 1. Life insurance (protect dependent and mortgage) = CRITICAL 2. Medical insurance (family healthcare) 3. Critical illness (income protection) 4. Other priorities Exam Tip: New dependent + mortgage = Life insurance becomes #1 priority

29. A property investor concerned about tenant defaults should use: - A. Risk avoidance (don’t rent out) - B. Risk transfer (insurance for tenant defaults) - C. Risk control (background checks) + Retention (emergency fund) ✅ - D. Only risk retention
Explanation: - Tenant default = moderate frequency, moderate severity - CONTROL: Background checks reduce likelihood - RETENTION: Emergency fund to cover temporary loss - Combination approach most appropriate Exam Tip: Moderate risks often need COMBINATION of techniques

30. Which statement about risk management is TRUE? - A. All identified risks must be insured - B. Risk management is a one-time process - C. Risk retention means doing nothing about the risk - D. Risk management techniques can be used in combination ✅
Explanation: - A = False (not all risks need insurance) - B = False (continuous process - Step 6 is ongoing review) - C = False (active retention involves planning and reserves) - D = TRUE (often use multiple techniques together) Exam Tip: Real-world risk management = combination of techniques, not single approach

title: Chapter 2: Risk Management and Insurance Planning
text:
This chapter builds on Chapter 1’s foundation and introduces the systematic process of managing risks in financial planning. Understanding the 6-step risk management process is CRITICAL for exam success, as it forms the framework for all practical risk management questions.
Exam Weight: Expect 15-20% of exam questions from this chapter - one of the highest weighted chapters.
Study Time Recommendation: 10-12 hours

title: Chapter 2: Risk Management and Insurance Planning
text:
By the end of this chapter, you must be able to:

Distinguish between speculative and pure risks in financial planning contexts
Apply the 6-step risk management process systematically
Evaluate and select appropriate risk management techniques for different scenarios
Analyze case studies to recommend suitable risk management strategies
Identify different types of pure risks (personal, property, liability)

📌 CRITICAL DISTINCTION: - Speculative Risk = Possibility of GAIN or LOSS (investment activities) - Pure Risk = Possibility of LOSS or NO LOSS (insurable events)




Definition: Risks involving the possibility of gaining or losing based on market fluctuations or economic conditions.
Key Characteristics: 1. Potential for profit 2. Voluntarily undertaken 3. NOT insurable through traditional insurance 4. Managed through investment strategies

Impact on Financial Planning Decisions: - Asset allocation strategies - Portfolio diversification requirements - Risk tolerance assessment - Cash holdings for liquidity
⚠️ EXAM TIP: If question mentions “investment”, “market volatility”, or “potential for gain” → Speculative Risk




Definition: Risks representing the possibility of losses WITHOUT the opportunity for gain.
Key Characteristics: 1. No potential for profit 2. Fortuitous (happen by chance) 3. INSURABLE 4. Definite and measurable
Three Main Types of Pure Risks:









Type
Definition
Malaysian Examples
Insurance Solutions




Personal Risks
Risks affecting individual’s earning capacity and life
Premature death, disability, critical illness, unemployment
Life insurance, disability income, critical illness, medical insurance


Property Risks
Risks of financial loss from damage/destruction of property
House fire, flood damage, car accidents, burglary
Fire insurance, home insurance, motor insurance


Liability Risks
Risks of being held legally responsible for injury/damage to others
Car accident injuring others, domestic worker injury, professional negligence
Third-party motor insurance, employer’s liability, professional indemnity



📌 MEMORY AID - “PPL”: - Personal (affects YOU) - Property (affects YOUR STUFF) - Liability (affects OTHERS through YOUR actions)




Four Major Categories (MUST MEMORIZE):









Risk Type
Definition

⚠️ EXAM QUESTION PATTERN: “Which pure risk situations fall under personal risks?” Answer: ALL FOUR categories above (Premature death, Retirement, Health deterioration, Unemployment)







MEMORIZE THIS: Risk management is the systematic process of dealing with risks faced by an individual.
⚠️ EXAM TRAP: - ❌ NOT “eliminating all risks” (impossible) - ❌ NOT “using insurance as sole method” (only one technique) - ❌ NOT “reducing risk exposures to increase wealth” (too narrow) - ✅ “Systematic process of DEALING with risks”




Key Concept: Risks are NOT static; they evolve with changes in: - Individual circumstances (marriage, children, career changes) - Economic conditions (recession, inflation, market crashes) - Regulatory environment (new laws, tax changes) - Technology (cybersecurity risks, digital fraud) - Demographics (aging population, healthcare advances)
