Risk Evaluation Criteria:
Frequency Analysis: - High Frequency, Low Severity → Risk Retention or Loss Control (e.g., minor car scratches - use own funds) - Low Frequency, High Severity → Risk Transfer/Insurance (e.g., death - buy life insurance) - High Frequency, High Severity → Risk Avoidance (e.g., dangerous activities - don’t do them) - Low Frequency, Low Severity → Risk Retention (e.g., losing wallet - accept and budget for replacement)
Matrix for Decision Making:
              HIGH SEVERITY                    LOW SEVERITY
HIGH      |  AVOID or TRANSFER  |         |  CONTROL or RETAIN  |
FREQUENCY |  (Very Risky)       |         |  (Nuisance Risks)   |
----------|---------------------|---------|---------------------|
LOW       |  TRANSFER           |         |  RETAIN             |
FREQUENCY |  (Insurance)        |         |  (Self-Insure)      |
⚠️ EXAM STRATEGY: When evaluating risks in case studies, always consider BOTH frequency AND severity.

Making Informed Decisions:
Key Principles: 1. Not every risk needs to be managed - Prioritize based on impact and probability 2. Resource limitations require prioritization - Focus on most significant risks first 3. Transparent communication with client - Explain which risks are addressed and which are not 4. Document unmitigated risks - Client must understand consequences of gaps
📌 EXAM TIP: If question asks “which risk should be prioritized?”, look for low frequency + high severity = Insurance priority.




Purpose: Select and apply cost-effective risk management techniques.
Four Main Risk Management Techniques (MUST MEMORIZE)










Technique
Description
When to Use
Strategies
Examples




1. Risk Avoidance
Completely avoid the risk
When risk is unacceptable and can be avoided
Elimination, Substitution, Separation, Rational Planning
Don’t engage in dangerous hobbies; Don’t invest in extremely volatile assets; Don’t drive if vision impaired


2. Risk Control (Loss Control)
Reduce likelihood or severity of losses
When risk cannot be avoided but can be managed
Loss Prevention, Loss Reduction, Loss Sharing
Install fire alarm (prevention); Use sprinkler system (reduction); Form business partnership (sharing)


3. Risk Retention
Accept and retain the risk, cover losses yourself
When risk impact is affordable or unavoidable
Active Retention (deliberate), Passive Retention (unintentional)
Maintain emergency fund; Self-insure small losses; Accept deductibles in insurance


4. Risk Transfer
Transfer risk to another party
When risk impact is too high to retain
Non-insurance Transfer, Insurance Transfer
Lease instead of buy equipment; Purchase life insurance; Buy property insurance




Detailed Breakdown of Each Technique:
1. RISK AVOIDANCE
Sub-Strategies:








Strategy
Definition
Example




Elimination
Remove the source of risk entirely
Sell investment property in flood-prone area


Substitution
Replace risky activity with safer alternative
Take train instead of motorcycle for daily commute


Separation
Divide assets/activities to prevent concentrated loss
Store cash in multiple banks (not all in one)


Rational Planning
Careful planning to develop alternatives
Create multiple income streams instead of single source



Malaysian Examples: - Avoid buying property in flood-prone areas (Kelantan, Pahang low-lying areas) - Choose stable job over volatile commission-based work (if risk-averse) - Don’t keep all savings in one bank (separation) - Avoid high-risk investments if approaching retirement
⚠️ EXAM TIP: Avoidance is NOT always the best solution - sometimes it means missing opportunities.

2. RISK CONTROL (LOSS CONTROL)
Three Sub-Techniques:









Sub-Technique
Focus
Mechanism
Example




Loss Prevention
REDUCE FREQUENCY (prevent loss from happening)
Reduce likelihood of risk occurrence
Install alarm system to prevent burglary; Annual medical checkup to detect illness early; Fire drills in office


Loss Reduction
REDUCE SEVERITY (minimize damage when loss occurs)
Minimize impact when loss happens
Install sprinkler system to limit fire damage; Wear seatbelt to reduce injury severity; Keep fire extinguisher in kitchen


Loss Sharing
SPREAD RISK (distribute impact among parties)
Share risk with others
Business partnership (share business risks); Join takaful (Islamic risk-sharing); Form neighborhood watch

Risk

Malaysian-Specific Measure

Sprinkler system, fire extinguisher

Build house on elevated ground
Keep valuables on upper floors, sandbags
Check JPS (Department of Irrigation and Drainage) flood maps before buying property


Car Accident
Defensive driving course, avoid speeding
Airbags, crumple zones, ABS brakes
Install dashcam (common in Malaysia for evidence)


Health Issues
Regular exercise, balanced diet, no smoking
Early health screening, maintain healthy weight
Participate in employer wellness programs, use SOCSO health screening



📌 MEMORY TRICK: - Prevention = Prevent = BEFORE it happens - Reduction = Reduce damage = AFTER it starts

3. RISK RETENTION
Two Types:









Type
Description
When It Happens
Example




Active (Intentional) Retention
Deliberately accept risk, often with planning
Conscious decision with preparation
Keep RM10,000 emergency fund for small medical expenses instead of insuring; Accept insurance deductible


Passive (Unintentional) Retention
Unknowingly retain risk due to lack of awareness
Accidental, no preparation
Unaware of flood risk in new property; Forgot to renew insurance policy



When Risk Retention is Appropriate: 1. Low-severity risks - Impact is affordable (e.g., small scratches on car) 2. High-frequency, low-severity - Insurance would be too expensive (e.g., minor medical consultations) 3. Deliberate cost management - Build emergency fund instead of comprehensive insurance 4. Unavoidable residual risks - After all other techniques applied
Malaysian Examples: - Keep emergency fund of 3-6 months expenses (active retention) - Accept RM500 deductible on car insurance to lower premiums - Self-fund minor medical consultations (under RM200) - Budget for smartphone replacement every 2-3 years
⚠️ EXAM TRAP: Retention ≠ Doing Nothing. Active retention requires planning and reserves.
📌 CRITICAL POINT: Risk retention does NOT change frequency or severity of loss - it only determines HOW you’ll pay for it when it occurs.

title: Chapter 2: Risk Management and Insurance Planning
text:
1. Simon Lim bought a house for RM600,000. Which best describes the pure risk situation? - A. Risk that house may be burnt down in a fire accident ✅ - B. Risk that house value may drop in a downturn - C. Risk of losing money had he invested elsewhere - D. None of the above
Explanation: - A = Pure risk (only loss or no loss, no gain) - B = Speculative risk (property value can go up or down) - C = Opportunity cost/speculative risk Exam Tip: Pure risk = NO possibility of profit, only loss or no loss.

2. Which best defines risk management? - A. Methods used in eliminating all risks faced by an individual - B. Systematic process of dealing with risks faced by an individual ✅ - C. Use of insurance as the sole method to manage risks - D. Process of increasing wealth by reducing risk exposures
Explanation: - A = Wrong - cannot eliminate ALL risks - B = Correct definition - SYSTEMATIC PROCESS of DEALING (not eliminating) - C = Wrong - insurance is only ONE technique - D = Wrong - too narrow, focus is on managing risks not just wealth increase Exam Tip: Word-for-word definition question - memorize “systematic process of dealing with risks”

3. As a financial practitioner, which best describes “risk”? - A. Uncertainty about financial losses from an exposure ✅ - B. Certainty about financial losses from an exposure - C. Exposure to investment risks - D. Exposure to systemic risks
Explanation: - A = Correct - exact definition from Chapter 1 & 2 - B = Wrong - UNCERTAINTY not certainty - C = Wrong - too narrow (only investment) - D = Wrong - too narrow (only systemic) Exam Tip: This is the MODULE 2 definition of risk - know it word-for-word

4. Fill in the blanks: In risk management, _____ is the unpleasant outcome of _____. - A. Loss; risk ✅ - B. Risk; Loss - C. Exposure; loss - D. Loss; business ventures
Explanation: - LOSS is the unpleasant OUTCOME (result) - RISK is what might cause it (the possibility) - Therefore: Loss is outcome OF risk Exam Tip: Think cause and effect - Risk causes Loss

5. There are two forms of loss. _____ is a loss that may happen; _____ is a loss that has precipitated. - A. Occurred loss; loss exposure - B. Loss exposure; occurred loss ✅ - C. Loss event; loss risk - D. Potential loss; actual loss (also acceptable, but B is the terminology used in the text)
Explanation: - Loss EXPOSURE = potential/may happen (future) - Occurred/Precipitated loss = already happened (past) Exam Tip: “Exposure” = future possibility; “Occurred/Precipitated” = already happened

6. Harban Singh (construction worker, high-risk area, large accident policy, single, no dependents, pressed by credit card debt). Insurer turns down proposal. What are likely grounds?

High physical hazard: works in high-risk area
Likely moral hazard: in debts
Possible morale hazard: no dependents


A. i only
B. i & ii
C. None of the above
D. All the above ✅

Explanation: - i = TRUE: High-risk job = physical hazard - ii = TRUE: Debt + large policy = potential fraud (moral hazard) - iii = TRUE: No dependents + large policy = may not care about safety (morale hazard) All three concerns valid - insurer right to decline Exam Tip: Multiple hazards can exist simultaneously in one scenario

7. _____ is a risk that affects the entire economy; _____ is a risk that affects only individuals. - A. Fundamental risk; particular risk ✅ - B. Particular risk; fundamental risk - C. Speculative risk; pure risk - D. Static risk; dynamic risk
Explanation: - Fundamental = affects MANY (economy/community) - Particular = affects FEW (individuals) Exam Tip: “Fundamental” sounds big = affects everyone; “Particular” sounds specific = affects specific person

8. Which are the three main types of pure risk faced by individuals? - A. Group risks, personal risks, and liability risks - B. Insurable risks, property risks, and liability risks - C. Personal risks, property risks, and liability risks ✅ - D. Death risks, disability risks, and illness risks
Explanation: The “PPL” framework: - Personal risks - Property risks - Liability risks Exam Tip: Memorize “PPL” - these are the three categories of pure risks




9. Which pure risk situations fall under personal risks?

Risk of Premature death
Risk of Retirement
Risk of Health Deterioration
Risk of Unemployment


A. i & ii only
B. ii & iii only
C. i, ii & iii only
D. All of the above ✅

Explanation: ALL FOUR are personal risks: - Premature death = affects earning capacity - Retirement = outliving resources - Health deterioration = medical costs + lost income - Unemployment = loss of income Exam Tip: When in doubt with personal risks, usually “all of the above” if all relate to the person’s earning/living capacity

10. (Fire scenario - Mr. Kong’s factory) Property loss can be direct or indirect. Which loss is classified as INDIRECT? - A. Loss of the factory - B. Loss of the special printing machines - C. Loss of profits ✅ - D. Loss of printing materials
Explanation: - Direct loss = Physical damage (factory, machines, materials) - Indirect loss = Consequential/resulting loss (profits, rental income, business interruption) Exam Tip: Direct = You can TOUCH it (physical); Indirect = You CANNOT touch it (consequential)

11. Which of the following is a speculative risk? - A. Risk of house fire - B. Risk of car accident - C. Risk of starting a new business ✅ - D. Risk of critical illness
Explanation: - A, B, D = Pure risks (only loss or no loss) - C = Speculative (business can profit OR lose) Exam Tip: If there’s potential for GAIN/PROFIT = Speculative

12. A young family with a new baby is considering insurance. Which risk should be the HIGHEST priority? - A. Travel insurance - B. Investment-linked policy - C. Life insurance for breadwinner ✅ - D. Car comprehensive insurance
Explanation: Priority for family with dependent: 1. Life insurance (protect dependent if breadwinner dies) = CRITICAL 2. Medical insurance (healthcare for family) 3. Critical illness (protect income) 4. Others (travel, car comprehensive) = lower priority Exam Tip: Dependent child = Life insurance becomes CRITICAL priority




13. Which risk management technique involves completely avoiding the risk? - A. Risk control - B. Risk avoidance ✅ - C. Risk retention - D. Risk transfer
Explanation: Four techniques: - Avoidance = Eliminate completely - Control = Reduce frequency/severity - Retention = Accept and self-pay - Transfer = Shift to others Exam Tip: “Avoid” = “Eliminate” = don’t do the risky activity

14. Installing a fire alarm system is an example of: - A. Risk avoidance - B. Loss prevention ✅ - C. Loss reduction - D. Risk transfer
Explanation: - Fire alarm = Detects early = PREVENTS fire from growing - Fire alarm is part of RISK CONTROL technique - Specifically: LOSS PREVENTION (reduces FREQUENCY) Exam Tip: Prevention = BEFORE/STOP it happening; Reduction = MINIMIZE damage AFTER it starts

15. Installing sprinkler systems in a building is an example of: - A. Risk avoidance - B. Loss prevention - C. Loss reduction ✅ - D. Risk retention
Explanation: - Sprinklers activate AFTER fire starts = don’t prevent, but REDUCE damage - Part of RISK CONTROL - Specifically: LOSS REDUCTION (reduces SEVERITY) Exam Tip: Sprinkler/fire extinguisher = REDUCTION (fire already started, minimize damage)

16. Maintaining an emergency fund to cover unexpected medical expenses is: - A. Risk avoidance - B. Risk control - C. Risk retention ✅ - D. Risk transfer
Explanation: - Emergency fund = Prepare to SELF-PAY when loss occurs - This is RISK RETENTION (accept risk, plan to cover it yourself) - Specifically: ACTIVE retention (deliberate with preparation) Exam Tip: Emergency fund = Retention (you’re retaining/accepting the risk)

17. Purchasing comprehensive motor insurance is an example of: - A. Risk avoidance - B. Risk control - C. Risk retention - D. Risk transfer ✅
Explanation: - Buying insurance = Transfer risk to insurer - Pay premium, insurer pays claims - This is INSURANCE-BASED TRANSFER Exam Tip: Buying insurance = always TRANSFER technique

18. Which technique is most appropriate for LOW frequency, HIGH severity risks? - A. Risk avoidance - B. Risk control - C. Risk retention - D. Risk transfer (Insurance) ✅
Explanation: Frequency-Severity Matrix: - Low frequency + High severity = INSURANCE (transfer) - Rarely happens, but devastating when it does - Examples: Death, major accident, house fire Exam Tip: Low frequency + High severity = classic insurance situation

19. Which technique is most appropriate for HIGH frequency, LOW severity risks? - A. Risk avoidance - B. Risk control - C. Risk retention ✅ - D. Risk transfer
Explanation: - High frequency + Low severity = Self-pay (retention) - Happens often but small impact - Insurance would be too expensive - Examples: Minor car scratches, small medical consultations Exam Tip: High frequency + Low severity = too expensive to insure, better to self-pay

20. Leasing equipment instead of buying it is an example of: - A. Risk avoidance - B. Risk control - C. Non-insurance transfer ✅ - D. Insurance transfer
Explanation: - Leasing = Lessor retains ownership and risks - Risk transferred through CONTRACT, not insurance - This is NON-INSURANCE TRANSFER Exam Tip: Contract-based shift = Non-insurance transfer; Premium-based = Insurance transfer




21. What is the FIRST step in the risk management process? - A. Gather information - B. Establish risk management objectives ✅ - C. Analyze risks - D. Develop a plan
Explanation: 6-Step Process: 1. Establish objectives (define what you want to achieve) 2. Gather information 3. Analyze and evaluate 4. Develop plan 5. Implement 6. Review and revise Exam Tip: Must know goals BEFORE gathering data

22. Which step involves identifying whether risks are high or low priority? - A. Step 2: Gather information - B. Step 3: Analyze and evaluate risks ✅ - C. Step 4: Develop plan - D. Step 5: Implement plan
Explanation: - Step 3 = ANALYZE information to IDENTIFY and EVALUATE (prioritize) risks - Evaluation includes assessing frequency, severity, and priority Exam Tip: “Evaluate” and “prioritize” happen in Step 3 (Analysis)

23. EPF death benefit is classified as: - A. Cash in bank - B. Cash resources ✅ - C. Cash equivalent resources - D. Non-liquid resources
Explanation: Table 2-1 Classifications: - Cash in bank = Immediately accessible - Cash resources = Received in cash on death within reasonable time (EPF, insurance, gratuities) - Cash equivalent = Can convert to cash (unit trusts, shares) - Non-liquid = Hard to convert (property) Exam Tip: EPF death benefit = Cash Resources (NOT cash in bank - needs processing time)

24. Listed shares on Bursa Malaysia are classified as: - A. Cash in bank - B. Cash resources - C. Cash equivalent resources ✅ - D. Non-liquid resources
Explanation: - Listed shares = Can sell on exchange = Convert to cash easily - Not immediate like bank account - Not cash received on death - Therefore: CASH EQUIVALENT Exam Tip: Shares, unit trusts, bonds = Cash Equivalent (can liquidate fairly easily)

25. Which is NOT a step in the risk management process? - A. Gather information for analysis - B. Develop a risk management plan - C. Eliminate all identified risks ✅ - D. Review, monitor, and revise the plan
Explanation: - Cannot eliminate ALL risks (unrealistic) - Risk management = MANAGE risks (not eliminate all) - Options A, B, D are actual steps in the 6-step process Exam Tip: “Eliminate all risks” = red flag wrong answer

26. How often should a risk management plan be reviewed? - A. Only when a claim is made - B. Once every 5 years - C. Annually and when life circumstances change ✅ - D. Never - set it and forget it
Explanation: Review triggers: - Annual review (comprehensive) - Major life changes (marriage, child, job change) - Financial changes (promotion, inheritance) - Asset acquisition (house, car) Exam Tip: Risk management is CONTINUOUS, not one-time




27. A retiree couple on fixed income is choosing medical insurance. They should prioritize: - A. Lowest premium regardless of deductible - B. Highest deductible to save on premium - C. Lower deductible even if premium is higher ✅ - D. No insurance - use government hospitals
Explanation: - Fixed income = predictable expenses important - Lower deductible = lower out-of-pocket when claim - Higher premium = predictable monthly cost - Better than high deductible with unpredictable large out-of-pocket Exam Tip: Fixed income + retiree = prefer predictable costs = lower deductible

28. A young couple with first child and mortgage should prioritize: - A. Investment-linked policy for returns - B. Term life insurance covering mortgage and family expenses ✅ - C. Saving for child’s university - D. Comprehensive motor insurance
Explanation: Priority ranking: 1. Life insurance (protect dependent and mortgage) = CRITICAL 2. Medical insurance (family healthcare) 3. Critical illness (income protection) 4. Other priorities Exam Tip: New dependent + mortgage = Life insurance becomes #1 priority

29. A property investor concerned about tenant defaults should use: - A. Risk avoidance (don’t rent out) - B. Risk transfer (insurance for tenant defaults) - C. Risk control (background checks) + Retention (emergency fund) ✅ - D. Only risk retention
Explanation: - Tenant default = moderate frequency, moderate severity - CONTROL: Background checks reduce likelihood - RETENTION: Emergency fund to cover temporary loss - Combination approach most appropriate Exam Tip: Moderate risks often need COMBINATION of techniques

30. Which statement about risk management is TRUE? - A. All identified risks must be insured - B. Risk management is a one-time process - C. Risk retention means doing nothing about the risk - D. Risk management techniques can be used in combination ✅
Explanation: - A = False (not all risks need insurance) - B = False (continuous process - Step 6 is ongoing review) - C = False (active retention involves planning and reserves) - D = TRUE (often use multiple techniques together) Exam Tip: Real-world risk management = combination of techniques, not single approach

title: Chapter 3: Insurance Needs Analysis
text:
Exam Weight: 20-25% (HIGHEST weighted chapter - critical for exam success)
Study Time: 12-15 hours





Master TWO life insurance valuation methods (HLV & Capital Needs)
Calculate coverage for death, disability, critical illness, retirement, education
Distinguish between Capital Liquidation vs. Capital Conservation
Apply Total Needs vs. Single Needs approach
Analyze business-related insurance needs







FOUR Key Functions: 1. Risk Protection - Guard against immediate financial risks 2. Goal Achievement - Secure long-term financial aspirations 3. Legacy Planning - Ensure intergenerational wealth transfer (critical in Malaysia) 4. Estate Liquidity - Provide funds for settlement of obligations
⚠️ EXAM ALERT: Malaysia has NO estate taxes, but insurance still crucial for: - Settlement of debts - Legal fees - Providing liquidity (avoid forced asset sale) - Equal distribution among heirs













Risk Type
Definition
Insurance Solution
Exam Frequency




Mortality Risk
Premature death
Life insurance
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐


Health Risk
Illness/medical expenses
Medical insurance, critical illness
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐


Disability Risk
Unable to work
Disability income insurance
⭐⭐⭐⭐

Life insurance for estate planning

📌 Memory Aid - “MHDDLE”: Mortality, Health, Disability, Dependency, Longevity, Education, Legacy







Concept: Present value of future income that would be lost if person dies.
Formula:
HLV = A × (1 + r) × [(1 - (1 + r)^-n) / r]

Where:
A = Annual income for dependents
r = Interest rate (discount rate)
n = Years to retirement
CRITICAL: Set calculator to BEGIN mode (income received at start of year)
Example 3-1: Mr. Aziz - Age: 30, Retirement: 55 (n = 25 years) - Annual income: RM60,000 - Income for dependents: RM40,000 (2/3 of income) - Interest rate: 6%
Calculator Steps: 1. Set to BEGIN mode 2. n = 25 3. i = 6 4. PMT = 40,000 5. Compute PV = RM542,014.30
Interpretation: RM542,014.30 is the total present value of income lost if Mr. Aziz dies prematurely.

Limitations of HLV (MUST KNOW for exam):







Limitation
Reality




❌ Assumes salary unchanged
✅ Salary typically increases


❌ Assumes constant interest rate
✅ Rates fluctuate


❌ Ignores inflation
✅ Inflation erodes purchasing power


❌ Ignores lifestyle changes
✅ Needs change (marriage, children)


❌ Assumes zero value at retirement
✅ May have post-retirement income


❌ HLV decreases as age increases
✅ Actually may increase with salary growth



⚠️ EXAM TRAP: Questions may present scenario where HLV seems to decrease with age, but ask you to identify this as a limitation.
📌 EXAM TIP: Despite limitations, HLV is “a good method to get started - at least there’s a numerical value to focus on with client.”




Concept: Calculate total capital needed to meet ALL financial needs of dependents.
TWO Sub-Methods:


Concept: Both principal AND interest consumed over time. Capital eventually depleted.
Formula:
Capital Needed = PV of income needs (using PVIFA)

Where income is consumed over fixed period
Example: RM60,000 annual income, 7 years, 6% interest
Calculator Steps: 1. Set to BEGIN mode 2. n = 7 3. i = 6 4. PMT = 60,000 5. Compute PV = RM374,457
Interpretation: RM374,457 needed if capital will be fully used up over 7 years.




Concept: Only interest consumed. Principal preserved intact for heirs.
Formula:
Capital Needed = Annual Income Needed / Interest Rate

Capital Needed = A / r
Example: RM60,000 annual income, 6% interest
Capital Needed = RM60,000 / 0.06 = RM1,000,000
Interpretation: RM1,000,000 invested at 6% generates RM60,000 annually FOREVER, principal intact.

Comparison Table (CRITICAL for Exam):








Aspect
Capital Liquidation
Capital Conservation




Principal
Consumed with interest
Preserved (not touched)


Duration
Fixed period only
Indefinite (perpetuity)


Amount Needed
Lower
Higher (always more)


Purpose
Income for dependents only
Income + Legacy for heirs


Formula
PVIFA calculation
A / r


Example (RM60k, 6%)
RM374,457 (7 years)
RM1,000,000 (forever)



⚠️ EXAM ALERT: Capital Conservation ALWAYS requires MORE capital than Liquidation.
📌 EXAM PATTERN: Questions often ask “which requires more capital?” Answer: Conservation





Total Life Insurance Need Formula:
Total Need = [Cash Needs + Income Replacement + Legacy Needs] - Available Resources

Where:
Cash Needs = Debts + Funeral + Final expenses
Income Replacement = Liquidation OR Conservation amount
Legacy Needs = Charitable giving, inheritance
Available Resources = Cash, EPF, existing insurance, investments
Example 3-4: Raymond Wong
Given: - Cash/equivalent resources: RM300,000 - Annual income needs: RM60,000 for 5 years - Interest rate: 6% - Cash needs at death: RM200,000 - Legacy (charity): RM80,000
Method 1: Capital Liquidation
Income Replacement (5 years, 6%):
PV = RM267,908 (calculator: BEGIN mode, n=5, i=6, PMT=60,000)

Total Need = [200,000 + 267,908 + 80,000] - 300,000
          = 547,908 - 300,000
          = RM247,908 (DEFICIENCY)
Method 2: Capital Conservation
Income Replacement (perpetual, 6%):
Capital = 60,000 / 0.06 = RM1,000,000

Total Need = [200,000 + 1,000,000 + 80,000] - 300,000
          = 1,280,000 - 300,000
          = RM980,000 (DEFICIENCY)
⚠️ EXAM TIP: Deficiency = Insurance amount to buy. If negative (surplus), no insurance needed for that component.





Growing Need in Malaysia: - Rising medical costs (10-15% annual increase) - Common critical illnesses: Cancer, heart disease, stroke, kidney failure - Private hospital costs: RM50,000-300,000+ per major treatment

Component
Calculation
Malaysian Context




Immediate Costs
Hospital, surgery, initial treatment
RM50,000-100,000 typical


Long-term Costs
Follow-up, rehabilitation, modifications
RM20,000+ annually


Income Replacement
Lost income during recovery
(Monthly income × Recovery months)


Inflation Adjustment
Apply medical inflation rate
Use 10-15% (higher than general inflation)


Existing Coverage
Deduct current insurance/savings
Company medical, personal savings


Lifestyle Costs
Home care, dependent support
RM10,000-30,000 annually



Example 3-5: Abdullah Family
Immediate medical: RM50,000
Ongoing treatment (annual): RM20,000
Income replacement (2 years): RM200,000 (RM100k × 2)
Lifestyle/care: RM10,000 annually
Less: Existing coverage: (RM30,000)
Less: Emergency savings: (RM50,000)

Total Critical Illness Need = RM200,000+
⚠️ EXAM TIP: Questions may ask to calculate total need - add all costs, subtract existing resources.




Formula (Capital Conservation):
Capital Needed = Annual Income to Replace / Interest Rate

Capital = A / r
Example: - Annual income to replace: RM72,000 - Interest rate: 7% - Capital Needed = 72,000 / 0.07 = RM1,028,571
Important Considerations: - Disability often more financially devastating than death (ongoing costs) - May need lifetime coverage (vs. death which is one-time) - Include medical costs + income replacement - Social Security (SOCSO) provides some disability coverage but often insufficient




Approach: Calculate future cost and work backwards to present value.
Process: 1. Estimate total education cost (university 4 years) 2. Apply education inflation (typically 6-8% in Malaysia) 3. Calculate lump sum needed TODAY to fund future cost 4. OR calculate annual savings needed
Malaysian Context: - Local public university: RM30,000-50,000 total - Local private university: RM100,000-200,000 total - Overseas (UK/US): RM400,000-800,000 total
Solutions: - Education insurance plans - SSPN (National Education Savings Scheme) - Life insurance with education rider - Investment-linked plans




Key Risks for Business Owners:








Risk
Impact
Insurance Solution




Death of Owner

Buy-sell agreement funded by life insurance


Disability of Owner
Business operations disrupted
Disability income, key person insurance


Key Person Loss

Key man insurance


Property Damage

Business property, interruption insurance


Employee Benefits
Retirement, death gratuity obligations
Group insurance, retirement plans



Buy-Sell Agreement Funding: - Partners insure each other - Upon death, proceeds buy deceased’s share - Ensures smooth transition, fair value for heirs




Critical Distinction:








Approach
Scenario
Calculation




Single Needs
Single individual, no dependents
Own debts + final expenses + personal goals


Total Needs
Married with dependents
Both spouses’ income replacement + family obligations



Married Couples - TWO Approaches:
Option 1: Single Need Per Person - Calculate husband’s need independently - Calculate wife’s need independently - Buy separate policies
Option 2: Total Combined Need - Calculate total family need if breadwinner dies - May result in different coverage amounts - Often more accurate for joint expenses
⚠️ EXAM SCENARIO: Question presents married couple, asks for insurance calculation. - If asks for “husband’s coverage” = Single need for husband - If asks for “family protection” = Total needs approach




MUST MEMORIZE:
1. Human Life Value (BEGIN mode)
HLV = A × (1+r) × [(1-(1+r)^-n)/r]
or use PV function with BEGIN mode
2. Capital Conservation
Capital = Annual Income / Interest Rate
Capital = A / r
3. Capital Liquidation
Use PVIFA / PV calculation with END or BEGIN mode
4. Total Insurance Need
Need = [Cash + Income Replacement + Legacy] - Resources
5. Income Replacement (Disability)
Capital = Annual Income × (1 - Tax Rate) / Interest Rate






1. Premature death in Malaysia is typically defined as death before age: - A. 50 - B. 55 ✅ - C. 60 - D. 65
Exam Tip: Standard retirement age in Malaysia is 55.

2. The Human Life Value approach calculates: - A. Total assets of the deceased - B. Present value of future income for dependents ✅ - C. Future value of current assets - D. Replacement cost of the person
Exam Tip: HLV = PV of income stream lost.

3. Which is a limitation of the HLV method? - A. Too complex to calculate - B. Assumes salary remains constant ✅ - C. Requires medical examination - D. Cannot be used for self-employed
Exam Tip: Know all 5-6 limitations by heart.

4. In HLV calculation, the financial calculator should be set to: - A. END mode - B. BEGIN mode ✅ - C. Either mode - D. Continuous compounding mode
Exam Tip: BEGIN mode because income received at start of each year.

5. Capital Conservation approach differs from Liquidation because: - A. It uses lower interest rate - B. Principal is preserved, not consumed ✅ - C. It has shorter time period - D. It ignores inflation
Exam Tip: “Conservation” = “Conserve the principal”

6. Which approach requires MORE capital? - A. Capital Liquidation - B. Capital Conservation ✅ - C. Both require same amount - D. Depends on interest rate
Exam Tip: Conservation ALWAYS requires more (principal preserved).

7. The formula Capital = A/r is used for: - A. Human Life Value - B. Capital Liquidation - C. Capital Conservation ✅ - D. Education funding
Exam Tip: Simple perpetuity formula = Conservation approach.

8. If annual income need is RM60,000 and interest rate is 6%, capital conservation requires: - A. RM360,000 - B. RM600,000 - C. RM1,000,000 ✅ - D. RM1,200,000
Calculation: 60,000 / 0.06 = 1,000,000

9. Legacy planning in Malaysia focuses on: - A. Minimizing estate taxes - B. Ensuring smooth wealth transfer ✅ - C. Avoiding insurance - D. Reducing liabilities
Exam Tip: Malaysia has NO estate tax, but smooth transfer still critical.

10. Critical illness insurance inflation rate in Malaysia is typically: - A. 3-5% - B. 6-8% - C. 10-15% ✅ - D. 20-25%
Exam Tip: Medical inflation higher than general inflation.




11. Mr. Ali, age 30, retires at 55. Annual income for dependents: RM50,000. Interest: 5%. HLV (approx): - A. RM500,000 - B. RM710,000 ✅ - C. RM850,000 - D. RM1,000,000
Calculation: n=25, i=5, PMT=50,000, BEGIN mode, PV ≈ 710,000

12. Capital liquidation for RM80,000 annual income, 6 years, 7% interest (approx): - A. RM420,000 ✅ - B. RM480,000 - C. RM540,000 - D. RM600,000
Calculation: n=6, i=7, PMT=80,000, BEGIN mode, PV ≈ 420,000

13. Capital conservation for RM90,000 annual income, 6% interest: - A. RM1,200,000 - B. RM1,350,000 - C. RM1,500,000 ✅ - D. RM1,800,000
Calculation: 90,000 / 0.06 = 1,500,000

14. Total need: Cash RM100k, Income RM500k, Legacy RM50k. Resources: RM200k. Deficiency: - A. RM350,000 - B. RM400,000 - C. RM450,000 ✅ - D. RM650,000
Calculation: (100+500+50) - 200 = 450,000

15. Disability income replacement: RM72,000 annually, 8% interest. Capital needed: - A. RM800,000 - B. RM850,000 - C. RM900,000 ✅ - D. RM950,000
Calculation: 72,000 / 0.08 = 900,000

16. Critical illness immediate cost RM60k, ongoing RM25k annually for 2 years, income loss RM150k. Existing coverage RM40k. Total need: - A. RM195,000 - B. RM220,000 ✅ - C. RM260,000 - D. RM300,000
Calculation: 60,000 + (25,000×2) + 150,000 - 40,000 = 220,000

17. If HLV at age 30 is RM800k, at age 35 with higher salary, HLV is: - A. Definitely lower (less years to retirement) - B. Could be higher despite fewer years ✅ - C. Must be exactly RM800k - D. Cannot calculate
Exam Tip: This tests understanding of HLV limitation - can increase with salary growth.

18. Annual income RM100k, 60% for dependents, 20 years to retirement, 6% interest. HLV (approx): - A. RM689,000 ✅ - B. RM720,000 - C. RM850,000 - D. RM1,000,000
Calculation: PMT = 60,000 (60% of 100k), n=20, i=6, BEGIN, PV ≈ 689,000

19. Conservation vs Liquidation (same income, same rate). Conservation is approx: - A. 50% more - B. Same amount - C. 100-200% more - D. 300-400% more ✅
Exam Tip: Conservation typically 3-4x liquidation amount (depends on years).

20. Education funding: RM200k needed in 10 years, 5% interest. Lump sum needed today (approx): - A. RM122,000 ✅ - B. RM150,000 - C. RM175,000 - D. RM200,000
Calculation: FV=200,000, n=10, i=5, PV ≈ 122,782




21. A single person with no dependents needs coverage for: - A. Income replacement for dependents - B. Own debts and final expenses ✅ - C. Children’s education - D. Spouse’s retirement
Exam Tip: Single, no dependents = only own obligations.

22. For married couple with 2 children, MOST critical coverage is: - A. Breadwinner’s life insurance ✅ - B. Car insurance - C. Travel insurance - D. Investment-linked plan
Exam Tip: Dependents = Life insurance priority #1.

23. Capital conservation approach is preferred when: - A. Client wants to leave inheritance ✅ - B. Client has limited budget - C. Coverage is temporary need - D. Interest rates are low
Exam Tip: Conservation = preserve capital for heirs.

24. Business buy-sell agreement is typically funded by: - A. Bank loans - B. Life insurance on partners ✅ - C. Business savings - D. Government grants
Exam Tip: Cross-purchase insurance on partners.

25. Key person insurance protects against: - A. Employee theft - B. Loss of critical employee ✅ - C. Property damage - D. Market competition
Exam Tip: Compensates business for loss of key employee.

26. For critical illness, which cost typically HIGHEST? - A. Funeral expenses - B. Income replacement during recovery ✅ - C. Immediate medical treatment - D. Insurance premiums
Exam Tip: Lost income over months/years > one-time medical bill.

27. EPF death benefit is considered: - A. Cash in bank - B. Cash resources ✅ - C. Cash equivalent - D. Non-liquid asset
Exam Tip: Received in cash on death = Cash Resources (from Chapter 2 Table 2-1).

28. SOCSO provides coverage for: - A. Retirement only - B. Disability and employment injury ✅ - C. Critical illness only - D. Education funding
Exam Tip: Employment injury, disability, survivors’ benefits.

29. In calculating total needs for married couple, if both work: - A. Only consider higher earner - B. Calculate each spouse’s contribution ✅ - C. Ignore lower earner - D. Use average of both incomes
Exam Tip: Both incomes matter for family lifestyle.

30. Legacy planning through insurance is important in Malaysia because: - A. High estate taxes - B. Provides liquidity and smooth transfer ✅ - C. Required by law - D. Reduces family conflict (partially true, but B is primary reason)
Exam Tip: No estate tax, but liquidity and smooth transfer crucial.

Section B: 11-B, 12-A, 13-C, 14-C, 15-C, 16-B, 17-B, 18-A, 19-D, 20-A
Section C: 21-B, 22-A, 23-A, 24-B, 25-B, 26-B, 27-B, 28-B, 29-B, 30-B

Week 3: Understand Concepts - [ ] Know all HLV limitations - [ ] Understand Conservation vs Liquidation differences - [ ] Learn 7 personal risk types - [ ] Study business insurance needs
Week 4: Application - [ ] Complete all 30 self-assessment questions - [ ] Create own calculation scenarios - [ ] Practice total needs calculation - [ ] Review Malaysian context (no estate tax, EPF, SOCSO)

“BEGIN” Mode for HLV: - Because income received at BEGINning of year
“Conservation = Conserve Principal”: - Capital CONSERVation = CONSERVE the capital
“A / R” for Conservation: - Annual income / Rate = Capital needed

Solutions: - Education insurance plans - SSPN (National Education Savings Scheme) - Life insurance with education rider - Investment-linked plans

title: Chapter 3: Insurance Needs Analysis
text:
MUST MEMORIZE:
1. Human Life Value (BEGIN mode)
HLV = A × (1+r) × [(1-(1+r)^-n)/r]
or use PV function with BEGIN mode
2. Capital Conservation
Capital = Annual Income / Interest Rate
Capital = A / r
3. Capital Liquidation
Use PVIFA / PV calculation with END or BEGIN mode
4. Total Insurance Need
Need = [Cash + Income Replacement + Legacy] - Resources
5. Income Replacement (Disability)

title: Chapter 3: Insurance Needs Analysis
text:
1. Premature death in Malaysia is typically defined as death before age: - A. 50 - B. 55 ✅ - C. 60 - D. 65
Exam Tip: Standard retirement age in Malaysia is 55.

2. The Human Life Value approach calculates: - A. Total assets of the deceased - B. Present value of future income for dependents ✅ - C. Future value of current assets - D. Replacement cost of the person
Exam Tip: HLV = PV of income stream lost.

3. Which is a limitation of the HLV method? - A. Too complex to calculate - B. Assumes salary remains constant ✅ - C. Requires medical examination - D. Cannot be used for self-employed
Exam Tip: Know all 5-6 limitations by heart.

4. In HLV calculation, the financial calculator should be set to: - A. END mode - B. BEGIN mode ✅ - C. Either mode - D. Continuous compounding mode
Exam Tip: BEGIN mode because income received at start of each year.

5. Capital Conservation approach differs from Liquidation because: - A. It uses lower interest rate - B. Principal is preserved, not consumed ✅ - C. It has shorter time period - D. It ignores inflation
Exam Tip: “Conservation” = “Conserve the principal”

6. Which approach requires MORE capital? - A. Capital Liquidation - B. Capital Conservation ✅ - C. Both require same amount - D. Depends on interest rate
Exam Tip: Conservation ALWAYS requires more (principal preserved).

7. The formula Capital = A/r is used for: - A. Human Life Value - B. Capital Liquidation - C. Capital Conservation ✅ - D. Education funding
Exam Tip: Simple perpetuity formula = Conservation approach.

8. If annual income need is RM60,000 and interest rate is 6%, capital conservation requires: - A. RM360,000 - B. RM600,000 - C. RM1,000,000 ✅ - D. RM1,200,000
Calculation: 60,000 / 0.06 = 1,000,000

9. Legacy planning in Malaysia focuses on: - A. Minimizing estate taxes - B. Ensuring smooth wealth transfer ✅ - C. Avoiding insurance - D. Reducing liabilities
Exam Tip: Malaysia has NO estate tax, but smooth transfer still critical.

10. Critical illness insurance inflation rate in Malaysia is typically: - A. 3-5% - B. 6-8% - C. 10-15% ✅ - D. 20-25%
Exam Tip: Medical inflation higher than general inflation.




11. Mr. Ali, age 30, retires at 55. Annual income for dependents: RM50,000. Interest: 5%. HLV (approx): - A. RM500,000 - B. RM710,000 ✅ - C. RM850,000 - D. RM1,000,000
Calculation: n=25, i=5, PMT=50,000, BEGIN mode, PV ≈ 710,000

12. Capital liquidation for RM80,000 annual income, 6 years, 7% interest (approx): - A. RM420,000 ✅ - B. RM480,000 - C. RM540,000 - D. RM600,000
Calculation: n=6, i=7, PMT=80,000, BEGIN mode, PV ≈ 420,000

13. Capital conservation for RM90,000 annual income, 6% interest: - A. RM1,200,000 - B. RM1,350,000 - C. RM1,500,000 ✅ - D. RM1,800,000
Calculation: 90,000 / 0.06 = 1,500,000

14. Total need: Cash RM100k, Income RM500k, Legacy RM50k. Resources: RM200k. Deficiency: - A. RM350,000 - B. RM400,000 - C. RM450,000 ✅ - D. RM650,000
Calculation: (100+500+50) - 200 = 450,000

15. Disability income replacement: RM72,000 annually, 8% interest. Capital needed: - A. RM800,000 - B. RM850,000 - C. RM900,000 ✅ - D. RM950,000
Calculation: 72,000 / 0.08 = 900,000

16. Critical illness immediate cost RM60k, ongoing RM25k annually for 2 years, income loss RM150k. Existing coverage RM40k. Total need: - A. RM195,000 - B. RM220,000 ✅ - C. RM260,000 - D. RM300,000
Calculation: 60,000 + (25,000×2) + 150,000 - 40,000 = 220,000

17. If HLV at age 30 is RM800k, at age 35 with higher salary, HLV is: - A. Definitely lower (less years to retirement) - B. Could be higher despite fewer years ✅ - C. Must be exactly RM800k - D. Cannot calculate
Exam Tip: This tests understanding of HLV limitation - can increase with salary growth.

18. Annual income RM100k, 60% for dependents, 20 years to retirement, 6% interest. HLV (approx): - A. RM689,000 ✅ - B. RM720,000 - C. RM850,000 - D. RM1,000,000
Calculation: PMT = 60,000 (60% of 100k), n=20, i=6, BEGIN, PV ≈ 689,000

19. Conservation vs Liquidation (same income, same rate). Conservation is approx: - A. 50% more - B. Same amount - C. 100-200% more - D. 300-400% more ✅
Exam Tip: Conservation typically 3-4x liquidation amount (depends on years).

20. Education funding: RM200k needed in 10 years, 5% interest. Lump sum needed today (approx): - A. RM122,000 ✅ - B. RM150,000 - C. RM175,000 - D. RM200,000
Calculation: FV=200,000, n=10, i=5, PV ≈ 122,782




21. A single person with no dependents needs coverage for: - A. Income replacement for dependents - B. Own debts and final expenses ✅ - C. Children’s education - D. Spouse’s retirement
Exam Tip: Single, no dependents = only own obligations.

22. For married couple with 2 children, MOST critical coverage is: - A. Breadwinner’s life insurance ✅ - B. Car insurance - C. Travel insurance - D. Investment-linked plan
Exam Tip: Dependents = Life insurance priority #1.

23. Capital conservation approach is preferred when: - A. Client wants to leave inheritance ✅ - B. Client has limited budget - C. Coverage is temporary need - D. Interest rates are low
Exam Tip: Conservation = preserve capital for heirs.

24. Business buy-sell agreement is typically funded by: - A. Bank loans - B. Life insurance on partners ✅ - C. Business savings - D. Government grants
Exam Tip: Cross-purchase insurance on partners.

25. Key person insurance protects against: - A. Employee theft - B. Loss of critical employee ✅ - C. Property damage - D. Market competition
Exam Tip: Compensates business for loss of key employee.

26. For critical illness, which cost typically HIGHEST? - A. Funeral expenses - B. Income replacement during recovery ✅ - C. Immediate medical treatment - D. Insurance premiums
Exam Tip: Lost income over months/years > one-time medical bill.

27. EPF death benefit is considered: - A. Cash in bank - B. Cash resources ✅ - C. Cash equivalent - D. Non-liquid asset
Exam Tip: Received in cash on death = Cash Resources (from Chapter 2 Table 2-1).

28. SOCSO provides coverage for: - A. Retirement only - B. Disability and employment injury ✅ - C. Critical illness only - D. Education funding
Exam Tip: Employment injury, disability, survivors’ benefits.

29. In calculating total needs for married couple, if both work: - A. Only consider higher earner - B. Calculate each spouse’s contribution ✅ - C. Ignore lower earner - D. Use average of both incomes
Exam Tip: Both incomes matter for family lifestyle.

30. Legacy planning through insurance is important in Malaysia because: - A. High estate taxes - B. Provides liquidity and smooth transfer ✅ - C. Required by law - D. Reduces family conflict (partially true, but B is primary reason)
Exam Tip: No estate tax, but liquidity and smooth transfer crucial.

title: Chapter 6: Annuities
text:
Annuities are the OPPOSITE of life insurance - they protect against living TOO LONG, not dying too soon. This chapter covers retirement income products that convert lump sums into steady income streams.
Exam Weight: 8-10% of total exam
Study Time Recommendation: 6-8 hours




By the end of this chapter, you must be able to:

Comprehend the role of annuities in retirement planning (longevity risk)
Distinguish between types of annuities (fixed vs variable, immediate vs deferred, etc.)
Understand the two phases of annuities (accumulation vs liquidation)
Evaluate tax treatment of annuities in Malaysia
Analyze suitability of annuities for different demographics
Compare annuities with other retirement products







The Core Problem: Risk of “Living Too Long” and outliving savings
Solution: Annuities = systematic liquidation of capital to provide lifetime income

🔑 KEY CONCEPT - The Opposite of Life Insurance:









Product
Protects Against
Focus
Payment Direction




Life Insurance
Dying TOO SOON (premature death)
Mortality risk
You pay premiums → Insurer pays beneficiaries on death


Annuity
Living TOO LONG (outliving savings)
Longevity risk
You pay lump sum → Insurer pays you periodic income



📌 EXAM TIP: Annuity = REVERSE life insurance. Life insurance converts small payments into large sum; annuity converts large sum into small periodic payments.

Malaysian Context:








Status
Details
Reason




Current Popularity
LOW - not actively promoted
Limited public awareness


Future Trend
Expected to GROW
Tax changes, aging population, EPF concerns


Global Comparison
USA, Japan = Very popular
Aging population, inflation concerns, retirement needs



⚠️ EXAM ALERT: While not currently popular in Malaysia, annuities are expected to become more important as population ages.

📝 EXAM QUESTION 1 (Links to Section 6.0 - Introduction)
Question: “Which is most suited product for client’s retirement years? A. Whole life policy with profits B. Endowment policy maturing at age 60 C. A life annuity ✅ D. All of the above”
Answer: C (A life annuity)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: For RETIREMENT INCOME needs, annuity is the BEST solution!
WHY ANNUITY IS BEST: - ✅ Provides LIFETIME income (can’t outlive it) - ✅ Regular payments for living expenses - ✅ Specifically designed for retirement years - ✅ Protects against longevity risk
WHY OTHERS ARE LESS SUITABLE: - A. Whole Life: Pays on DEATH, not for retirement income - Benefit goes to beneficiaries, not you - Doesn’t provide regular income stream

B. Endowment (age 60): ONE-TIME lump sum at maturity

What if you live to 90? (30 more years!)
Must manage lump sum yourself
Can outlive the money


KEYWORDS: - “Retirement years” = Need INCOME ✅ - “Most suited” = Annuity = PURPOSE-BUILT for retirement ✅ - “Life annuity” = LIFETIME payments ✅
MEMORY TIP:
RETIREMENT = Need INCOME (not lump sum)
INCOME for LIFE = ANNUITY




Definition: Contract with insurer where insurer makes periodic payments to annuitant, starting immediately or future date, for lifetime or specified term.
Formal Definition (memorize): > “An annuity is a contract with an insurance company providing periodic payments to the annuitant for a lifetime or specified term, serving as reverse life insurance focusing on longevity risk.”




Primary Function: Mitigate LONGEVITY RISK
What is Longevity Risk? - Risk of outliving your assets - Living longer than expected - Running out of money in old age
How Annuities Help: - Convert lump sum → steady income stream - Provide financial security - Give peace of mind (guaranteed income) - Can’t outlive payments (if lifetime annuity)

📝 EXAM QUESTION 2 (Links to Section 6.1.a - Function)
Question: “What is basic function of annuity? A. To provide lifetime replacement or supplementary income immediately ✅ B. To provide inflation adjusted living during retirement C. To protect against medical expenses in old age D. To guarantee high income and enjoyable retirement”
Answer: A (Provide lifetime replacement/supplementary income)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Basic function = INCOME PROVISION, nothing fancy!
ANALYSIS OF EACH OPTION:
A ✅ CORRECT - The BASIC function: - “Lifetime” = Core feature (longevity protection) - “Replacement or supplementary” = Can replace work income OR supplement other income - “Immediately” = For immediate annuities (can also be deferred) - This is the FUNDAMENTAL purpose
B ❌ WRONG - Too specific: - Inflation adjustment is OPTIONAL feature, not basic function - Not all annuities are inflation-adjusted - This is a NICE-TO-HAVE, not core purpose
C ❌ WRONG - Wrong product! - Medical expenses = HEALTH INSURANCE function - Annuities = INCOME, not medical coverage - Completely different purpose
D ❌ WRONG - Too optimistic/unrealistic: - “Guarantee high income” = FALSE (depends on amount invested) - “Enjoyable retirement” = Subjective, not insurance function - Overpromises what annuity can do
KEYWORDS: - “Basic function” = CORE purpose (income provision) - “Lifetime” = LONGEVITY protection - “Replacement/supplementary” = INCOME focus
EXAM TIP: Don’t be distracted by fancy features (inflation, medical, “enjoyable”). Basic function = PROVIDE INCOME.




TWO PHASES (CRITICAL to understand):
ANNUITY LIFE CYCLE

Phase 1: ACCUMULATION → Phase 2: LIQUIDATION
(Building)              (Paying Out)



Definition: Period of capital investment into annuity.
What Happens:








Activity
Description
Result




Premium Payment
Annuity holder pays premiums
Fund grows


Payment Type
Lump-sum OR periodic
Flexibility


Interest Accrual
Invested amount earns interest
Principal increases


Investment Growth
Based on underlying investment strategy
Fund accumulation



Example:
Age 30-60 (30 years accumulation):
Monthly premium: RM500
Total paid: RM500 × 12 × 30 = RM180,000
With 5% annual return: Fund grows to ~RM416,000
📌 EXAM TIP: Accumulation phase = PAY IN period (you’re building the fund).




Definition: Period where accumulated funds distributed back to annuitant.
What Happens:








Activity
Description
Result




Payment Commencement
Regular payments begin
Income stream starts


Payment Structure
Fixed period OR lifetime
Depends on annuity type


Fund Depletion
Systematic withdrawal of capital
Provides income


Longevity Protection
Payments continue (lifetime annuity)
Can’t outlive



Example:
Age 60+ (liquidation begins):
Accumulated fund: RM416,000
Monthly payment: RM3,000 (calculated actuarially)
Duration: Lifetime (even if live to 100+)
If live 30 years: Receive RM3,000 × 12 × 30 = RM1,080,000!
(Much more than paid in due to pooling and mortality credits)
📌 EXAM TIP: Liquidation phase = PAY OUT period (insurer pays you income).

Comparison Table:



Aspect
Accumulation Phase
Liquidation Phase




Direction
Money IN (you → insurer)
Money OUT (insurer → you)


Duration
Variable (years/decades)
Fixed period OR lifetime


Purpose
Build capital
Provide income


Who Benefits
Future you
Current you


Risk
Investment risk
Longevity risk covered








FIVE Classification Bases (memorize):

Number of Lives Covered

Single life
Multiple lives (e.g., husband & wife)

Method of Premium Payment

Single premium
Periodic premiums

Timing of Income Payments

Immediate (starts now)
Deferred (starts later)

Method of Disposing Proceeds

Immediate distribution
Deferred to specific date
Payments to certain age (e.g., age 65)

Denomination of Benefits

Various currencies (USD, RM, etc.)


📌 EXAM TIP: These classifications form the basis for understanding different annuity types.




SIX Main Type Distinctions:
ANNUITY TYPES
├── 1. Fixed-Sum vs Variable
├── 2. Immediate vs Deferred
├── 3. Individual vs Group
├── 4. Single Payment vs Instalment
├── 5. Single Life vs Joint Life
└── 6. Pure Life vs Annuity Certain



Fixed-Sum (Fixed) Annuity:








Feature
Description
Example




Payment Amount
FIXED, predetermined
RM2,000/month (never changes)


Guarantee
Amount guaranteed
Certainty of income


Inflation Risk
HIGH - purchasing power erodes
RM2,000 today ≠ RM2,000 in 20 years


Investment Risk
LOW - insurer bears risk
Safe but inflexible


Suitability
Conservative, risk-averse
Those wanting certainty



Example:
Fixed Annuity: RM2,000/month
Year 1: RM2,000 (buys 1,000 eggs @ RM2 each)
Year 20: RM2,000 (inflation: eggs now RM4, buys only 500 eggs)
Result: Same nominal amount, LESS real purchasing power
⚠️ EXAM ALERT: Fixed annuities = INFLATION RISK (purchasing power erodes over time).

Variable Annuity:








Feature
Description
Example




Payment Amount
VARIES based on investment performance
RM2,000-4,000/month (fluctuates)


Guarantee
NO guarantee on amount
Uncertainty


Inflation Risk
LOWER - can keep pace with inflation
Payments may increase


Investment Risk
HIGH - annuitant bears risk
Market exposure


Suitability
Growth-oriented, can handle volatility
Those wanting potential growth



Example:
Variable Annuity tied to equity index:
Good year: RM3,500/month (index up 15%)
Bad year: RM1,800/month (index down 10%)
Average: ~RM2,500/month (better than fixed over long term if markets grow)
📌 EXAM TIP: - Fixed = Certainty but inflation risk - Variable = Growth potential but market risk




Immediate Annuity:








Feature
Description
Malaysian Context




Payment Start
IMMEDIATELY (within 1 year)
Right after purchase


Purchase
Lump sum only
EPF lump sum, inheritance, retirement gratuity


Accumulation Phase
NONE
No growth period


Typical Buyer
Already retired, needs income NOW
Age 60+



Example:
Mr. Tan retires at 60:
EPF lump sum: RM500,000
Buys immediate annuity: RM3,500/month for life
Payments start: Next month
No accumulation needed - income begins immediately

Deferred Annuity:








Feature
Description
Malaysian Context




Payment Start
LATER (after accumulation period)
10-30 years later


Purchase
Single OR periodic premiums
Regular savings during working years


Accumulation Phase
YES - fund grows
Important growth period


Typical Buyer
Still working, planning ahead
Age 30-50



Example:
Ms. Lee age 35:
Buys deferred annuity: RM500/month premium
Accumulation: Age 35-60 (25 years)
Fund grows with interest
Payments start: Age 60
Monthly income: RM4,000/month for life
📌 EXAM TIP: - Immediate = For those who need income NOW (already retired) - Deferred = For those PLANNING AHEAD (still working)

Historical Note - Malaysia:
EPF Life Annuity Scheme (discontinued):
- Launched to convert EPF to lifetime income
- Two versions: Conventional & Takaful
- Both immediate and deferred options
- Discontinued due to pricing, administration, sales practice issues
⚠️ EXAM ALERT: EPF annuity scheme existed but DISCONTINUED - know this for Malaysian context questions.




Single Payment (Single Premium) Annuity:








Feature
Immediate Annuity
Deferred Annuity




Payment
ONE lump sum
ONE lump sum


Income Start
Immediately
After deferral period


Refund if Death
N/A (already paying out)
Purchase price refundable (with/without interest)


Surrender Value
N/A
Allowed during deferral



Example:
Immediate Single Premium:
Pay: RM500,000 (one time)
Receive: RM3,500/month immediately

Deferred Single Premium:
Pay: RM200,000 (one time, age 40)
Wait: 20 years (accumulation with interest)
Receive: RM4,000/month starting age 60

Instalment (Periodic Premium) Annuity:



Feature
Details




Payment
Regular premiums over time (monthly, annually)


Nature
ALWAYS deferred (need time to accumulate)


Refund if Death
Premiums paid refundable during accumulation


Surrender Value
Available during accumulation period


Flexibility
Can adjust payments (some plans)



Example:
Instalment Annuity:
Pay: RM500/month for 25 years (age 35-60)
Total paid: RM150,000
Fund grows: ~RM300,000 (with interest)
Receive: RM3,000/month starting age 60

If death at age 45 (during accumulation):
Beneficiaries receive: Premiums paid + interest
📌 EXAM TIP: Instalment plans are ALWAYS DEFERRED (by nature, need time to pay installments).




Single Life Annuity:








Feature
Description
Example




Coverage
ONE person only
Mr. Tan only


Payment Duration
As long as annuitant lives
Until Mr. Tan dies


Death of Annuitant
Payments STOP
No more payments to anyone


Cost
Lower (shorter expected duration)
Pays for one life



Example:
Mr. Tan, age 60:
Buys single life annuity: RM3,500/month
Lives to 85 (25 years): Receives RM3,500 × 12 × 25 = RM1,050,000
Dies at 85: Payments STOP, nothing to wife/children
⚠️ EXAM ALERT: Single life = Payments stop at death, NOTHING to beneficiaries (unless annuity certain - see later).

Joint-Life Annuity:








Feature
Description
Example




Coverage
TWO people (usually spouses)
Mr. & Mrs. Tan


Payment Duration
Until FIRST death
Stops when EITHER dies


Death of First
Payments STOP completely
Surviving spouse gets NOTHING


Cost
Moderate
Shorter than survivorship



Example:
Mr. & Mrs. Tan:
Joint-life annuity: RM4,000/month
Mr. Tan dies age 75: Payments STOP
Mrs. Tan (still alive age 72): NO MORE PAYMENTS
Problem: Left survivor without income!
⚠️ EXAM ALERT: Joint-life = Stops at FIRST death (not ideal for protecting survivor).

Survivorship Annuity (Last-to-Die):








Feature
Description
Example




Coverage
TWO people
Mr. & Mrs. Tan


Payment Duration
Until LAST death
Continues as long as ONE alive


Death of First
Payments CONTINUE to survivor
Protects surviving spouse


Cost
HIGHEST (longest expected duration)
Pays longest


Variation
Reduced payment after first death (e.g., 75% of original)
Common structure



Example:
Mr. & Mrs. Tan:
Survivorship annuity: RM4,000/month
Mr. Tan dies age 75: Payments CONTINUE
Mrs. Tan receives: RM4,000/month (or reduced to RM3,000)
Until Mrs. Tan dies age 88
Total duration: 28 years (age 60-88)
📌 EXAM TIP: Survivorship = Most expensive but BEST protection for couples (survivor continues to receive income).

📝 EXAM QUESTION 5 (Links to Section 6.1.d.v - Joint Life vs Survivorship)
Question: “For , annuity payments cease on first death. For , annuity payments until death of last annuitant. A. survivorship annuity; joint-life B. joint-life; survivorship annuity ✅ C. Single life annuity; joint life annuity D. Immediate life annuity; survivorship annuity”
Answer: B (joint-life; survivorship annuity)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Distinguish between FIRST death vs LAST death!
ANALYSIS:
First blank: “cease on FIRST death” - = JOINT-LIFE annuity ✅ - When EITHER person dies (first death), payments STOP - Survivor gets NOTHING
Second blank: “until death of LAST annuitant” - = SURVIVORSHIP annuity ✅ - Payments continue as long as ONE person alive - Stops only when BOTH dead (last death)
MEMORY TIP:
JOINT-LIFE = JOINS together, DIES together
(Stops at FIRST death - both must be alive)

SURVIVORSHIP = SURVIVOR continues
(Continues until LAST death - protects survivor)
VISUAL AID:
Joint-Life:
Husband dies → STOP ❌
Wife still alive, but no payments

Survivorship:
Husband dies → CONTINUE ✅
Wife still receives payments
Until wife dies → STOP
KEYWORDS: - “Cease on FIRST death” = JOINT-LIFE - “Until LAST annuitant” = SURVIVORSHIP




Pure Life Annuity (Straight Life Annuity):








Feature
Description
Risk/Benefit




Payment Duration
Lifetime of annuitant ONLY
Can’t outlive ✅


At Death
Payments STOP immediately
Nothing to heirs ❌


Fully Liquidated
Fund considered fully used up
No residual value ❌


Payment Amount
HIGHEST (for same premium)
Maximum income ✅


Gamble
If die early, lose money; if live long, win
Longevity bet



Example:
Mr. Ahmad age 60:
Pure life annuity: RM4,000/month
Paid: RM500,000 premium

Scenario 1: Dies age 62 (2 years)
Received: RM4,000 × 12 × 2 = RM96,000
Lost: RM404,000 (insurer keeps) ❌

Scenario 2: Lives age 90 (30 years)
Received: RM4,000 × 12 × 30 = RM1,440,000
Gained: RM940,000 more than paid! ✅

Scenario 3: Dies age 70 (10 years)
Received: RM480,000
About break-even
⚠️ EXAM ALERT: Pure life = HIGHEST monthly payment but NOTHING to beneficiaries at death.

📝 EXAM QUESTION 4 (Links to Section 6.1.d.vi - Pure Life Annuity)
Question: “Ah Seng purchased annuity, receives payments as long as he lives. Amount invested fully liquidated on death. This is: A. Pure life annuity ✅ B. Deferred annuity C. Instalment annuity D. Annuity certain”
Answer: A (Pure life annuity)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Two key phrases identify PURE LIFE: 1. “As long as he lives” = LIFETIME payments 2. “Fully liquidated on death” = NOTHING left for heirs
KEYWORD ANALYSIS:
✅ “Receives payments as long as he lives” - = LIFETIME duration - Continues until death - Can’t outlive payments
✅ “Amount invested fully liquidated on death” - = NO residual value - Nothing to beneficiaries - Fund completely used up - This is THE defining feature of PURE LIFE!
WHY NOT OTHERS:

📝 EXAM QUESTION 3 (Links to Section 6.1.d - Types of Annuities)
Question: “Which is generally true of annuity? A. For those who expect to live long, annuity not good option B. Computation exactly same as life insurance C. Lump sum deposited with insurer in exchange for stream of payments ✅ D. Younger person receives larger annuity payment than older”
Answer: C (Lump sum deposited for stream of payments)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: This is the FUNDAMENTAL DEFINITION of how annuities work!
ANALYSIS OF EACH OPTION:
C ✅ CORRECT - This IS what annuity does: - “Lump sum deposited” = You give money upfront (or accumulate) - “Exchange for” = Contract trade - “Stream of payments” = Regular periodic income - “In future” = Over time (liquidation phase) - This is the ESSENCE of annuity concept!
A ❌ FALSE - Complete OPPOSITE of truth! - Annuities are PERFECT for those expecting to live long - Live longer = Get more total payments - Protects against outliving savings - This statement is BACKWARDS!
B ❌ FALSE - Computation is OPPOSITE: - Life Insurance: Small premiums → Large lump sum (mortality focus) - Annuity: Large lump sum → Small periodic payments (longevity focus) - Actuarial methods related but NOT the same
D ❌ FALSE - OPPOSITE is true: - OLDER person receives LARGER payment (shorter life expectancy) - YOUNGER person receives SMALLER payment (longer life expectancy) - Same fund must last longer for younger = smaller per payment
Example Proof (Why D is wrong):
Fund: RM500,000

Age 60 annuitant:
Life expectancy: 20 more years
Payment: RM500,000 / 20 years = RM2,083/month

Age 40 annuitant:
Life expectancy: 40 more years
Payment: RM500,000 / 40 years = RM1,042/month

OLDER person gets LARGER payment (same fund, shorter expected duration)
KEYWORDS: - “Lump sum” = UPFRONT capital - “Stream of payments” = REGULAR income - “Exchange” = CONVERSION process
MEMORY TIP:
ANNUITY = OPPOSITE of saving
SAVING: Little by little → Build big amount
ANNUITY: Big amount → Distribute little by little

Inflation Sensitivity (CRITICAL ISSUE):
Problem with Fixed Annuities:
Year 1: RM3,000/month (buys basket of goods)
Year 10 (3% inflation): RM3,000/month (buys 25% less goods)
Year 20 (3% inflation): RM3,000/month (buys 45% less goods)
Year 30 (3% inflation): RM3,000/month (buys 58% less goods)

Purchasing power ERODED!
Solution: Cost-of-Living Adjustments (COLAs) - Payments increase with inflation - Maintain purchasing power - Higher initial cost (lower starting payment) - Better long-term protection

📝 EXAM QUESTION 7 (Links to Section 6.4.b - Annuity Limitations)
Question: “Which is FALSE regarding purchase of annuity? A. With fixed-income annuities, inflation can erode purchasing power B. Those who cannot risk lump sum should consider annuity C. Converting funds to annuity ensures regular income D. Converting savings to annuity is way to provide for annuitant’s heirs ✅”
Answer: D (Provide for heirs - FALSE)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Annuities are for ANNUITANT’S INCOME, not for LEAVING INHERITANCE!
ANALYSIS OF EACH:
A ✅ TRUE statement: - Fixed annuities DO suffer from inflation - RM3,000 today ≠ RM3,000 in 20 years - This is a KNOWN PROBLEM with fixed annuities
B ✅ TRUE statement: - If can’t handle investment risk with lump sum - Annuity = Professional management - Guaranteed income (especially fixed) - Good option for risk-averse
C ✅ TRUE statement: - Annuity = Conversion of lump sum to income stream - Regular, predictable payments - This IS what annuity does!
D ❌ FALSE statement - This is the WRONG answer: - Annuities are for ANNUITANT’S RETIREMENT INCOME - NOT designed to leave money to heirs - Pure life annuity: NOTHING to heirs - If you want to leave inheritance: BUY LIFE INSURANCE instead!
DISTINCTION TO UNDERSTAND:
Want regular income for self? → ANNUITY ✅
Want to leave money to heirs? → LIFE INSURANCE ✅

Annuity = LIVE TOO LONG protection (for you)
Life Insurance = DIE TOO SOON protection (for heirs)
EXCEPTION TO NOTE: - Annuity certain: CAN provide for heirs (if die during certain period) - But this is NOT the PRIMARY purpose - Main purpose still = Income for annuitant
KEYWORDS: - “Provide for heirs” = LIFE INSURANCE function, not annuity - “FALSE” = Look for incorrect statement - “Annuitant’s heirs” = Wrong product focus
EXAM TIP: Don’t confuse annuity (income for living) with life insurance (money for heirs)!

📝 EXAM QUESTION 9 (Links to Section 6.1 - Annuity Definition)
Question: “An annuity may be defined as insurance contract that provides ___. A. Fixed sum for fixed period to annuitant’s heirs on death B. Variable sum of money payable to those reaching age 55 C. Answer: C (Regular payment stream for specific period or lifetime)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Focus on KEY DEFINING FEATURES - regular payments, specific period OR lifetime.
ANALYSIS:
C ✅ CORRECT - Captures essence of annuity: - “Regular payment stream” = Not lump sum, but periodic ✅ - “Specific period” = Can be fixed term (annuity certain) ✅ - “OR lifetime” = Can be life-based (pure life) ✅ - Covers BOTH main types: certain and life annuities
A ❌ WRONG - Multiple errors: - “To heirs” = NO, annuities are for ANNUITANT, not heirs - “On death” = NO, annuities are for LIVING (longevity protection) - This describes LIFE INSURANCE, not annuity!
B ❌ WRONG - Too narrow/specific: - “Variable sum” = Only variable annuities (not fixed) - “Age 55” = Too specific, can start at any agreed age - Misses the essence of regular payments
D ❌ WRONG - Wrong structure: - “Lump sum” = Annuities provide REGULAR payments, not lump sums - “Intervals every 5 years” = Too infrequent (usually monthly/annually) - This is NOT how annuities work
DEFINITION TO MEMORIZE: > “Annuity = Contract providing REGULAR, PERIODIC payments for FIXED PERIOD or LIFETIME in exchange for premium/lump sum”
KEY ELEMENTS: 1. Regular = Not one-time 2. Periodic = At intervals (monthly, annually) 3. Fixed period OR Lifetime = Two duration options 4. Payment stream = Flow of income
MEMORY TIP:
ANNUITY = ANNUAL payments (historically yearly, now various periods)
Regular + Periodic + Lifetime option = Definition

Answer: D (All of the above)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Annuities can be purchased with ANY LUMP SUM - very flexible funding!
ANALYSIS OF EACH SOURCE:
i. EPF (Employees Provident Fund) ✅ VALID: - Common source in Malaysia - Lump sum withdrawal at retirement (age 55+) - Can convert to lifetime income via annuity - Historical note: EPF even had own annuity scheme (discontinued)
Example:
Mr. Wong retires age 60:
EPF Account 1: RM400,000
Option 1: Take lump sum, manage yourself
Option 2: Buy immediate annuity → RM3,000/month for life ✅
Many retirees choose annuity to ensure income can't run out
ii. Bank Savings ✅ VALID: - Any cash savings can be used - Fixed deposits, savings accounts - Accumulated wealth over years - Convert lump sum to income stream
Example:
Inherits RM500,000
Instead of keeping in bank at 3% interest (RM15,000/year)
Buy annuity: RM3,500/month for life (RM42,000/year)
Higher income + longevity protection
iii. Cash Values of Life Policy ✅ VALID: - Surrender life insurance policy - Use accumulated cash value - Convert death protection to income protection - Suitable when death protection no longer needed
Example:
Mr. Lee age 65:
Whole life policy cash value: RM300,000
Children grown, death coverage less important
Surrender policy, buy immediate annuity
Convert to retirement income: RM2,200/month
OTHER POSSIBLE SOURCES (Not in question but valid): - Inheritance/gift - Sale of property/business - Investment liquidation - Retirement gratuity/pension lump sum - Lottery/windfall
KEY PRINCIPLE: Annuity = LUMP SUM IN → INCOME STREAM OUT Source of lump sum doesn’t matter - ANY capital works!
KEYWORDS: - “Sources of capital sum” = Where lump sum comes from - “All the above” = Multiple sources valid - “EPF” = Common Malaysian source

Solution: Annuities = systematic liquidation of capital to provide lifetime income

📌 EXAM TIP: Annuity = REVERSE life insurance. Life insurance converts small payments into large sum; annuity converts large sum into small periodic payments.

📝 EXAM QUESTION 1 (Links to Section 6.0 - Introduction)
Question: “Which is most suited product for client’s retirement years? A. Whole life policy with profits B. Endowment policy maturing at age 60 C. A life annuity ✅ D. All of the above”
Answer: C (A life annuity)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: For RETIREMENT INCOME needs, annuity is the BEST solution!
WHY ANNUITY IS BEST: - ✅ Provides LIFETIME income (can’t outlive it) - ✅ Regular payments for living expenses - ✅ Specifically designed for retirement years - ✅ Protects against longevity risk
WHY OTHERS ARE LESS SUITABLE: - A. Whole Life: Pays on DEATH, not for retirement income - Benefit goes to beneficiaries, not you - Doesn’t provide regular income stream

B. Endowment (age 60): ONE-TIME lump sum at maturity

What if you live to 90? (30 more years!)
Must manage lump sum yourself
Can outlive the money


KEYWORDS: - “Retirement years” = Need INCOME ✅ - “Most suited” = Annuity = PURPOSE-BUILT for retirement ✅ - “Life annuity” = LIFETIME payments ✅
MEMORY TIP:
RETIREMENT = Need INCOME (not lump sum)
INCOME for LIFE = ANNUITY




Definition: Contract with insurer where insurer makes periodic payments to annuitant, starting immediately or future date, for lifetime or specified term.
Formal Definition (memorize): > “An annuity is a contract with an insurance company providing periodic payments to the annuitant for a lifetime or specified term, serving as reverse life insurance focusing on longevity risk.”




Primary Function: Mitigate LONGEVITY RISK
What is Longevity Risk? - Risk of outliving your assets - Living longer than expected - Running out of money in old age
How Annuities Help: - Convert lump sum → steady income stream - Provide financial security - Give peace of mind (guaranteed income) - Can’t outlive payments (if lifetime annuity)

📝 EXAM QUESTION 2 (Links to Section 6.1.a - Function)
Question: “What is basic function of annuity? A. To provide lifetime replacement or supplementary income immediately ✅ B. To provide inflation adjusted living during retirement C. To protect against medical expenses in old age D. To guarantee high income and enjoyable retirement”
Answer: A (Provide lifetime replacement/supplementary income)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Basic function = INCOME PROVISION, nothing fancy!
ANALYSIS OF EACH OPTION:
A ✅ CORRECT - The BASIC function: - “Lifetime” = Core feature (longevity protection) - “Replacement or supplementary” = Can replace work income OR supplement other income - “Immediately” = For immediate annuities (can also be deferred) - This is the FUNDAMENTAL purpose
B ❌ WRONG - Too specific: - Inflation adjustment is OPTIONAL feature, not basic function - Not all annuities are inflation-adjusted - This is a NICE-TO-HAVE, not core purpose
C ❌ WRONG - Wrong product! - Medical expenses = HEALTH INSURANCE function - Annuities = INCOME, not medical coverage - Completely different purpose
D ❌ WRONG - Too optimistic/unrealistic: - “Guarantee high income” = FALSE (depends on amount invested) - “Enjoyable retirement” = Subjective, not insurance function - Overpromises what annuity can do
KEYWORDS: - “Basic function” = CORE purpose (income provision) - “Lifetime” = LONGEVITY protection - “Replacement/supplementary” = INCOME focus
EXAM TIP: Don’t be distracted by fancy features (inflation, medical, “enjoyable”). Basic function = PROVIDE INCOME.




TWO PHASES (CRITICAL to understand):
ANNUITY LIFE CYCLE

(Building)              (Paying Out)

📝 EXAM QUESTION 5 (Links to Section 6.1.d.v - Joint Life vs Survivorship)
Question: “For , annuity payments cease on first death. For , annuity payments until death of last annuitant. A. survivorship annuity; joint-life B. joint-life; survivorship annuity ✅ C. Single life annuity; joint life annuity D. Immediate life annuity; survivorship annuity”
Answer: B (joint-life; survivorship annuity)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Distinguish between FIRST death vs LAST death!
ANALYSIS:
First blank: “cease on FIRST death” - = JOINT-LIFE annuity ✅ - When EITHER person dies (first death), payments STOP - Survivor gets NOTHING
Second blank: “until death of LAST annuitant” - = SURVIVORSHIP annuity ✅ - Payments continue as long as ONE person alive - Stops only when BOTH dead (last death)
MEMORY TIP:
JOINT-LIFE = JOINS together, DIES together
(Stops at FIRST death - both must be alive)

SURVIVORSHIP = SURVIVOR continues
(Continues until LAST death - protects survivor)
VISUAL AID:
Joint-Life:
Husband dies → STOP ❌
Wife still alive, but no payments

Survivorship:
Husband dies → CONTINUE ✅
Wife still receives payments
Until wife dies → STOP
KEYWORDS: - “Cease on FIRST death” = JOINT-LIFE - “Until LAST annuitant” = SURVIVORSHIP

📝 EXAM QUESTION 4 (Links to Section 6.1.d.vi - Pure Life Annuity)
Question: “Ah Seng purchased annuity, receives payments as long as he lives. Amount invested fully liquidated on death. This is: A. Pure life annuity ✅ B. Deferred annuity C. Instalment annuity D. Annuity certain”
Answer: A (Pure life annuity)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Two key phrases identify PURE LIFE: 1. “As long as he lives” = LIFETIME payments 2. “Fully liquidated on death” = NOTHING left for heirs
KEYWORD ANALYSIS:
✅ “Receives payments as long as he lives” - = LIFETIME duration - Continues until death - Can’t outlive payments
✅ “Amount invested fully liquidated on death” - = NO residual value - Nothing to beneficiaries - Fund completely used up - This is THE defining feature of PURE LIFE!
WHY NOT OTHERS:
❌ B. Deferred - This refers to WHEN payments START (immediate vs deferred), not the TYPE of payout structure
❌ C. Instalment - This refers to HOW PREMIUM IS PAID (single vs periodic), not payout characteristics
❌ D. Annuity Certain - This has GUARANTEED period payments regardless of life/death (opposite of pure life)
MEMORY TIP:
PURE LIFE = PURE gamble on longevity
- Live long = WIN BIG ✅
- Die early = LOSE ❌
- Nothing left = PURE (nothing for heirs)

📝 EXAM QUESTION 3 (Links to Section 6.1.d - Types of Annuities)
Question: “Which is generally true of annuity? A. For those who expect to live long, annuity not good option B. Computation exactly same as life insurance C. Lump sum deposited with insurer in exchange for stream of payments ✅ D. Younger person receives larger annuity payment than older”
Answer: C (Lump sum deposited for stream of payments)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: This is the FUNDAMENTAL DEFINITION of how annuities work!
ANALYSIS OF EACH OPTION:
C ✅ CORRECT - This IS what annuity does: - “Lump sum deposited” = You give money upfront (or accumulate) - “Exchange for” = Contract trade - “Stream of payments” = Regular periodic income - “In future” = Over time (liquidation phase) - This is the ESSENCE of annuity concept!
A ❌ FALSE - Complete OPPOSITE of truth! - Annuities are PERFECT for those expecting to live long - Live longer = Get more total payments - Protects against outliving savings - This statement is BACKWARDS!
B ❌ FALSE - Computation is OPPOSITE: - Life Insurance: Small premiums → Large lump sum (mortality focus) - Annuity: Large lump sum → Small periodic payments (longevity focus) - Actuarial methods related but NOT the same
D ❌ FALSE - OPPOSITE is true: - OLDER person receives LARGER payment (shorter life expectancy) - YOUNGER person receives SMALLER payment (longer life expectancy) - Same fund must last longer for younger = smaller per payment
Example Proof (Why D is wrong):
Fund: RM500,000

Age 60 annuitant:
Life expectancy: 20 more years
Payment: RM500,000 / 20 years = RM2,083/month

Age 40 annuitant:
Life expectancy: 40 more years
Payment: RM500,000 / 40 years = RM1,042/month

OLDER person gets LARGER payment (same fund, shorter expected duration)
KEYWORDS: - “Lump sum” = UPFRONT capital - “Stream of payments” = REGULAR income - “Exchange” = CONVERSION process
MEMORY TIP:
ANNUITY = OPPOSITE of saving
SAVING: Little by little → Build big amount
ANNUITY: Big amount → Distribute little by little

🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Annuity income is FULLY TAX EXEMPT in Malaysia!
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: - Before 1995: Annuity income was taxable - From 1995 onwards: Tax exemption granted - Reaffirmed 2012: Public Ruling 4/2014 confirmed exemption - Purpose: Encourage retirement savings, make annuities attractive
WHY OTHERS WRONG:
❌ A. Taxed as income: FALSE - Was true before 1995, but NOT anymore
❌ B. Taxed as capital gain: FALSE - Not treated as capital gain at all
❌ C. Not taxed but as retirement gratuity: FALSE - Simply tax exempt, not reclassified as gratuity

Part-time work: RM20,000/year (TAXABLE) ❌

Tax savings significant!
KEYWORDS: - “Tax exempt” = NO TAX on annuity payments - “1995” = Year exemption started - “Life and Takaful” = Both covered

Tailored to needs

Maximize Tax Relief

Contribute RM3,000 annually (max deduction)
Coordinate with PRS contributions
Plan timing of contributions

Take advantage of tax-free status

Consult financial advisors
