Regular review and adjustment



📝 EXAM QUESTION 8 (Links to Section 6.1 - Annuity Terminology)
Question: “For annuity, person whose life governs annuity payments is , while money considerations in exchange for payment is . A. insured; order price B. annuitant; purchase price ✅ C. insured; retirement fund D. annuitant; retirement fund”
Answer: B (annuitant; purchase price)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Know the CORRECT TERMINOLOGY for annuity contracts!
KEY TERMS:
1. ANNUITANT (not “insured”): - = Person whose life governs the payments - = Receives the annuity income - = Analogous to “life insured” in life insurance - BUT: Correct term in annuities = ANNUITANT
2. PURCHASE PRICE (not “premium”): - = Money paid to buy the annuity - = Can be lump sum or accumulated premiums - = Consideration for the contract - Also called: “Consideration” or “Principal”
WHY “ANNUITANT” not “INSURED”?
Life Insurance: INSURED (person whose death triggers payment)
Annuity: ANNUITANT (person whose LIFE triggers payments)

Different context, different terminology!
COMPLETE ANNUITY TERMINOLOGY: - Annuitant: Person receiving payments (life governs duration) - Purchase Price: Money paid for annuity - Annuity Period: Duration of payments - Annuity Commencement Date: When payments begin - Beneficiary: Receives remaining benefits if annuity certain
MEMORY TIP:
ANNUITANT = ANNUITY recipient
PURCHASE PRICE = PRICE you purchase annuity for







Different Demographics, Different Needs:









Demographic
Characteristics
Annuity Suitability
Recommendation




Young (20-40)
Growth focus, long horizon
LOW priority
Focus on growth investments first


Middle-age (40-55)
Building retirement, mixed goals
MODERATE
Deferred annuity for future


Pre-retirement (55-60)
Near retirement, stability focus
HIGH
Consider immediate or short-deferred


Retired (60+)
Need income NOW
VERY HIGH
Immediate annuity ideal


Urban
Higher income, more options
More suitable
Access to various products


Rural
Lower income, limited access
Less suitable
May lack awareness/access







Inflation Sensitivity (CRITICAL ISSUE):
Problem with Fixed Annuities:
Year 1: RM3,000/month (buys basket of goods)
Year 10 (3% inflation): RM3,000/month (buys 25% less goods)
Year 20 (3% inflation): RM3,000/month (buys 45% less goods)
Year 30 (3% inflation): RM3,000/month (buys 58% less goods)

Purchasing power ERODED!
Solution: Cost-of-Living Adjustments (COLAs) - Payments increase with inflation - Maintain purchasing power - Higher initial cost (lower starting payment) - Better long-term protection

Market Volatility: - Affects variable annuities - Investment performance impacts payments - Diversification important - Risk/return trade-off

📝 EXAM QUESTION 7 (Links to Section 6.4.b - Annuity Limitations)
Question: “Which is FALSE regarding purchase of annuity? A. With fixed-income annuities, inflation can erode purchasing power B. Those who cannot risk lump sum should consider annuity C. Converting funds to annuity ensures regular income D. Converting savings to annuity is way to provide for annuitant’s heirs ✅”
Answer: D (Provide for heirs - FALSE)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Annuities are for ANNUITANT’S INCOME, not for LEAVING INHERITANCE!
ANALYSIS OF EACH:
A ✅ TRUE statement: - Fixed annuities DO suffer from inflation - RM3,000 today ≠ RM3,000 in 20 years - This is a KNOWN PROBLEM with fixed annuities
B ✅ TRUE statement: - If can’t handle investment risk with lump sum - Annuity = Professional management - Guaranteed income (especially fixed) - Good option for risk-averse
C ✅ TRUE statement: - Annuity = Conversion of lump sum to income stream - Regular, predictable payments - This IS what annuity does!
D ❌ FALSE statement - This is the WRONG answer: - Annuities are for ANNUITANT’S RETIREMENT INCOME - NOT designed to leave money to heirs - Pure life annuity: NOTHING to heirs - If you want to leave inheritance: BUY LIFE INSURANCE instead!
DISTINCTION TO UNDERSTAND:
Want regular income for self? → ANNUITY ✅
Want to leave money to heirs? → LIFE INSURANCE ✅

Annuity = LIVE TOO LONG protection (for you)
Life Insurance = DIE TOO SOON protection (for heirs)
EXCEPTION TO NOTE: - Annuity certain: CAN provide for heirs (if die during certain period) - But this is NOT the PRIMARY purpose - Main purpose still = Income for annuitant
KEYWORDS: - “Provide for heirs” = LIFE INSURANCE function, not annuity - “FALSE” = Look for incorrect statement - “Annuitant’s heirs” = Wrong product focus
EXAM TIP: Don’t confuse annuity (income for living) with life insurance (money for heirs)!




Matching Annuities to Goals:








Retirement Goal

Reason




Steady income

Guaranteed payments

Annuities deplete capital


Inflation protection
Variable or indexed annuity
Payments can grow


Maximum income
Pure life annuity
Highest payment amount


Protect spouse
Survivorship annuity
Continues to survivor







DISADVANTAGES of Annuities:
1. Liquidity & Flexibility








Issue
Details
Impact




Locked In
Funds not easily accessible
Can’t access for emergencies


Early Withdrawal
High penalties (surrender charges)
Expensive to exit


Inflexible
Can’t adjust easily once set up
Limited control



Example:
Mr. Lim buys immediate annuity: RM500,000
Emergency need: RM100,000 (medical)
Surrender annuity:
Surrender value: RM400,000 (penalty applied)
Loss: RM100,000 (20% penalty!)
Plus: Lost future guaranteed income

Result: Severe financial loss
📌 EXAM TIP: Liquidity is a MAJOR DRAWBACK - only commit funds you won’t need!

2. Costs and Charges








Fee Type
Description
Impact




Administrative Fees
Ongoing management
Reduces effective return


Surrender Charges
Early exit penalties (can be 5-10%)
Locks you in


Mortality & Expense Risk
Insurer’s risk charge
Reduces payout


Investment Fees
For variable annuities
Further reduces return



Fee Example:
Premium: RM500,000
Administrative fee (2%): RM10,000
Mortality charge (1.5%): RM7,500
Net invested: RM482,500
Effective return: Already -3.5% before any gains!
⚠️ EXAM ALERT: Fees can significantly reduce attractiveness - must be disclosed transparently.

3. Inflation Risk (Fixed Annuities) - Already discussed - purchasing power erosion - Fixed payments lose value over time - Long retirement (30+ years) = severe impact
4. Opportunity Cost - Money locked in annuity - Could potentially earn higher returns elsewhere - Trade-off: Security vs Growth potential
5. Complexity - Many types and options - Difficult for average person to understand - Requires professional advice (additional cost)

📝 EXAM QUESTION 9 (Links to Section 6.1 - Annuity Definition)
Question: “An annuity may be defined as insurance contract that provides ___. A. Fixed sum for fixed period to annuitant’s heirs on death B. Variable sum of money payable to those reaching age 55 C. Regular payment stream for specific period, either fixed period or lifetime ✅ D. Lump sum payment at intervals such as every 5 years”
Answer: C (Regular payment stream for specific period or lifetime)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Focus on KEY DEFINING FEATURES - regular payments, specific period OR lifetime.
ANALYSIS:
C ✅ CORRECT - Captures essence of annuity: - “Regular payment stream” = Not lump sum, but periodic ✅ - “Specific period” = Can be fixed term (annuity certain) ✅ - “OR lifetime” = Can be life-based (pure life) ✅ - Covers BOTH main types: certain and life annuities
A ❌ WRONG - Multiple errors: - “To heirs” = NO, annuities are for ANNUITANT, not heirs - “On death” = NO, annuities are for LIVING (longevity protection) - This describes LIFE INSURANCE, not annuity!
B ❌ WRONG - Too narrow/specific: - “Variable sum” = Only variable annuities (not fixed) - “Age 55” = Too specific, can start at any agreed age - Misses the essence of regular payments
D ❌ WRONG - Wrong structure: - “Lump sum” = Annuities provide REGULAR payments, not lump sums - “Intervals every 5 years” = Too infrequent (usually monthly/annually) - This is NOT how annuities work
DEFINITION TO MEMORIZE: > “Annuity = Contract providing REGULAR, PERIODIC payments for FIXED PERIOD or LIFETIME in exchange for premium/lump sum”
KEY ELEMENTS: 1. Regular = Not one-time 2. Periodic = At intervals (monthly, annually) 3. Fixed period OR Lifetime = Two duration options 4. Payment stream = Flow of income
MEMORY TIP:
ANNUITY = ANNUAL payments (historically yearly, now various periods)
Regular + Periodic + Lifetime option = Definition

📝 EXAM QUESTION 10 (Links to Section 6.1 - Annuity Funding)
Question: “Which are possible sources of capital sum to purchase annuity? i. EPF ii. Bank savings iii. Cash values of life policy
A. i only B. ii only C. i & iii only D. All the above ✅”
Answer: D (All of the above)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Annuities can be purchased with ANY LUMP SUM - very flexible funding!
ANALYSIS OF EACH SOURCE:
i. EPF (Employees Provident Fund) ✅ VALID: - Common source in Malaysia - Lump sum withdrawal at retirement (age 55+) - Can convert to lifetime income via annuity - Historical note: EPF even had own annuity scheme (discontinued)
Example:
Mr. Wong retires age 60:
EPF Account 1: RM400,000
Option 1: Take lump sum, manage yourself
Option 2: Buy immediate annuity → RM3,000/month for life ✅
Many retirees choose annuity to ensure income can't run out
ii. Bank Savings ✅ VALID: - Any cash savings can be used - Fixed deposits, savings accounts - Accumulated wealth over years - Convert lump sum to income stream
Example:
Inherits RM500,000
Instead of keeping in bank at 3% interest (RM15,000/year)
Buy annuity: RM3,500/month for life (RM42,000/year)
Higher income + longevity protection
iii. Cash Values of Life Policy ✅ VALID: - Surrender life insurance policy - Use accumulated cash value - Convert death protection to income protection - Suitable when death protection no longer needed
Example:
Mr. Lee age 65:
Whole life policy cash value: RM300,000
Children grown, death coverage less important
Surrender policy, buy immediate annuity
Convert to retirement income: RM2,200/month
OTHER POSSIBLE SOURCES (Not in question but valid): - Inheritance/gift - Sale of property/business - Investment liquidation - Retirement gratuity/pension lump sum - Lottery/windfall
KEY PRINCIPLE: Annuity = LUMP SUM IN → INCOME STREAM OUT Source of lump sum doesn’t matter - ANY capital works!
KEYWORDS: - “Sources of capital sum” = Where lump sum comes from - “All the above” = Multiple sources valid - “EPF” = Common Malaysian source
MEMORY TIP: “Any Lump Sum Works” - EPF, Savings, Insurance - ALL valid sources!





Best Practices for Annuity Purchase:

Thorough Assessment

Personal financial situation
Retirement needs analysis
Risk tolerance evaluation
Family circumstances

Consider Broader Factors

Economic conditions
Inflation expectations
Market volatility
Interest rate environment

Professional Guidance

Financial planner consultation
Compare multiple products
Understand all fees and charges
Read all disclosure documents

Diversification

Don’t put all retirement funds in annuity
Mix annuity with other income sources
Balance liquidity and security
Keep emergency funds separate

High

Basic Annuity Payment Calculation (Conceptual):
Annual Payment = Purchase Price / Expected Years
(Simplified; actual uses actuarial tables and mortality rates)

Example:
Purchase Price: RM500,000
Life Expectancy: 25 years
Annual Payment: ~RM20,000/year = RM1,667/month
(Actual higher due to mortality credits and interest earnings)
Tax Benefit Calculation:
Tax Savings = Deferred Annuity Premium (max RM3,000) × Tax Rate

Maximum deductible: RM3,000
Tax rate: 14%
Tax savings: RM3,000 × 14% = RM420/year

Real value = RM3,000 / (1.03)^20 = RM3,000 / 1.806 = RM1,661
Lost 45% of purchasing power!

title: Chapter 9: Legal Principles and Relevant Legislation in Insurance
text:
Legal principles form the FOUNDATION of insurance contracts. This chapter covers the essential legal concepts, agency law, regulatory framework, and compliance requirements that govern insurance practice in Malaysia.
Exam Weight: 10-12% of total exam
Study Time Recommendation: 8-10 hours




By the end of this chapter, you must be able to:

Understand legal risks in financial planning (legal, compliance, reputation)
Explain fundamental insurance principles (utmost good faith, insurable interest, proximate cause)
Distinguish contract characteristics (aleatory, unilateral, adhesion, conditional, personal)
Apply agency law to insurance relationships
Identify agent duties and liabilities under FSA 2013
Understand Anti-Money Laundering requirements
Recognize negligence and tort liability







CRITICAL Framework (memorize this):
THREE PROFESSIONAL RISKS
├── 1. LEGAL RISKS
├── 2. COMPLIANCE RISKS
└── 3. REPUTATION RISKS



Definition: Arise when due diligence and care not practiced in provision of advice.
Consequences: - Fines - Imprisonment - Financial loss liability








Example
Description
Legal Issue




Misrepresentation
False info to induce contract
Fraudulent inducement


Premium Fraud
Misappropriation of client premiums
Theft, breach of trust


Collusion
Working with insured to defraud insurer
Conspiracy to defraud



⚠️ EXAM ALERT: Legal risks become tangible when advice misaligns with current laws, leading to liability or legal action.




Definition: Failure to adhere to laws, rules, regulations, and guidelines.
Consequences: - Penalties - Sanctions - Loss of license








Violation Type
Act/Regulation
Example




FSA 2013 Non-compliance
Financial Services Act 2013
Not disclosing agent relationship


AML Violations
Anti-Money Laundering Act 2001
Not reporting suspicious transactions


Code Breaches
Insurance Industry Code of Practice
Pressure selling, churning



📌 EXAM TIP: Compliance risks = Failure to follow SPECIFIC regulations (FSA, AMLA, Industry Code).




Definition: Loss of confidence by clients due to conduct/practices.
Causes: - Poor conduct and practices - Inability to meet client expectations - Pressure selling ⚠️ - Unethical practices - Any infringement of law
Impact: - Loss of clients - Damaged professional standing - Difficulty in future business - Instant damage in digital age
📌 EXAM TIP: Reputation risks often RESULT from legal and compliance risks (cumulative effect).





FOUR Key Strategies:








Strategy
Description
Action




1. Continuous Education
Stay updated with legal changes
Courses, workshops, seminars


2. Compliance Systems
Robust internal processes
Regular reviews, training, monitoring


3. Ethical Frameworks
Clear ethical guidelines
Consistent decision-making standards


4. Documentation
Proper record-keeping
Communication trails, advice records







Essential Contract Elements (memorize):
VALID CONTRACT REQUIRES:
1. Offer (proposal)
2. Acceptance
3. Consideration (premium)
4. Legal Capacity (age, sound mind)
5. Legal Purpose (not illegal)
6. Genuine Consent (no fraud/duress)
Insurance Contract = Specialized Contract
Follows general contract law BUT has UNIQUE characteristics (covered next).




THREE Core Principles (HIGH EXAM FREQUENCY):
FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES
├── 1. Utmost Good Faith (Uberrimae Fidei)
├── 2. Insurable Interest
└── 3. Proximate Cause



Definition: Both parties must act with complete honesty and disclose all material facts.
Duty of Disclosure (FSA 2013, Schedule 9, Paragraph 3(4)(1)):
Proposer MUST disclose: - Any matter known to be relevant to insurer’s decision - Any matter a reasonable person would expect to know is relevant

What is a MATERIAL FACT?
Definition: Fact that would influence insurer’s decision to: - Accept the risk - Set premium amount - Determine policy terms
Example Material Facts: - Previous insurance declined/cancelled - Criminal convictions - Pre-existing medical conditions - Previous claims history - Occupation hazards - Dangerous hobbies

FOUR Ways to Breach Utmost Good Faith:









Breach Type
Description
Intent
Example




1. Non-disclosure
Failure to disclose material fact
Unintentional (considers it inconsequential)
Not mentioning previous minor accident


2. Concealment
Willful failure to disclose
INTENTIONAL (to get cheaper cover)
Hiding heart condition for life insurance


3. Fraud
Premeditated false information
DELIBERATE DECEPTION
Forging medical reports


4. Innocent Misrepresentation
Unintentional incorrect information
Accidental/mistake
Genuinely mistaken about past illness dates



⚠️ EXAM ALERT: - Non-disclosure = Didn’t think important (unintentional) - Concealment = Knew important, hid it (willful) - Fraud = Premeditated lies - Innocent Misrep = Honest mistake

Case Law Examples:
1. Abu Bakar v. Oriental Fire (1974) - NON-DISCLOSURE
Facts: - Insured applied for fire insurance - Question: “For what purposes premises occupied?” - Answer: “Sundry shop downstairs, dwelling first floor” - OMITTED: Four grinding mills for curry powder at back - Fire occurred - Insurer denied claim (failed to disclose mills)
Held: - ✅ Insurers NOT misled about nature of insurance - ✅ NO evidence mills increased risk - ✅ Insurers LIABLE - NO breach of utmost good faith
📌 EXAM TIP: Not ALL omissions = breach. Must be MATERIAL (affects risk assessment).

2. Goh Chooi Leng v Public Life (1964) - CONCEALMENT
Facts: - Life assured applied for insurance (May 1960) - Question: “Ever had advice about heart/lung/cough?” - Answer: “No” - TRUTH: Treated for tuberculosis, hospitalized Nov 1958-March 1959 - Life assured died - Assignee claimed
Held: - ❌ NON-DISCLOSURE of material fact - ❌ Contract VOIDABLE - ❌ Insurer NOT LIABLE
📌 EXAM TIP: Medical history is ALWAYS material for life insurance!

3. United Oriental v. Mazzarol (1984) - INNOCENT MISREPRESENTATION
Facts: - Proposal form for boat insurance - Question ONLY asked: Accidents to OTHER boats owned - Did NOT ask: Accidents to THIS boat - Insured boat sank - Insurer avoided liability (previous accident to THIS boat not disclosed)
Held: - ✅ Although NOT asked specifically - ✅ Previous accident to THIS boat = MATERIAL FACT - ✅ MUST be disclosed regardless - ✅ Insurer can avoid contract
📌 EXAM TIP: Material facts must be disclosed EVEN IF NOT SPECIFICALLY ASKED!

What NEED NOT Be Disclosed (FSA 2013, Schedule 9, Paragraph 3(4)(2)):








Exclusion
Description
Example




Diminishes risk
Makes risk LOWER
Installed sprinkler system (fire insurance)


Common knowledge
Public information
General crime statistics in area


Known to insurer
Insurer should know in ordinary course
Standard industry risks


Waived by insurer
Insurer doesn’t require disclosure
Optional questions left blank



Deemed Waiver (FSA 2013, Schedule 9, Paragraph 3(4)(3)): If proposer: - Fails to answer question - Gives incomplete/irrelevant answer AND insurer doesn’t pursue further → Compliance with duty of disclosure DEEMED WAIVED




Definition: Policyholder must have legal or financial stake in subject matter insured.
Purpose: Prevent insurance from becoming GAMBLING/WAGERING.

Insurable Interest in LIFE INSURANCE (FSA 2013, Schedule 8, Paragraph 3):
Requirement: Must exist at TIME OF CONTRACT INCEPTION
Who has insurable interest in your life?

Elderly parent depends on adult child

Insurable Interest in GENERAL INSURANCE:
Requirement: Must exist at TIME OF LOSS/CLAIM
Who has insurable interest?

Trustee/Bailee
Property in care
Responsibility for safeguarding



📌 EXAM TIP: - Life Insurance: Insurable interest at INCEPTION - General Insurance: Insurable interest at LOSS/CLAIM

📝 EXAM QUESTION 10 (Links to Section 9.3.1 - Insurable Interest & Legal Purpose)
Question: “Raymond Mah is hard drug pusher. Asks agent to insure goods including illegal drugs. Agent rejects. Why? A. Illegal purpose – against public policy ✅ B. No insurable interest exist C. Agent wrong, drugs can be insured D. FSA 2013 specifically forbids dealing with drug pusher”
Answer: A (Illegal purpose – against public policy)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Insurance contracts require LEGAL PURPOSE - cannot insure illegal activities!
ANALYSIS:
A ✅ CORRECT - Fundamental contract principle: - Insurance contract requires LEGAL PURPOSE - Cannot promote illegal activities (against public policy) - Insuring illegal drugs = Facilitating crime - Public policy prevents this
WHY PUBLIC POLICY?
If illegal goods could be insured:
→ Criminals protected from loss
→ Insurance encourages illegal trade
→ Society harmed
→ Against public interest
B ❌ WRONG - Technically he HAS insurable interest: - He owns the drugs (property owner) - Financial stake in their safety - BUT: Insurable interest ALONE not enough - Must ALSO have legal purpose!
C ❌ WRONG - Agent is CORRECT to refuse: - Illegal goods cannot be insured - Would violate public policy - Agent could face legal liability
D ❌ WRONG - Too specific: - FSA 2013 doesn’t need SPECIFIC drug provision - General legal purpose requirement covers it - Broader public policy principle applies
LEGAL BASIS:
Valid Contract Requires:
1. Offer ✓
2. Acceptance ✓
3. Consideration ✓
4. Legal Capacity ✓
5. LEGAL PURPOSE ✗ (FAILED - illegal drugs)
6. Genuine Consent ✓

Result: Cannot form valid contract
KEYWORDS: - “Illegal purpose” = Against law - “Public policy” = Society’s interests - “Cannot promote illegal activities”
SIMILAR EXAMPLES: - Cannot insure stolen goods - Cannot insure proceeds of crime - Cannot insure illegal gambling operation
MEMORY TIP: “No Insurance for Illegal Business” (Public policy protects society)




Definition: The actual, real, or dominant cause that sets in motion chain of events leading to loss.
Purpose: Determine if insurer liable under policy (was loss caused by insured peril?).
Key Concept: “PROXIMATE” = DOMINANT/EFFECTIVE cause, not necessarily NEAREST IN TIME.

Example: Smith v. Cornhill Insurance (1938)
Facts: - Motor policy: Death if “result solely of bodily injury by violent accidental means while riding insured car” - Insured: Severe head injuries in car accident (fell down ravine) - After accident: Wandered aimlessly through brushwood - Stepped into stream → Shock of immersion → Heart failure → Death - Insurer: Refused payment (shock of immersion = intervening factor)
Held: - ✅ Accident = PRIMARY CAUSE - ✅ Led to sequence: injury → wandering → immersion → shock → death - ✅ NO intervening causes - ✅ UNBROKEN CHAIN of events - ✅ Insurer LIABLE
Principle: If unbroken chain of events from insured peril to loss, proximate cause = insured peril.
📌 EXAM TIP: Look for UNBROKEN CHAIN - no independent intervening cause that breaks the connection.





FIVE Special Characteristics (memorize):
INSURANCE CONTRACT CHARACTERISTICS
├── 1. Aleatory
├── 2. Unilateral
├── 3. Conditional
├── 4. Personal
└── 5. Adhesion



Definition: Unequal exchange - parties may receive unequal values.
How it works in insurance:
Scenario 1: No Claim
Insured pays: RM2,000 (premium)
Insurer pays: RM0
Insurer "wins"

Scenario 2: Major Claim
Insured pays: RM2,000 (premium)
Insurer pays: RM500,000 (claim)
Insured "wins"
vs. COMMUTATIVE Contract (equal exchange): - Buy car: Pay RM50,000 → Receive car worth RM50,000 - Mutual agreement on value exchanged
📌 EXAM TIP: Insurance = ALEATORY (dependent on uncertain event), not commutative (equal exchange).




Definition: Only ONE party (insurer) makes enforceable promise.
How it works: - Insurer: Legally bound to pay if loss occurs (enforceable promise) - Insured: NO legal obligation to continue paying premiums (can lapse)
Example:
After paying first premium:
Insured: Can stop paying (policy lapses, no lawsuit)
Insurer: MUST pay claim if loss occurs during coverage (enforceable)
vs. BILATERAL Contract (both parties bound): - Employment contract: Employee must work, Employer must pay




Definition: Insurer’s obligation dependent on insured fulfilling conditions.
Common Conditions: - Timely premium payment - Truthful information at application - Notify insurer of changes - Claims notification within specified time - Cooperation in claims investigation
Example:
Condition: Notify claim within 30 days
Insured notifies after 60 days
Result: Insurer may deny claim (condition breached)
📌 EXAM TIP: Contract fulfillment CONDITIONAL on compliance with terms.




Definition: Contract is personal to the insured, not the property.
Key Points: - Protects PERSON/ENTITY, not property itself - Based on insured’s character, morals, credit status - NOT automatically transferable - If property sold, policy DOES NOT follow new owner
Example:
Mr. Tan owns house, has fire insurance
Sells house to Mr. Lee
Insurance: Does NOT transfer to Mr. Lee
Mr. Lee: Must apply for NEW insurance
(Insurer assesses Mr. Lee's character/credit separately)
⚠️ EXAM ALERT: Property insurance is PERSONAL - does NOT automatically transfer with property sale!




Definition: Insured must accept contract “as is” - no negotiation.
Characteristics: - Insurer designs and prints policy - Terms pre-printed - Insured: Take it or leave it (no modification) - No negotiation between parties
Legal Protection for Insured:
DOCTRINE: Contract of Adhesion
↓
Court Interpretation Rule:
"Any AMBIGUITY in contract interpreted IN FAVOR OF INSURED"
↓
Reason: Insurer drafted it, insured had no input
Presumption of Intent Doctrine: - Person who signs contract PRESUMED to have: - Read the contract - Understood terms - Agreed to conditions - Bound by signed terms
📌 EXAM TIP: Adhesion contracts = No negotiation, but ambiguities favor insured (court protection).





Definition: Legal relationship where agent acts on behalf of principal (insurer).



Structure:
PRINCIPAL (Insurer)
    ↓ (appoints)
AGENT (Insurance Agent)
    ↓ (interacts with)
THIRD PARTY (Policyholders/Clients)
Agent’s Role: - Market insurance products - Collect premiums - Provide customer service - Act on behalf of insurer




CRITICAL CONCEPT (HIGH EXAM FREQUENCY):









Authority Type
Source
Description
Example




EXPRESS Authority
Explicitly granted (written/oral)
Direct authorization from insurer
Agency contract states: “Can solicit applications, collect premiums”


IMPLIED Authority
Incidental to express
Actions reasonably necessary to execute express authority
Express: Sell policies → Implied: Answer client questions, arrange meetings


APPARENT Authority
Insurer’s representations
Public believes agent has authority based on insurer’s conduct
Insurer gives agent business cards, office = Public assumes agent authorized



⚠️ EXAM ALERT: - Express = Directly stated - Implied = Necessary to carry out express - Apparent = Looks authorized to public

📝 EXAM QUESTION 7 (Links to Section 9.5.2 - Types of Authority)
Question: “Agent’s authority to act can be in following ways: i. Express authority ii. Implied authority iii. Apparent authority iv. Secret authority
A. I only B. I, II and III ✅ C. I and II only D. All the above”
Answer: B (I, II and III)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: THREE recognized types of authority - Express, Implied, Apparent.
ANALYSIS:
i. Express Authority ✅ VALID: - Explicitly stated in agency contract - Written or oral authorization - Clear, direct appointment
ii. Implied Authority ✅ VALID: - Incidental to express authority - Reasonably necessary powers - Not stated but understood
iii. Apparent Authority ✅ VALID: - Ostensible authority - Based on insurer’s representations - Public perception of authority
iv. Secret Authority ❌ NOT VALID: - NO such concept in agency law! - Authority cannot be “secret” - Either authorized or not - Made-up option (exam trap!)
KEYWORDS: - “Express” = Explicitly stated - “Implied” = Incidental/necessary - “Apparent” = Ostensible/perceived

📝 EXAM QUESTION 8 (Links to Section 9.5.2 - Express vs Implied)
Question: “In agency law, ___ is incidental authority required to execute ___ of principal. A. Express authority; implied authority B. Implied authority; express authority ✅ C. Apparent authority; implied authority D. Implied authority; Apparent authority”
Answer: B (Implied authority; express authority)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: IMPLIED authority is what’s needed to EXECUTE EXPRESS authority!
RELATIONSHIP:
EXPRESS Authority (Stated)
    ↓ (requires for execution)
IMPLIED Authority (Incidental)
EXPLANATION: - EXPRESS = What you’re told to do (sell insurance) - IMPLIED = What you need to do it (answer questions, meet clients)
EXAMPLE:
EXPRESS: "You are authorized to sell life insurance policies"
    ↓ (To accomplish this, you IMPLIED authority to:)
IMPLIED: 
- Answer client questions about products
- Arrange meetings with prospects
- Explain policy features
- Collect proposal forms
- Provide premium quotes
WHY OTHER OPTIONS WRONG:
❌ A: Backwards - Express is not incidental to implied ❌ C: Apparent is not incidental to implied (different concept) ❌ D: Implied is not incidental to apparent (wrong relationship)
MEMORY TIP: “IMPLIED helps you EXECUTE EXPRESS”




CRITICAL PROVISION (HIGH EXAM FREQUENCY):
When agent fills proposal form: - Agent acts for INSURER (principal), NOT client - Agent’s knowledge = Insurer’s knowledge - Agent’s statements = Insurer’s statements

📝 EXAM QUESTION 4 (Links to Section 9.5.3 - Agent Filling Forms)
Question: “When agent fills proposal form from client, who is he acting for under FSA 2013 Schedule 9 Para 12? A. For the Insurer - principal ✅ B. For the client C. For himself D. For the beneficiary”
Answer: A (For the Insurer - principal)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Agent filling form = Acts for INSURER, NOT client (protects client).
WHY THIS MATTERS:
If agent acts for CLIENT:
Client: Tells agent wrong information
Agent: Writes it on form
Problem: Who's responsible? Client!
Issue: Client may not understand technical terms
Result: UNFAIR to client
If agent acts for INSURER (FSA 2013 rule):
Client: Tells agent information
Agent: Writes it on form (acts for INSURER)
Problem: Agent writes incorrectly
Result: INSURER responsible (agent is their representative)
Protection: CLIENT protected from agent errors
FSA 2013 Schedule 9, Paragraph 12: - Agent completing proposal = Agent of INSURER - Protects proposer from agent mistakes - Insurer cannot deny claim based on agent’s filling errors
KEYWORDS: - “Filling proposal form” = Critical activity - “Acting for insurer” = Agent represents principal - “Schedule 9 Para 12” = Specific provision

📝 EXAM QUESTION 5 (Links to Section 9.5.3 - Agent Fraudulent Statement)
Question: “If agent Jeffery makes fraudulent statement to induce client to buy policy, his statement deemed to be statement made by ___, under Para 12(2) Schedule 9 FSA 2013. A. Agent himself B. Agent’s manager C. Principal-insurer ✅ D. CEO of company”
Answer: C (Principal-insurer)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Agent’s fraudulent statement = INSURER’S statement (insurer bears liability).
LEGAL PRINCIPLE:
Agent's Actions = Principal's Actions
Agent's Knowledge = Principal's Knowledge
Agent's Statements = Principal's Statements
WHY THIS RULE?: 1. Protection for Client: Client relies on agent as insurer’s representative 2. Agency Law: Principal liable for agent’s acts within scope of authority 3. Fair Attribution: Insurer hired agent, insurer bears risk
EXAMPLE:
Agent Jeffery: "This policy covers ALL diseases" (FALSE - fraud)
Client: Buys policy based on this statement
Reality: Policy excludes certain diseases
Claim: Denied for excluded disease

Legal Position:
- Jeffery's fraudulent statement = INSURER'S statement
- Insurer liable for agent's fraud
- Cannot deny claim based on exclusion
- Client protected
FSA 2013 Schedule 9, Paragraph 12(2): Statement by agent = Statement by insurer (for purpose of proposal)
KEYWORDS: - “Fraudulent statement” = False info to induce - “Deemed to be” = Legally treated as - “Principal-insurer” = Liability rests with insurer




CRITICAL REQUIREMENT (HIGH EXAM FREQUENCY):
Agent MUST disclose to clients THREE things:








Disclosure
What to Tell
Purpose




1. Insurer Name
Name of licensed insurer
Know who insurer is


2. Agent Relationship
Agent’s relationship with insurer
Understand connection


3. (NOT premiums)
-
Transparency in agency



⚠️ EXAM TRAP: Agent does NOT disclose “premiums charged” (not one of the three).

📝 EXAM QUESTION 6 (Links to Section 9.5.4 - Disclosure Requirements)
Question: “To increase transparency (Section 186(1)), agent must disclose three things. Choose: i. Name of insurance agency agent works under ii. Name of licensed insurer iii. Agent’s relationship with licensed insurer iv. Premiums charged by insurer
A. I only B. I, II and III C. II, III, & IV ✅ D. All the above”
Answer: C (II, III, & IV) - WAIT! ERROR IN MATERIALS
CORRECTION: Should be B (I, II and III) based on FSA 2013 Section 186(1)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: THREE disclosures for transparency - Agency name, Insurer name, Relationship.
ACTUAL THREE DISCLOSURES: 1. ✅ Name of insurance AGENCY (i) 2. ✅ Name of licensed INSURER (ii) 3. ✅ Agent’s RELATIONSHIP with insurer (iii)
NOT REQUIRED: - ❌ Premiums charged (iv) - NOT part of Section 186(1) requirement
PURPOSE: - Client knows WHO they’re dealing with - Transparency in representation - Understand agent’s connection to insurer - Informed decision-making
EXAM NOTE: If this exact question appears, check answer key carefully. Based on FSA 2013, answer should be B (I, II, III), not C.







TORT = Private wrong/civil wrong (not criminal)
Key Quote (memorize): > “Tortious liability arises from breach of duty primarily fixed by law; duty is towards persons generally; breach is redressible by action for unliquidated damages.”

📝 EXAM QUESTION 1 (Links to Section 9.6.1 - Tort Definition)
Question: “A private wrong is violation of rights of another person, such wrong is , wrongdoer is . A. crime; criminal B. liability; risk taker C. penalty; criminal D. tort; tort feasor ✅”
Answer: D (tort; tort feasor)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Know the correct TERMINOLOGY - Tort & Tort Feasor!
DEFINITIONS: - TORT = Private/civil wrong (violation of another’s rights) - TORT FEASOR = Person who commits tort (wrongdoer)
vs. CRIME:
CRIME (Public Wrong):
- Wrong against STATE/SOCIETY
- Prosecuted by government
- Punishment: Fine, imprisonment
- Person: CRIMINAL

TORT (Private Wrong):
- Wrong against INDIVIDUAL
- Sued by injured party
- Remedy: DAMAGES (money)
- Person: TORT FEASOR
EXAMPLES OF TORTS: - Negligence (car accident) - Trespass (entering property without permission) - Defamation (false statements damaging reputation) - Nuisance (interfering with enjoyment of property)
KEYWORDS: - “Private wrong” = Not crime, civil matter - “Tort” = Civil wrong - “Tort feasor” = Wrongdoer in tort
MEMORY TIP: “TORTfeasor = MADE-a-TORT” (person who made the tort)




TWO Categories:









Type
Description
Intent
Examples




INTENTIONAL Torts
Carried out with malicious intent
DELIBERATE
Assault, battery, slander, fraud


UNINTENTIONAL Torts
Result of negligence/carelessness
ACCIDENTAL
Car accidents, professional errors



⚠️ EXAM ALERT: Most insurance-related torts = UNINTENTIONAL (negligence).

📝 EXAM QUESTION 2 (Links to Section 9.6.2 - Intentional Torts)
Question: “___ are those tortuous behaviours carried out with malicious intent. A. Intentional torts ✅ B. Unintentional torts C. Negligence D. Professional negligence”
Answer: A (Intentional torts)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: “Malicious intent” = Key phrase for INTENTIONAL torts!
INTENTIONAL TORTS: - Malicious = With bad intent - Premeditated = Planned - Deliberate = On purpose
EXAMPLES: - Assault: Threatening harm intentionally - Battery: Intentional harmful touching - Slander: Deliberately false spoken statements - Fraud: Intentional deception for gain
vs. UNINTENTIONAL: - Negligence: Carelessness (no intent to harm) - Professional negligence: Professional error (no malice)
KEYWORDS: - “Malicious intent” = Deliberately harmful - “Intentional” = On purpose




Definition: Breach of legal duty to take care, resulting in undesired damage.
Three Elements Required: 1. Duty of Care existed 2. Breach of that duty 3. Damage/Loss resulted from breach
Examples: - Flower pot on ledge blown by wind, injures pedestrian - Lawyer designs poor contract → client loses money - Surgeon leaves scissors in patient’s abdomen

Financial Planner’s Duty of Care: - Provide prudent and diligent advice - Effect appropriate instruments for client’s intention - Exercise professional competence
Breach Example:
Financial planner drafts will
Error: Didn't get two witnesses to sign
OR: Got beneficiary to sign as witness
Result: Will invalid, beneficiary loses inheritance
Liability: Financial planner breached duty of care
Remedy: Client can sue for damages
📌 EXAM TIP: Duty of care = Professional must act with reasonable care and skill.




Definition: Injured party hurt partly due to OWN negligence.
Principle: Everyone has duty to look after own safety.

📝 EXAM QUESTION 3 (Links to Section 9.6.4 - Contributory Negligence)
Question: “___ means injured party hurt partly due to own negligence. A. Intentional negligence B. Unintentional negligence C. Contributory negligence ✅ D. Professional negligence”
Answer: C (Contributory negligence)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: “OWN negligence” = Contributory negligence (injured party contributed).
CONCEPT:
Total Damage: RM100,000
Defendant's fault: 70%
Plaintiff's fault: 30% (own negligence = CONTRIBUTORY)

Damages Awarded: RM70,000 (reduced by 30%)
EXAMPLE:
Car Accident:
- Driver A: Speeding (negligent)
- Driver B: Not wearing seatbelt (contributory negligence)

Driver B injured:
Medical bills: RM50,000
Court finds:
- Driver A: 80% at fault
- Driver B: 20% contributory negligence (no seatbelt)

Damages awarded: RM40,000 (RM50,000 × 80%)
Reduced by B's contribution
Legal Basis (Malaysia): Civil Law Act 1956, Section 12: - Damages reduced by claimant’s share of responsibility - Court determines “just and equitable” reduction
KEYWORDS: - “Contributory” = Contributing to - “Own negligence” = Plaintiff’s fault too - “Partly due to” = Shared responsibility
MEMORY TIP: “Contributed to OWN harm” = Contributory negligence




Definition: Negligent acts by professionals causing breach of duty and damage.
Professionals Subject to This: - Doctors - Lawyers - Accountants - Architects - Financial Planners
Not ALL professional acts = liability: Only negligent acts that: 1. Breach duty 2. Cause damage/loss/injury
Example - Doctor:
Scenario 1: NOT Negligence
- Surgery performed with due care
- Patient dies (surgery complication)
- Result: NO breach (inherent risk, not negligence)

Scenario 2: NEGLIGENCE
- Surgery performed with due care
- BUT: Left scissors inside patient
- Scissors pierce organs → excessive bleeding → death
- Result: PROFESSIONAL NEGLIGENCE (breach of duty)
Coverage: Professional Indemnity Insurance





Full Name: Anti-Money Laundering, Anti-Terrorism Financing, and Proceeds of Unlawful Activities Act 2001
Background: - Based on FATF (Financial Action Task Force) recommendations - FATF: Inter-governmental organization (Paris, 1989) - 40 + 9 recommendations (money laundering + terrorism financing) - Malaysia enacted: July 5, 2001 - Effective: January 15, 2002 - Latest amendment: November 8, 2014



CRITICAL CONCEPT (HIGH EXAM FREQUENCY):








Stage
Description
Insurance Example




1. PLACEMENT
Introduce illicit funds into financial system
Purchase insurance policies with large cash payments


2. LAYERING
Move funds through transactions to obscure origin
Borrow against policies, make claims on insured valuables, switch policies


3. INTEGRATION
Integrate laundered money into economy as legitimate
Receive claim payouts, use for business investments



📌 EXAM TIP: Memorize the THREE STAGES - Placement, Layering, Integration (order matters!).




Front-End Indicators (at application):







Red Flag
Example

Reluctant to provide details
Avoids personal/corporate information

Buy many, cancel together (>RM50,000 cash)

Meets red flag criteria

Red Flag
Example

Series of policy loans
Multiple loans/repayments short period

Unrelated person, other country


High risk acceptance
Willing to pay for cases likely rejected/claimed







Record-Keeping: - Minimum: 6 years post-transaction - All transactions documented - Customer interactions recorded - Audit trail maintained
Reporting: - Suspicious transactions → Financial Intelligence Unit (Bank Negara Malaysia) - Mandatory reporting - Timely submission
Training: - Initial AML/CFT training - Ongoing training - Risk-based approach - Agent awareness of legal responsibilities
Customer Due Diligence (CDD): - Verify identity - Assess risk profile - Understand nature of business - Source of funds





Age Requirements:








Age
Capacity
Requirement




10-16 years
Can enter life insurance contract
WITH written consent from parent/guardian


16+ years
Can enter contract independently
NO consent needed (full capacity)




📝 EXAM QUESTION 9 (Links to Section 9.8 - Minor’s Capacity)
Question: “Para 4 Schedule 8 FSA 2013, minor may enter life insurance contract on: A. Age 9, no consent B. Age 10, no consent C. Age 9, with consent D. Age 10, with consent ✅”
Answer: D (Age 10, with parental consent)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Age 10 is the threshold, but CONSENT required until age 16.
AGE FRAMEWORK:
Below Age 10: CANNOT enter contract (even with consent)
Age 10-15: CAN enter WITH written parental/guardian consent
Age 16+: CAN enter INDEPENDENTLY (no consent needed)
WHY Age 10?: - Legal capacity starts at 10 (Malaysian law) - Balance between protection and autonomy - Parental oversight until 16
WHAT MINOR CAN DO (ages 10-16 with consent): - Enter life insurance on OWN life - Enter life insurance on ANOTHER life (with insurable interest) - Assign policies - Receive assignments
KEYWORDS: - “Age 10” = Minimum age - “With consent” = Parent/guardian written approval - “Minor” = Under 18 (but 16+ has full capacity for insurance)







1. Three Professional Risks: - Legal Risks - Compliance Risks - Reputation Risks
2. Three Fundamental Principles: - Utmost Good Faith (Uberrimae Fidei) - Insurable Interest - Proximate Cause
3. Four Ways to Breach Utmost Good Faith: - Non-disclosure (unintentional) - Concealment (willful) - Fraud (premeditated) - Innocent Misrepresentation (accidental)
4. Three Types of Agent Authority: - Express Authority (explicitly granted) - Implied Authority (incidental to express) - Apparent Authority (ostensible/perceived)

6. Three Money Laundering Stages: - Placement (introduce to system) - Layering (obscure origin) - Integration (legitimize)
7. Three Agent Disclosures (Section 186): - Name of insurance agency - Name of licensed insurer - Agent’s relationship with insurer

text:

Strategy

Communication trails, advice records







Essential Contract Elements (memorize):
VALID CONTRACT REQUIRES:
1. Offer (proposal)
2. Acceptance
3. Consideration (premium)
4. Legal Capacity (age, sound mind)
5. Legal Purpose (not illegal)
6. Genuine Consent (no fraud/duress)
Insurance Contract = Specialized Contract
Follows general contract law BUT has UNIQUE characteristics (covered next).




THREE Core Principles (HIGH EXAM FREQUENCY):
FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES
├── 1. Utmost Good Faith (Uberrimae Fidei)
├── 2. Insurable Interest
└── 3. Proximate Cause



Definition: Both parties must act with complete honesty and disclose all material facts.
Duty of Disclosure (FSA 2013, Schedule 9, Paragraph 3(4)(1)):
Proposer MUST disclose: - Any matter known to be relevant to insurer’s decision - Any matter a reasonable person would expect to know is relevant

What is a MATERIAL FACT?
Definition: Fact that would influence insurer’s decision to: - Accept the risk - Set premium amount - Determine policy terms
Example Material Facts: - Previous insurance declined/cancelled - Criminal convictions - Pre-existing medical conditions - Previous claims history - Occupation hazards - Dangerous hobbies

FOUR Ways to Breach Utmost Good Faith:









Breach Type
Description
Intent
Example




1. Non-disclosure
Failure to disclose material fact
Unintentional (considers it inconsequential)
Not mentioning previous minor accident


2. Concealment
Willful failure to disclose
INTENTIONAL (to get cheaper cover)
Hiding heart condition for life insurance


3. Fraud
Premeditated false information
DELIBERATE DECEPTION
Forging medical reports


4. Innocent Misrepresentation
Unintentional incorrect information
Accidental/mistake
Genuinely mistaken about past illness dates



⚠️ EXAM ALERT: - Non-disclosure = Didn’t think important (unintentional) - Concealment = Knew important, hid it (willful) - Fraud = Premeditated lies - Innocent Misrep = Honest mistake

Case Law Examples:
1. Abu Bakar v. Oriental Fire (1974) - NON-DISCLOSURE
Facts: - Insured applied for fire insurance - Question: “For what purposes premises occupied?” - Answer: “Sundry shop downstairs, dwelling first floor” - OMITTED: Four grinding mills for curry powder at back - Fire occurred - Insurer denied claim (failed to disclose mills)
Held: - ✅ Insurers NOT misled about nature of insurance - ✅ NO evidence mills increased risk - ✅ Insurers LIABLE - NO breach of utmost good faith
📌 EXAM TIP: Not ALL omissions = breach. Must be MATERIAL (affects risk assessment).

2. Goh Chooi Leng v Public Life (1964) - CONCEALMENT
Facts: - Life assured applied for insurance (May 1960) - Question: “Ever had advice about heart/lung/cough?” - Answer: “No” - TRUTH: Treated for tuberculosis, hospitalized Nov 1958-March 1959 - Life assured died - Assignee claimed
Held: - ❌ NON-DISCLOSURE of material fact - ❌ Contract VOIDABLE - ❌ Insurer NOT LIABLE
📌 EXAM TIP: Medical history is ALWAYS material for life insurance!

3. United Oriental v. Mazzarol (1984) - INNOCENT MISREPRESENTATION
Facts: - Proposal form for boat insurance - Question ONLY asked: Accidents to OTHER boats owned - Did NOT ask: Accidents to THIS boat - Insured boat sank - Insurer avoided liability (previous accident to THIS boat not disclosed)
Held: - ✅ Although NOT asked specifically - ✅ Previous accident to THIS boat = MATERIAL FACT - ✅ MUST be disclosed regardless - ✅ Insurer can avoid contract
📌 EXAM TIP: Material facts must be disclosed EVEN IF NOT SPECIFICALLY ASKED!

What NEED NOT Be Disclosed (FSA 2013, Schedule 9, Paragraph 3(4)(2)):








Exclusion
Description
Example




Diminishes risk
Makes risk LOWER
Installed sprinkler system (fire insurance)


Common knowledge
Public information
General crime statistics in area


Known to insurer
Insurer should know in ordinary course
Standard industry risks


Waived by insurer
Insurer doesn’t require disclosure
Optional questions left blank



Deemed Waiver (FSA 2013, Schedule 9, Paragraph 3(4)(3)): If proposer: - Fails to answer question - Gives incomplete/irrelevant answer AND insurer doesn’t pursue further → Compliance with duty of disclosure DEEMED WAIVED




Definition: Policyholder must have legal or financial stake in subject matter insured.
Purpose: Prevent insurance from becoming GAMBLING/WAGERING.

Insurable Interest in LIFE INSURANCE (FSA 2013, Schedule 8, Paragraph 3):
Requirement: Must exist at TIME OF CONTRACT INCEPTION
Who has insurable interest in your life?








Relationship
Insurable Interest
Example




Yourself
Unlimited
Own life policy


Spouse
YES
Husband insures wife’s life


Child (under 18)
YES
Parent insures child


Ward (under 18)
YES
Guardian insures ward


Employee
YES
Employer insures key employee


Person you depend on
YES (wholly/partly dependent)
Elderly parent depends on adult child



⚠️ EXAM ALERT: Life insurance insurable interest needed at INCEPTION only, NOT at claim time.

Insurable Interest in GENERAL INSURANCE:
Requirement: Must exist at TIME OF LOSS/CLAIM
Who has insurable interest?








Party
Property
Reason




Owner
Own property
Direct financial interest


Mortgagee/Bank
Mortgaged property
Loan security


Business Partner
Partner’s contribution
Business continuity


Creditor
Debtor’s property/life
Debt repayment ability


Trustee/Bailee
Property in care
Responsibility for safeguarding



📌 EXAM TIP: - Life Insurance: Insurable interest at INCEPTION - General Insurance: Insurable interest at LOSS/CLAIM

📝 EXAM QUESTION 10 (Links to Section 9.3.1 - Insurable Interest & Legal Purpose)
Question: “Raymond Mah is hard drug pusher. Asks agent to insure goods including illegal drugs. Agent rejects. Why? A. Illegal purpose – against public policy ✅ B. No insurable interest exist C. Agent wrong, drugs can be insured D. FSA 2013 specifically forbids dealing with drug pusher”
Answer: A (Illegal purpose – against public policy)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Insurance contracts require LEGAL PURPOSE - cannot insure illegal activities!
ANALYSIS:
A ✅ CORRECT - Fundamental contract principle: - Insurance contract requires LEGAL PURPOSE - Cannot promote illegal activities (against public policy) - Insuring illegal drugs = Facilitating crime - Public policy prevents this
WHY PUBLIC POLICY?
If illegal goods could be insured:
→ Criminals protected from loss
→ Insurance encourages illegal trade
→ Society harmed
→ Against public interest
B ❌ WRONG - Technically he HAS insurable interest: - He owns the drugs (property owner) - Financial stake in their safety - BUT: Insurable interest ALONE not enough - Must ALSO have legal purpose!
C ❌ WRONG - Agent is CORRECT to refuse: - Illegal goods cannot be insured - Would violate public policy - Agent could face legal liability
D ❌ WRONG - Too specific: - FSA 2013 doesn’t need SPECIFIC drug provision - General legal purpose requirement covers it - Broader public policy principle applies
LEGAL BASIS:
Valid Contract Requires:
1. Offer ✓
2. Acceptance ✓
3. Consideration ✓
4. Legal Capacity ✓
5. LEGAL PURPOSE ✗ (FAILED - illegal drugs)
6. Genuine Consent ✓

Result: Cannot form valid contract
KEYWORDS: - “Illegal purpose” = Against law - “Public policy” = Society’s interests - “Cannot promote illegal activities”
SIMILAR EXAMPLES: - Cannot insure stolen goods - Cannot insure proceeds of crime - Cannot insure illegal gambling operation
MEMORY TIP: “No Insurance for Illegal Business” (Public policy protects society)




Definition: The actual, real, or dominant cause that sets in motion chain of events leading to loss.
Purpose: Determine if insurer liable under policy (was loss caused by insured peril?).
Key Concept: “PROXIMATE” = DOMINANT/EFFECTIVE cause, not necessarily NEAREST IN TIME.

Example: Smith v. Cornhill Insurance (1938)
Facts: - Motor policy: Death if “result solely of bodily injury by violent accidental means while riding insured car” - Insured: Severe head injuries in car accident (fell down ravine) - After accident: Wandered aimlessly through brushwood - Stepped into stream → Shock of immersion → Heart failure → Death - Insurer: Refused payment (shock of immersion = intervening factor)
Held: - ✅ Accident = PRIMARY CAUSE - ✅ Led to sequence: injury → wandering → immersion → shock → death - ✅ NO intervening causes - ✅ UNBROKEN CHAIN of events - ✅ Insurer LIABLE
Principle: If unbroken chain of events from insured peril to loss, proximate cause = insured peril.
📌 EXAM TIP: Look for UNBROKEN CHAIN - no independent intervening cause that breaks the connection.





FIVE Special Characteristics (memorize):
INSURANCE CONTRACT CHARACTERISTICS
├── 1. Aleatory
├── 2. Unilateral
├── 3. Conditional
├── 4. Personal
└── 5. Adhesion



Definition: Unequal exchange - parties may receive unequal values.
How it works in insurance:
Scenario 1: No Claim
Insured pays: RM2,000 (premium)
Insurer pays: RM0
Insurer "wins"

Scenario 2: Major Claim
Insured pays: RM2,000 (premium)
Insurer pays: RM500,000 (claim)
Insured "wins"
vs. COMMUTATIVE Contract (equal exchange): - Buy car: Pay RM50,000 → Receive car worth RM50,000 - Mutual agreement on value exchanged
📌 EXAM TIP: Insurance = ALEATORY (dependent on uncertain event), not commutative (equal exchange).




Definition: Only ONE party (insurer) makes enforceable promise.
How it works: - Insurer: Legally bound to pay if loss occurs (enforceable promise) - Insured: NO legal obligation to continue paying premiums (can lapse)
Example:
After paying first premium:
Insured: Can stop paying (policy lapses, no lawsuit)
Insurer: MUST pay claim if loss occurs during coverage (enforceable)
vs. BILATERAL Contract (both parties bound): - Employment contract: Employee must work, Employer must pay




Definition: Insurer’s obligation dependent on insured fulfilling conditions.
Common Conditions: - Timely premium payment - Truthful information at application - Notify insurer of changes - Claims notification within specified time - Cooperation in claims investigation
Example:
Condition: Notify claim within 30 days
Insured notifies after 60 days
Result: Insurer may deny claim (condition breached)
📌 EXAM TIP: Contract fulfillment CONDITIONAL on compliance with terms.




Definition: Contract is personal to the insured, not the property.
Key Points: - Protects PERSON/ENTITY, not property itself - Based on insured’s character, morals, credit status - NOT automatically transferable - If property sold, policy DOES NOT follow new owner
Example:
Mr. Tan owns house, has fire insurance
Sells house to Mr. Lee
Insurance: Does NOT transfer to Mr. Lee
Mr. Lee: Must apply for NEW insurance
(Insurer assesses Mr. Lee's character/credit separately)
⚠️ EXAM ALERT: Property insurance is PERSONAL - does NOT automatically transfer with property sale!




Definition: Insured must accept contract “as is” - no negotiation.
Characteristics: - Insurer designs and prints policy - Terms pre-printed - Insured: Take it or leave it (no modification) - No negotiation between parties
Legal Protection for Insured:
DOCTRINE: Contract of Adhesion
↓
Court Interpretation Rule:
"Any AMBIGUITY in contract interpreted IN FAVOR OF INSURED"
↓
Reason: Insurer drafted it, insured had no input
Presumption of Intent Doctrine: - Person who signs contract PRESUMED to have: - Read the contract - Understood terms - Agreed to conditions - Bound by signed terms
📌 EXAM TIP: Adhesion contracts = No negotiation, but ambiguities favor insured (court protection).





Definition: Legal relationship where agent acts on behalf of principal (insurer).



Structure:
PRINCIPAL (Insurer)
    ↓ (appoints)
AGENT (Insurance Agent)
    ↓ (interacts with)
THIRD PARTY (Policyholders/Clients)
Agent’s Role: - Market insurance products - Collect premiums - Provide customer service - Act on behalf of insurer




CRITICAL CONCEPT (HIGH EXAM FREQUENCY):









Authority Type
Source
Description
Example




EXPRESS Authority
Explicitly granted (written/oral)
Direct authorization from insurer
Agency contract states: “Can solicit applications, collect premiums”


IMPLIED Authority
Incidental to express
Actions reasonably necessary to execute express authority
Express: Sell policies → Implied: Answer client questions, arrange meetings


APPARENT Authority
Insurer’s representations
Public believes agent has authority based on insurer’s conduct
Insurer gives agent business cards, office = Public assumes agent authorized



⚠️ EXAM ALERT: - Express = Directly stated - Implied = Necessary to carry out express - Apparent = Looks authorized to public

📝 EXAM QUESTION 7 (Links to Section 9.5.2 - Types of Authority)
Question: “Agent’s authority to act can be in following ways: i. Express authority ii. Implied authority iii. Apparent authority iv. Secret authority
A. I only B. I, II and III ✅ C. I and II only D. All the above”
Answer: B (I, II and III)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: THREE recognized types of authority - Express, Implied, Apparent.
ANALYSIS:
i. Express Authority ✅ VALID: - Explicitly stated in agency contract - Written or oral authorization - Clear, direct appointment
ii. Implied Authority ✅ VALID: - Incidental to express authority - Reasonably necessary powers - Not stated but understood
iii. Apparent Authority ✅ VALID: - Ostensible authority - Based on insurer’s representations - Public perception of authority
iv. Secret Authority ❌ NOT VALID: - NO such concept in agency law! - Authority cannot be “secret” - Either authorized or not - Made-up option (exam trap!)
KEYWORDS: - “Express” = Explicitly stated - “Implied” = Incidental/necessary - “Apparent” = Ostensible/perceived

📝 EXAM QUESTION 8 (Links to Section 9.5.2 - Express vs Implied)
Question: “In agency law, ___ is incidental authority required to execute ___ of principal. A. Express authority; implied authority B. Implied authority; express authority ✅ C. Apparent authority; implied authority D. Implied authority; Apparent authority”
Answer: B (Implied authority; express authority)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: IMPLIED authority is what’s needed to EXECUTE EXPRESS authority!
RELATIONSHIP:
EXPRESS Authority (Stated)
    ↓ (requires for execution)
IMPLIED Authority (Incidental)
EXPLANATION: - EXPRESS = What you’re told to do (sell insurance) - IMPLIED = What you need to do it (answer questions, meet clients)
EXAMPLE:
EXPRESS: "You are authorized to sell life insurance policies"
    ↓ (To accomplish this, you IMPLIED authority to:)
IMPLIED: 
- Answer client questions about products
- Arrange meetings with prospects
- Explain policy features
- Collect proposal forms
- Provide premium quotes
WHY OTHER OPTIONS WRONG:
❌ A: Backwards - Express is not incidental to implied ❌ C: Apparent is not incidental to implied (different concept) ❌ D: Implied is not incidental to apparent (wrong relationship)
MEMORY TIP: “IMPLIED helps you EXECUTE EXPRESS”




CRITICAL PROVISION (HIGH EXAM FREQUENCY):
When agent fills proposal form: - Agent acts for INSURER (principal), NOT client - Agent’s knowledge = Insurer’s knowledge - Agent’s statements = Insurer’s statements

📝 EXAM QUESTION 4 (Links to Section 9.5.3 - Agent Filling Forms)
Question: “When agent fills proposal form from client, who is he acting for under FSA 2013 Schedule 9 Para 12? A. For the Insurer - principal ✅ B. For the client C. For himself D. For the beneficiary”
Answer: A (For the Insurer - principal)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Agent filling form = Acts for INSURER, NOT client (protects client).
WHY THIS MATTERS:
If agent acts for CLIENT:
Client: Tells agent wrong information
Agent: Writes it on form
Problem: Who's responsible? Client!
Issue: Client may not understand technical terms
Result: UNFAIR to client
If agent acts for INSURER (FSA 2013 rule):
Client: Tells agent information
Agent: Writes it on form (acts for INSURER)
Problem: Agent writes incorrectly
Result: INSURER responsible (agent is their representative)
Protection: CLIENT protected from agent errors
FSA 2013 Schedule 9, Paragraph 12: - Agent completing proposal = Agent of INSURER - Protects proposer from agent mistakes - Insurer cannot deny claim based on agent’s filling errors
KEYWORDS: - “Filling proposal form” = Critical activity - “Acting for insurer” = Agent represents principal - “Schedule 9 Para 12” = Specific provision

📝 EXAM QUESTION 5 (Links to Section 9.5.3 - Agent Fraudulent Statement)
Question: “If agent Jeffery makes fraudulent statement to induce client to buy policy, his statement deemed to be statement made by ___, under Para 12(2) Schedule 9 FSA 2013. A. Agent himself B. Agent’s manager C. Principal-insurer ✅ D. CEO of company”
Answer: C (Principal-insurer)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Agent’s fraudulent statement = INSURER’S statement (insurer bears liability).
LEGAL PRINCIPLE:
Agent's Actions = Principal's Actions
Agent's Knowledge = Principal's Knowledge
Agent's Statements = Principal's Statements
WHY THIS RULE?: 1. Protection for Client: Client relies on agent as insurer’s representative 2. Agency Law: Principal liable for agent’s acts within scope of authority 3. Fair Attribution: Insurer hired agent, insurer bears risk
EXAMPLE:
Agent Jeffery: "This policy covers ALL diseases" (FALSE - fraud)
Client: Buys policy based on this statement
Reality: Policy excludes certain diseases
Claim: Denied for excluded disease

Legal Position:
- Jeffery's fraudulent statement = INSURER'S statement
- Insurer liable for agent's fraud
- Cannot deny claim based on exclusion
- Client protected
FSA 2013 Schedule 9, Paragraph 12(2): Statement by agent = Statement by insurer (for purpose of proposal)
KEYWORDS: - “Fraudulent statement” = False info to induce - “Deemed to be” = Legally treated as - “Principal-insurer” = Liability rests with insurer




CRITICAL REQUIREMENT (HIGH EXAM FREQUENCY):
Agent MUST disclose to clients THREE things:








Disclosure
What to Tell
Purpose




1. Insurer Name
Name of licensed insurer
Know who insurer is


2. Agent Relationship
Agent’s relationship with insurer
Understand connection


3. (NOT premiums)
-
Transparency in agency



⚠️ EXAM TRAP: Agent does NOT disclose “premiums charged” (not one of the three).

📝 EXAM QUESTION 6 (Links to Section 9.5.4 - Disclosure Requirements)
Question: “To increase transparency (Section 186(1)), agent must disclose three things. Choose: i. Name of insurance agency agent works under ii. Name of licensed insurer iii. Agent’s relationship with licensed insurer iv. Premiums charged by insurer
A. I only B. I, II and III C. II, III, & IV ✅ D. All the above”
Answer: C (II, III, & IV) - WAIT! ERROR IN MATERIALS
CORRECTION: Should be B (I, II and III) based on FSA 2013 Section 186(1)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: THREE disclosures for transparency - Agency name, Insurer name, Relationship.
ACTUAL THREE DISCLOSURES: 1. ✅ Name of insurance AGENCY (i) 2. ✅ Name of licensed INSURER (ii) 3. ✅ Agent’s RELATIONSHIP with insurer (iii)
NOT REQUIRED: - ❌ Premiums charged (iv) - NOT part of Section 186(1) requirement
PURPOSE: - Client knows WHO they’re dealing with - Transparency in representation - Understand agent’s connection to insurer - Informed decision-making
EXAM NOTE: If this exact question appears, check answer key carefully. Based on FSA 2013, answer should be B (I, II, III), not C.







TORT = Private wrong/civil wrong (not criminal)
Key Quote (memorize): > “Tortious liability arises from breach of duty primarily fixed by law; duty is towards persons generally; breach is redressible by action for unliquidated damages.”

📝 EXAM QUESTION 1 (Links to Section 9.6.1 - Tort Definition)
Question: “A private wrong is violation of rights of another person, such wrong is , wrongdoer is . A. crime; criminal B. liability; risk taker C. penalty; criminal D. tort; tort feasor ✅”
Answer: D (tort; tort feasor)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Know the correct TERMINOLOGY - Tort & Tort Feasor!
DEFINITIONS: - TORT = Private/civil wrong (violation of another’s rights) - TORT FEASOR = Person who commits tort (wrongdoer)
vs. CRIME:
CRIME (Public Wrong):
- Wrong against STATE/SOCIETY
- Prosecuted by government
- Punishment: Fine, imprisonment
- Person: CRIMINAL

TORT (Private Wrong):
- Wrong against INDIVIDUAL
- Sued by injured party
- Remedy: DAMAGES (money)
- Person: TORT FEASOR
EXAMPLES OF TORTS: - Negligence (car accident) - Trespass (entering property without permission) - Defamation (false statements damaging reputation) - Nuisance (interfering with enjoyment of property)
KEYWORDS: - “Private wrong” = Not crime, civil matter - “Tort” = Civil wrong - “Tort feasor” = Wrongdoer in tort
MEMORY TIP: “TORTfeasor = MADE-a-TORT” (person who made the tort)




TWO Categories:









Type
Description
Intent
Examples




INTENTIONAL Torts
Carried out with malicious intent
DELIBERATE
Assault, battery, slander, fraud


UNINTENTIONAL Torts
Result of negligence/carelessness
ACCIDENTAL
Car accidents, professional errors



⚠️ EXAM ALERT: Most insurance-related torts = UNINTENTIONAL (negligence).

📝 EXAM QUESTION 2 (Links to Section 9.6.2 - Intentional Torts)
Question: “___ are those tortuous behaviours carried out with malicious intent. A. Intentional torts ✅ B. Unintentional torts C. Negligence D. Professional negligence”
Answer: A (Intentional torts)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: “Malicious intent” = Key phrase for INTENTIONAL torts!
INTENTIONAL TORTS: - Malicious = With bad intent - Premeditated = Planned - Deliberate = On purpose
EXAMPLES: - Assault: Threatening harm intentionally - Battery: Intentional harmful touching - Slander: Deliberately false spoken statements - Fraud: Intentional deception for gain
vs. UNINTENTIONAL: - Negligence: Carelessness (no intent to harm) - Professional negligence: Professional error (no malice)
KEYWORDS: - “Malicious intent” = Deliberately harmful - “Intentional” = On purpose




Definition: Breach of legal duty to take care, resulting in undesired damage.
Three Elements Required: 1. Duty of Care existed 2. Breach of that duty 3. Damage/Loss resulted from breach
Examples: - Flower pot on ledge blown by wind, injures pedestrian - Lawyer designs poor contract → client loses money - Surgeon leaves scissors in patient’s abdomen

Financial Planner’s Duty of Care: - Provide prudent and diligent advice - Effect appropriate instruments for client’s intention - Exercise professional competence
Breach Example:
Financial planner drafts will
Error: Didn't get two witnesses to sign
OR: Got beneficiary to sign as witness
Result: Will invalid, beneficiary loses inheritance
Liability: Financial planner breached duty of care
Remedy: Client can sue for damages
📌 EXAM TIP: Duty of care = Professional must act with reasonable care and skill.




Definition: Injured party hurt partly due to OWN negligence.
Principle: Everyone has duty to look after own safety.

📝 EXAM QUESTION 3 (Links to Section 9.6.4 - Contributory Negligence)
Question: “___ means injured party hurt partly due to own negligence. A. Intentional negligence B. Unintentional negligence C. Contributory negligence ✅ D. Professional negligence”
Answer: C (Contributory negligence)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: “OWN negligence” = Contributory negligence (injured party contributed).
CONCEPT:
Total Damage: RM100,000
Defendant's fault: 70%
Plaintiff's fault: 30% (own negligence = CONTRIBUTORY)

Damages Awarded: RM70,000 (reduced by 30%)
EXAMPLE:
Car Accident:
- Driver A: Speeding (negligent)
- Driver B: Not wearing seatbelt (contributory negligence)

Driver B injured:
Medical bills: RM50,000
Court finds:
- Driver A: 80% at fault
- Driver B: 20% contributory negligence (no seatbelt)

Damages awarded: RM40,000 (RM50,000 × 80%)
Reduced by B's contribution
Legal Basis (Malaysia): Civil Law Act 1956, Section 12: - Damages reduced by claimant’s share of responsibility - Court determines “just and equitable” reduction
KEYWORDS: - “Contributory” = Contributing to - “Own negligence” = Plaintiff’s fault too - “Partly due to” = Shared responsibility
MEMORY TIP: “Contributed to OWN harm” = Contributory negligence




Definition: Negligent acts by professionals causing breach of duty and damage.
Professionals Subject to This: - Doctors - Lawyers - Accountants - Architects - Financial Planners
Not ALL professional acts = liability: Only negligent acts that: 1. Breach duty 2. Cause damage/loss/injury
Example - Doctor:
Scenario 1: NOT Negligence
- Surgery performed with due care
- Patient dies (surgery complication)
- Result: NO breach (inherent risk, not negligence)

Scenario 2: NEGLIGENCE
- Surgery performed with due care
- BUT: Left scissors inside patient
- Scissors pierce organs → excessive bleeding → death
- Result: PROFESSIONAL NEGLIGENCE (breach of duty)
Coverage: Professional Indemnity Insurance





Full Name: Anti-Money Laundering, Anti-Terrorism Financing, and Proceeds of Unlawful Activities Act 2001
Background: - Based on FATF (Financial Action Task Force) recommendations - FATF: Inter-governmental organization (Paris, 1989) - 40 + 9 recommendations (money laundering + terrorism financing) - Malaysia enacted: July 5, 2001 - Effective: January 15, 2002 - Latest amendment: November 8, 2014



CRITICAL CONCEPT (HIGH EXAM FREQUENCY):








Stage
Description
Insurance Example




1. PLACEMENT
Introduce illicit funds into financial system
Purchase insurance policies with large cash payments


2. LAYERING
Move funds through transactions to obscure origin
Borrow against policies, make claims on insured valuables, switch policies


3. INTEGRATION
Integrate laundered money into economy as legitimate
Receive claim payouts, use for business investments



📌 EXAM TIP: Memorize the THREE STAGES - Placement, Layering, Integration (order matters!).




Front-End Indicators (at application):







Red Flag
Example




Not proportionate to financial standing
Low-income person buying RM1 million policy


Reluctant to provide details
Avoids personal/corporate information


Multiple small policies cancelled
Buy many, cancel together (>RM50,000 cash)


Exceeds threshold
Meets red flag criteria


Frequently changing insurer
Pattern of switching


Different addresses
Home ≠ mailing address


Foreign client seeking lump sum
Offers foreign currency payment


Premiums exceed apparent means
Cannot afford based on stated income


Not interested in performance
Only asks about early cancellation/surrender


Change beneficiaries
To non-family, unusual parties


Anonymous payment instruments
Bearer instruments, cash equivalents


Unclear fund sources
Cannot explain where money from



Back-End Indicators (during policy):







Red Flag
Example




Claims to unusual beneficiaries
Not next of kin, no insurable interest


Series of policy loans
Multiple loans/repayments short period


Large payments to 3rd parties
Unrelated person, other country


High risk acceptance
Willing to pay for cases likely rejected/claimed







Record-Keeping: - Minimum: 6 years post-transaction - All transactions documented - Customer interactions recorded - Audit trail maintained
Reporting: - Suspicious transactions → Financial Intelligence Unit (Bank Negara Malaysia) - Mandatory reporting - Timely submission
Training: - Initial AML/CFT training - Ongoing training - Risk-based approach - Agent awareness of legal responsibilities
Customer Due Diligence (CDD): - Verify identity - Assess risk profile - Understand nature of business - Source of funds





Age Requirements:








Age
Capacity
Requirement




10-16 years
Can enter life insurance contract
WITH written consent from parent/guardian


16+ years
Can enter contract independently
NO consent needed (full capacity)




📝 EXAM QUESTION 9 (Links to Section 9.8 - Minor’s Capacity)
Question: “Para 4 Schedule 8 FSA 2013, minor may enter life insurance contract on: A. Age 9, no consent B. Age 10, no consent C. Age 9, with consent D. Age 10, with consent ✅”
Answer: D (Age 10, with parental consent)
🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Age 10 is the threshold, but CONSENT required until age 16.
AGE FRAMEWORK:
Below Age 10: CANNOT enter contract (even with consent)
Age 10-15: CAN enter WITH written parental/guardian consent
Age 16+: CAN enter INDEPENDENTLY (no consent needed)
WHY Age 10?: - Legal capacity starts at 10 (Malaysian law) - Balance between protection and autonomy - Parental oversight until 16
WHAT MINOR CAN DO (ages 10-16 with consent): - Enter life insurance on OWN life - Enter life insurance on ANOTHER life (with insurable interest) - Assign policies - Receive assignments
KEYWORDS: - “Age 10” = Minimum age - “With consent” = Parent/guardian written approval - “Minor” = Under 18 (but 16+ has full capacity for insurance)

title: Chapter 7: General Insurance Products in Insurance Planning
text:
General insurance protects against financial losses from specific risks. Unlike life insurance (person), general insurance covers PROPERTY, LIABILITY, and specific PERILS. This chapter covers motor, property, marine, liability, engineering insurance and more.
Exam Weight: 12-15% of total exam
Study Time Recommendation: 7-9 hours




By the end of this chapter, you must be able to:

Explain three core general insurance principles (Indemnity, Contribution, Subrogation)
Distinguish motor insurance types (Act, Third Party, Comprehensive)
Identify property insurance types (Fire, All Risk, Business Interruption)
Understand liability insurance categories
Explain engineering insurance (CAR, EAR, Machinery Breakdown)
Know bonds types (Tender, Performance, Advance Payment)
Apply general insurance in financial planning







CRITICAL FRAMEWORK (HIGH EXAM FREQUENCY):
THREE FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES
├── 1. INDEMNITY (Restore to original position)
├── 2. CONTRIBUTION (Share among insurers)
└── 3. SUBROGATION (Recover from third party)



Definition: Restore insured to financial position BEFORE loss - no profit, no loss.
Key Points: - Compensation = ACTUAL LOSS only - Cannot profit from insurance - Prevents unjust enrichment - Based on replacement/repair cost
Example:
House damaged by fire:
Original value: RM200,000
Damage: RM50,000 repairs needed

Insurance pays: RM50,000 (actual loss)
NOT: RM200,000 (full value)
NOT: RM60,000 (more than loss)

Result: House restored to pre-loss condition
What Indemnity Means: - Cannot claim more than loss - Cannot rebuild better than before - Cannot upgrade using insurance money - Return to SAME condition, not improved
📌 EXAM TIP: Indemnity = Compensate ACTUAL loss, no profit for insured.




Definition: When multiple policies cover same risk, insurers share claim proportionally.
Key Points: - Can have multiple policies on same asset - Cannot claim MORE than loss from all policies combined - Each insurer pays proportionate share - Prevents over-compensation
Formula:
Contribution = (Policy A Sum / Total Sum Insured) × Loss

Example:
Fire destroys warehouse worth RM500,000
Policy A: RM300,000
Policy B: RM200,000
Total: RM500,000

Loss: RM100,000

Policy A pays: (RM300,000 / RM500,000) × RM100,000 = RM60,000
Policy B pays: (RM200,000 / RM500,000) × RM100,000 = RM40,000
Total: RM100,000
Example Scenario:
Car insured with:
Insurer A: RM80,000
Insurer B: RM60,000
Total: RM140,000

Accident damage: RM28,000

Insurer A pays: (80/140) × 28,000 = RM16,000
Insurer B pays: (60/140) × 28,000 = RM12,000
Total: RM28,000 (actual loss)
📌 EXAM TIP: Contribution ensures fair sharing among multiple insurers - no double compensation.




Definition: After paying claim, insurer can recover from responsible third party.
Key Points: - Insurer “steps into shoes” of insured - Can sue third party for recovery - Only after insured fully compensated - Prevents insured from double recovery
When Applies: - Third party caused the loss - Third party legally liable - After insurer pays claim - Insured must cooperate
Example:
Your car hit by negligent driver:
Damage: RM20,000

STEP 1: Your insurer pays you RM20,000 (you're made whole)
STEP 2: Your insurer sues negligent driver (subrogation)
STEP 3: Insurer recovers RM20,000 from driver
STEP 4: Insurer keeps recovery (recoups claim payment)

You benefit: Immediate payment without lawsuit
Insurer benefit: Recovers claim cost
Negligent party: Pays for damage caused
Important: - Does NOT apply to life insurance (non-indemnity) - Insured cannot compromise third party’s liability - Insured must assist insurer in recovery
📌 EXAM TIP: Subrogation = Insurer’s right to recover from liable third party AFTER paying claim.





General Insurance Classification:
GENERAL INSURANCE
├── 1. MOTOR INSURANCE
│   └── Vehicles, accidents, liability
└── 2. NON-MOTOR INSURANCE
    ├── Property (Fire, Burglary, All Risk)
    ├── Marine (Hull, Cargo)
    ├── Liability (Public, Professional)
    ├── Engineering (CAR, EAR, Machinery)
    └── Others (Travel, PA, Bonds)






Mandatory: ALL vehicles on public roads MUST have motor insurance.
Minimum: Third-party coverage (Act Cover)
Penalties for Non-Compliance: - Fine: Up to RM1,000 - Imprisonment: Up to 3 months - Both fine AND imprisonment - License disqualification: 12 months
⚠️ EXAM ALERT: Motor insurance is COMPULSORY under RTA 1987.




FOUR Coverage Levels (MEMORIZE):

2. Third Party

4. Comprehensive

Most complete




Detailed Comparison:
COVERAGE LEVELS (Lowest → Highest)

ACT COVER (Minimum Legal):
✅ Third-party death/bodily injury
❌ Third-party property damage
❌ Own vehicle damage
❌ Fire/theft

THIRD PARTY:
✅ Third-party death/injury
✅ Third-party property damage
❌ Own vehicle damage
❌ Fire/theft

THIRD PARTY FIRE & THEFT:
✅ All Third Party coverage
✅ Own vehicle fire damage
✅ Own vehicle theft
❌ Own vehicle accident damage

COMPREHENSIVE:
✅ All TPFT coverage
✅ Own vehicle accident damage
✅ Most complete protection
Example Scenarios:
Scenario 1: You hit another car
Third Party: Covers other car damage ✅
Comprehensive: Covers other car + YOUR car ✅

Scenario 2: Your car stolen
Third Party: NO coverage ❌
TPFT: Covers theft ✅
Comprehensive: Covers theft ✅

Scenario 3: You hit tree (own fault)
Third Party: NO coverage ❌
TPFT: NO coverage ❌
Comprehensive: Covers your car ✅
📌 EXAM TIP: Comprehensive = Everything covered; Third Party = Only others’ loss; TPFT = TP + Fire + Theft.
